default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t10-p1.vietnamese:
Modern people who cannot eat properly at home often suffer from deficiencies in the nutrients necessary to sustain life.

Dietary supplements are products created to make up for those nutritional deficiencies. Although supplements are quick and convenient, many people mistakenly believe that simply taking them is enough.

Taking too many supplements can destroy other nutrients, and even taking large amounts may have little effect if they are not consumed together with certain foods.

Nevertheless, many people are currently taking supplements uselessly and wastefully because they are taking them incorrectly.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-p1.outline.0.note: Opens by posing the question of whether fever can be reduced through meals instead of relying on medicine.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-p1.outline.1.label: Rice porridge and green-onion miso soup to reduce fever
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-p1.outline.1.note: The passage analyzes the benefits of rice porridge, which is easy to digest and provides nutrients, and green-onion miso soup, in which green onion promotes sweating to reduce fever and miso replenishes minerals. default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-p1.outline.3.label: Summary and advice
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-p1.outline.3.note: A summary of the wide range of foods that help reduce fever, recommending that readers try these foods before relying only on medicine.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-p1.vietnamese:
When we have a fever, we usually take medicine. But what if we could reduce a fever through our diet without taking medicine?

The first representative food said to be effective for reducing a fever is rice porridge. It is easy to digest, and ingredients such as vegetables and eggs can be added, making it suitable for replenishing missing nutrients. Next, miso soup with green onions is also said to be effective against fever. Onions make us sweat, which helps reduce a fever, while the miso replenishes the minerals lost through sweating. In addition, people say that dried dandelion roots can help reduce a fever. Finally, there is matcha ice cream. Since ice cream melts in the mouth and is easy to eat, it may be best to start with it when you have no appetite.

As mentioned above, there are actually many different foods that may help reduce a fever. When you have a fever, why not try starting with foods like these instead of relying only on medicine?

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t14-p1.outline.1.note: Although many people prefer large supermarkets, the face-to-face relationships at local shops help ensure that food is safe and of good quality.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t14-p1.outline.2.label: Rethinking the value of shopping districts
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t14-p1.outline.2.note: The shopping district is ideal for food safety; consumers need to reconsider its distinctive advantages.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t14-p1.vietnamese:
Recently, more and more people are shopping at large supermarkets instead of shopping streets.

Large supermarkets are inexpensive above all. In addition, it is very convenient that many kinds of items, such as food and household goods, can be paid for at a single checkout counter. Shopping streets are inconvenient because you have to pay at each separate store, but when you visit a shop, a familiar clerk will kindly recommend inexpensive or delicious products.

Both options have advantages and disadvantages, but many people choose large supermarkets because they are "cheap and convenient." However, it is said that, to prevent food-safety problems, it is important for stores and shoppers to have a "face-to-face relationship." When a store knows its customers well, it naturally tends to sell only safe, high-quality products.

Does this not mean that the shopping streets that have recently been disappearing are actually ideal for food safety? Perhaps we should not seek only low prices and convenience, but reconsider the valuable qualities of shopping streets for the sake of food safety.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t16-p1.vietnamese:
Since the first convenience store in Japan opened in 1974, 24-hour convenience stores have steadily gained more customers. Their popularity is due not only to the constant introduction of new products but also to their wide range of services. At convenience stores, people can do many different things, such as reserve concert tickets, send packages by express delivery, and pay their gas, electricity, and water bills. ① Convenience stores are now no longer simply places that sell products.

However, recently, more supermarkets and other stores have begun staying open until late at night, and competition between convenience stores and these businesses has become fierce. Therefore, to prevent other stores from taking their customers, some convenience stores have begun offering ② a new service called 「goyoukiki」.

Goyoukiki means that store employees visit households to ask for orders and deliver products, something that old-fashioned neighborhood shops used to do. At convenience stores, employees do not visit each home; instead, they take orders by telephone or over the internet and deliver the products to customers’ homes. The service is used not only by elderly people who cannot shop regularly but has also become popular with busy homemakers. It will be interesting to see what additional services convenience stores introduce in the future.

(Note 1) Abundant (豊富な): Large in quantity or variety.

(Note 2) Public utility charges (公共料金): Household gas, electricity, and water bills.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t17-p1.vietnamese:
For people who feel, "Every day is boringly the same. I wonder if there is anything new," one suggestion is to choose a topic you like and make a map of your town. There are many possible topics, such as "good food," "cafés," and "walking routes for pets."

Once you have chosen a topic, go out into the streets, walk around on your own, and record what you discover.

① This activity is like taking photographs of the town's scenery to preserve it. For example, even if two people photograph the same street, the picture taken by someone interested in beautiful flowers will differ from the one taken by someone interested in the buildings there. Making a map is similar.

To make a good map, go out for walks many times and try observing the town with your own eyes. When you do so, you will realize that even in the town you thought was the same every day and never changed, there are countless things you had never noticed before and countless interesting things. By the time your own map of the town is complete, ② you will certainly see a completely new town.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t18-p1.outline.1.note: Unable to tolerate having Thursday left empty, the woman called a hair salon and asked to have her hair permed again the following Thursday to fill the blank in her planner, then smiled with satisfaction.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t18-p1.outline.3.label: Source of the work quotation
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t18-p1.outline.3.note: A citation note from the work “The Empty Thursday” by author Hoshino Hiromi.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t18-p1.vietnamese:
Some people feel anxious whenever they have no plans. The woman I happened to see at a café the other day was just like that. She took a red planner from her handbag and looked at it for a while. Then she suddenly began making phone calls, repeatedly arranging drinks, meals, and other outings, and filling the planner with one appointment after another. However, there seemed to be one day that she simply could not fill, no matter what she did.

It was the blank Thursday. This seemed unbearable to her. Finally, she called her usual hair salon and insisted that she had not liked the perm she had gotten the other time and wanted to have it redone. Since Thursday of the following week was the only day she was free, she asked for an appointment then. In the end, she managed to make a plan for Thursday. She stared at the page, now completely filled in, and smiled with satisfaction.

By contrast, my planner was completely blank. To be precise, the period up to yesterday contained many entries, but from today onward it looked like a blank sheet of paper. Nothing was written about the future. Like her, I opened my planner. However, no matter how long I stared at it, not a single plan came to mind.

※ Hiromi Hoshino, “The Empty Thursday,” from The Disaster Called Beauty (Bunshun Bunko)

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t25-p1.vietnamese:
Recruiting people to help with the Minamicho International Exchange Party

The Minamicho International Exchange Club will hold an “International Exchange Party” according to the schedule below.

We are currently recruiting people to help with the party.

The party schedule, location, and available volunteer positions are listed below. This is a great opportunity to make friends.

Would you like to help prepare for the party?

@ About the party

・Date: December 12 (Sunday)

・Location: 2nd-floor hall, Minamicho Community Center

・Event time: 13:00〜16:00 (Volunteers should gather at 12:00)

Volunteers are asked to clean the hall after the party ends.

The cleanup will take about 30 minutes.

@ Volunteer positions

Cooking Korean, Chinese, Vietnamese, and Thai dishes

| Games team | Preparing games and serving as MC during the games | 5 people |

Costume team | 1~2 people from each country (women only)

★ The games team will prepare before the party.

・1st session: November 27 (Saturday), 10:00 ~ 12:00

・2nd session: December 4 (Saturday), 10:00 ~ 12:00

・Location: 2nd-floor seminar room, Minamicho Community Center

★ The cooking team will hold a meeting to decide on the menu.

・December 5 (Sunday), 10:00 ~ 12:00

・Location: 2nd-floor seminar room, Minamicho Community Center

★ If you would like to help, please call.

Representative of the Minamicho International Exchange Club: Sato - Phone: 060-28XXX-33XX

(Note) Kitsuke: dressing someone else in clothing

Nguyen (male, 24), a Vietnamese man, wants to help with the party and make friends.

Nguyen has a job. On weekdays, he works from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and on Saturdays from 9 a.m. to noon. His day off is Sunday.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t29-p1.outline.0.note: States that the room must be completely dark for deep sleep, explaining that turning on a light prevents the brain from resting. This is the main basis for Question 1.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t29-p1.outline.1.note: Extends the principle to young children: their sleeping environment must allow both the brain and body to rest so they can develop.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t29-p1.vietnamese:
If you want to sleep soundly at night, making the room completely dark is the most effective method. Some people leave a little light on when they go to bed, but if you sleep in a bright room, your brain continues to function even while you are asleep, making it impossible to sleep deeply.

Therefore, when going to bed, it is very important to make the room as dark as possible before sleeping. The same is entirely true for young children.

Providing children with an environment in which both their minds and bodies can rest is very important for their development. For the same reason, it seems that we should also give up the habit of sleeping while listening to music.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t31-p1.vietnamese:
Nowadays, many junior high and high school students own mobile phones. They seem to have become indispensable in daily life. Why do so many junior high and high school students own mobile phones?

Having a mobile phone makes it easier to communicate with family and friends, and it is very convenient because people can contact one another immediately. In addition, students can use social networking services (SNS) to interact with many different people, and they can immediately look things up on the internet whenever there is something they do not understand.

However, mobile phones, which are convenient and enjoyable, can also lead to arguments with friends, playing games all night until one becomes ill, or having one's information stolen by strangers. They are becoming a social problem.

Adults around children, such as parents and teachers, need to protect them from problems like these. When students encounter difficulties, they too must immediately discuss them with the adults around them. For this reason, families and schools should carefully discuss how mobile phones should be used and establish rules for their use...

At the Sakura City Riding Center, we are recruiting participants for the 「Beginner Horseback Riding Class」 so that everyone can experience the joy of horseback riding firsthand.

We look forward to receiving applications from everyone.

・Address ・Name (with furigana) ・Age ・Gender ・Occupation ・Phone number ・Preferred session

Mail applications to: 〒111-0022

2-3-5 Sakura-machi, Sakura City

Beginner Horseback Riding Class, Sakura City Riding Center

＜To all residents of Hana Apartments＞

The garbage disposal rules will be partially changed as follows starting April 1. We ask for your cooperation.

1. Please put out garbage between 6:00 p.m. on the day before collection and 9:00 a.m. on the collection day.

Having a mobile phone makes it easier to communicate with family members and friends, and being able to contact them immediately is very convenient.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t40-p1.vietnamese:
As people age, their hair gradually turns gray. This is because the hair's pigment-producing function gradually weakens.

This pigment, melanin, is produced in cells called melanocytes located at the roots of the hair.

As people grow older, their ability to produce melanin gradually disappears.

Regardless of one's natural hair color, as people age, their hair eventually becomes unable to produce color and turns gray.

Because melanocytes are located at the roots of the hair, they cannot affect hair that has not yet grown gray.

An old story says that someone's hair turned completely white overnight because of a great shock, but (that is impossible).

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.outline.1.note: Advises checking one's bicycle and wearing a helmet, and explains that accidents causing harm led to the creation of bicycle insurance.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.outline.2.label: Safety precautions when carrying a small child
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.outline.2.note: Reminds people cycling with small children to pay attention to the child seat.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.outline.3.label: The author's conclusion and message
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.outline.3.note: Bicycles are convenient, but they must be used properly to prevent them from becoming dangerous vehicles.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.vietnamese:
Bicycles are used not only as a means of transportation but also for various purposes such as losing weight and exercising, yet apparently few people pay attention to safety when cycling.

Before riding a bicycle, you should check the brakes and tires and, just as when riding a motorcycle, wear a helmet.

Recently, accidents in which cyclists are the at-fault party have also been increasing, so bicycle insurance has been introduced.

In addition, I hope those who carry children on bicycles will also pay attention to the children's seats.

Bicycles are convenient means of transportation, but if they are not used properly, they can become dangerous.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t43-p1.outline.1.note: Whenever he goes out, the boy prefers taking the train to the car and excitedly photographs trains at the station.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t43-p1.outline.2.note: By researching trains, the boy learned to read even difficult kanji and was praised by everyone. Question 1 is based on this point.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t43-p1.vietnamese:
My son, who is in the second grade of elementary school, loves trains. He also has a video game console, but he hardly ever plays with it.

Whenever we go out, he prefers taking the train to going by car, and as soon as we arrive at a station, he takes out his camera and starts photographing things such as trains. At times like that, he looks genuinely happy. He also frequently looks things up and knows the names and locations of the stations well. As a result, he can read quite a lot of difficult kanji.

Everyone around us praises him, saying that he is remarkably capable for such a young child, and as his parent, I feel very happy too.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t46-p1.outline.1.note: Explains the appeal of handwritten letters: the writer thinks about the recipient while carefully choosing the wording, while also enjoying the time spent waiting for a reply. This provides the basis for Question 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t46-p1.outline.2.label: The significance of handwritten letters for young people today
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t46-p1.outline.2.note: Concludes that for young people accustomed to the high speed of email, handwritten letters may become an entirely new form of communication.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t46-p1.vietnamese:
Recently, it seems that more and more young people are becoming interested in “making friends by letter”—exchanging letters with strangers. Although email is convenient, why has exchanging letters become so popular?

It is said that with email, people sometimes feel tired because they think they have to reply immediately. With handwritten letters, however, they can think about what kind of person the other person is while carefully choosing each word to write, which gives them a refreshing feeling.

Moreover, the time spent waiting for a reply is said to be an exciting period of anticipation that email cannot provide. For young people who are too accustomed to email, handwritten letters may be a new form of communication.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.outline.0.note: Dry winter weather increases the risk of fires, so everyone is reminded to be careful with sources of flame.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.outline.1.label: Causes of fires and preventive measures
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.outline.1.note: Lists common causes: gas stoves (leaving while cooking), cigarettes (smoking in bed and discarding ashes carelessly), and heaters (forgetting to turn them off). The evidence for Question 1 is in Sentence 3, about the gas stove.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.vietnamese:
This winter, the weather is especially dry compared with previous years. When the air is dry, fires are likely to occur, so please be extremely careful with sources of heat and flame.

Things that can easily cause fires include gas stoves, cigarettes, and heaters. In particular, cooking-related accidents are the most common gas-stove accidents, so when cooking, be careful not to leave the area where the flame is. With cigarettes, smoking in bed or carelessly discarding cigarette butts can cause fires. In addition, forgetting to turn off a heater is also a major cause. Please pay close attention to these matters and do your best to prevent fires.

(注釈1) Smoking in bed: smoking under the covers or in bed.

(注釈2) Cigarette butt: a cigarette that has been smoked.

(注釈3) Carelessly discarding trash: throwing trash onto roads or in public places.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t54-p1.vietnamese:
Recently, it seems that more and more young people are becoming interested in exchanging letters「文通」with people they do not know.

Although email is convenient, why has exchanging handwritten letters become so popular?

It is said that with email, people sometimes feel tired because they think they have to reply immediately. With handwritten letters, however, they can think about what kind of person the other person is while carefully choosing their words, which gives them a refreshing feeling.

Moreover, the time spent waiting for a reply is also said to be an enjoyable period that email does not provide.

For young people who are accustomed to email, handwritten letters may be an entirely new means of communication.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t96-p1.vietnamese:
This time, we spoke with Mitsuo Tanaka, the director who founded a company that introduces jobs to foreign nationals.

Interviewer: What kind of work does your company specifically do?

More than 1,400 foreign nationals are currently registered with us. Simply put, we introduce them to companies as closely as possible according to their preferences.

So your company serves as a bridge between foreign nationals and businesses.

Interviewer: I see. But with the economy in a downturn recently, has it been difficult?

Yes. Even Japanese people are having difficulty finding good jobs, so it is even more difficult for foreign nationals. Only about 5% of the people registered with us are actually hired.

Interviewer: What advice would you give foreign nationals who hope to work in Japan in the future?

For those who want to work in Japan, I hope they will develop communication skills strong enough to travel together with Japanese people.

Especially for international students, what concerns me even more than their knowledge of honorific language or their vocabulary is their lack of experience interacting with Japanese people.

Without skills such as choosing topics of conversation, responding appropriately in dialogue, and sensing the atmosphere at the time, it will be very difficult to work with Japanese people.

Another important point is probably taking the initiative to learn about Japanese culture.

✅ Correct answer: (b) 1.600 円
The total for three fruit-juice sets (1,500 yen) and three cartons of fresh milk (300 yen) is 1,800 yen. Since purchases of at least 1,000 yen receive an additional 200-yen discount, the final total is 1,600 yen.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.explanation: According to the passage, one set of fruit juice remains 500 yen but includes two additional bottles (「1セット (3本入り )500円のジュースは、もう2本つけて、同じねだんで売ります」), while the milk is reduced to 100 yen per carton (「1本120円のぎゅうにゅうが100円になります」). Buying three sets of juice and three cartons of milk initially costs 1,500 + 300 = 1,800 yen. Under the discount condition 「1.000円以上、買っていただいたおきゃくさまは、ぜんぶを合計したねだんから200円安くなります」, the total qualifies for the 200-yen discount, so the actual amount to pay is 1,800 - 200 = 1,600 yen.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) Incorrect because 1,100 yen does not match any correct calculation based on the product price and the supermarket's promotions.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.1: ✓ (b) Correct, because 3 sets of fruit juice (500 × 3 = 1,500 yen) plus 3 cartons of milk (100 × 3 = 300 yen) totals 1,800 yen. A 200-yen discount applies to purchases of 1,000 yen or more, leaving 1,600 yen.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) This is incorrect because 1,660 円 is calculated using the original milk price of 120 yen per carton minus 200 yen, ignoring the discounted milk price of 100 yen per carton.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) Incorrect because 1,800 円 is only the subtotal of the products, before subtracting the 200-yen discount available for bills of 1,000 yen or more.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 正しく 飲ん で いな いた め に 、 本 来 の 効果 が 得 ら れ な いか ら 。
The passage explains that many people take supplements incorrectly, such as taking too much or failing to take them with suitable food, so they do not receive the products’ intended benefits.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.explanation: In the passage, the author points out problems with taking supplements: 「サプリメントは、飲みすぎるとほかの栄養を壊してしまったり、たくさん飲んでも、あるほかの食品と一緒にとらないとたいして効果がなかったりする。」(If you take too many supplements, they may destroy other nutrients; and even if you take a lot, they may have little effect unless taken with certain other foods.) The concluding sentence emphasizes: 「しかし、間違った飲み方のために、無駄に飲んでいる人が大勢いるのが現状なのだ。」The grammar pattern 「～ために」indicates the cause, stating that many people are taking supplements unnecessarily because they take them incorrectly. Therefore, users fail to obtain the supplements’ intended benefits precisely because they do not take them properly.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage does not say that drinking it every day is ineffective; it says that it does not work when consumed incorrectly.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.1: ✓ (b) The passage clearly states that many people are drinking it ineffectively because they are taking it incorrectly and are not receiving its intended benefits.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The passage does not mention the expense or effort involved in buying and using supplements.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The passage does not say that one becomes malnourished no matter how much one drinks; rather, nutritional supplements are designed to make up for nutritional deficiencies.

The passage advises people who live alone to pretend that someone else is inside when opening the door to enter, for safety.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.explanation: The passage explains ways for people living alone (一人暮らし) to avoid danger, emphasizing that they should avoid letting others know they live alone. The basis is the sentence: 「まるで家族が待っているように「ただいまー」と言いながらドアを開けるようにしましょう。」 (Open the door while saying “I’m home,” as if your family were waiting inside.) The grammar pattern 「まるで〜ように」 means “as if…” and describes pretending that someone else is in the house, which is exactly equivalent to 「誰か他の人がいるふりをする」 in choice d.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage is intended for people living alone (一人暮らし), so asking a family member to wait in the room does not fit the situation.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The passage does not mention leaving doors or windows open to make escaping easier.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The passage does not say that one should quickly close the door to block the thief's escape route.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.3: ✓ (d) The passage advises saying 「ただいまー」 when opening the door or ringing the doorbell, pretending that someone else is inside to avoid danger.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t12-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 「 や ま と 株 式 会 社 」 は 、 来 年 度 に お 客 様 に カレ ンダ ー を 配 ろ うと 思っ て いる 。
The passage confirms that Yamato Co. plans to choose a suitable calendar design and distribute it to customers in the coming fiscal year.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t12-q1.explanation: In the passage, a representative of Yamato clearly states: 「新年に、お客様に配るカレンダーとしての利用を検討させていただきたいと思います。」 (We would like to consider using it as a calendar to distribute to customers at New Year.) This sentence uses the humble expression 「検討させていただきたい」 together with 「～と思う」 (to think/intend) to express Yamato's intention, which is equivalent to the volitional grammar pattern 「～配ろうと思っている」 in answer choice (c). In addition, the structure 「N ＋ として」 (in the capacity or role of) clearly indicates that the mini calendar is intended to be given to customers next year.

default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 食べやすく、熱が出て食欲のないときにも簡単に食べられるから。
The passage states that matcha ice cream melts quickly and is easy to eat, making it the most suitable food to have first when one has a fever and no appetite.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-q1.explanation: The relevant quotation is: 「それから、抹茶アイスクリームだ。すっと溶けて食べやすいので、食欲のないときにはまずこれから食べるとよいだろう。」 It means: “Next is matcha ice cream. Since it melts quickly and is easy to eat, when you have no appetite, it would be best to start with this.” The key grammar point is 「V（ます-stem）＋やすい」, which expresses that an action is easy to perform (here, 食べやすい: easy to eat or swallow). It is combined with the gentle recommendation pattern 「V-dictionary form ＋ とよい」, suggesting a beneficial course of action in a particular situation. The author is saying that when a high fever causes a loss of appetite, ordinary food may be difficult to consume, so a cool, quick-melting, easily digestible food such as matcha ice cream is an ideal way to take in energy without the difficulty described in choice (c). In JLPT reading comprehension, choices (a) and (b) are classic traps that arbitrarily rearrange keywords from the porridge and onion miso soup, while (d) is an unsupported personal inference. Carefully match each property to the correct food mentioned in the passage.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) This incorrectly confuses the functions of rice porridge, which supplies missing nutrients, with green onions and miso soup, which promote sweating to reduce a fever and replenish salt.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because the passage only states that ham helps induce sweating and miso replenishes salt; it does not say that eating them together makes the food easier to eat.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) This is correct because it exactly matches the passage: matcha ice cream melts quickly and is easy to eat, making it suitable for people who have lost their appetite due to a fever.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t13-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) Incorrect because the passage does not mention simple preparation methods or whether someone with a fever can cook alone.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t14-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 商店 街 は 、 炎 型 スー パー に は な い 良 さ を 持っ て いる 。
The reading points out that although large supermarkets have advantages such as low prices and convenience, shopping streets (商店街) have their own unique strengths, including attentive advice from familiar staff and greater confidence in food safety.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t14-q1.explanation: The passage compares the advantages and disadvantages of large supermarkets (大型スーパー) and shopping streets (商店街), ultimately asserting that shopping streets have unique values that large supermarkets lack. The key evidence is the quotation:「店へ行くと、いつもの店員が安いものやおいしいものなどを丁寧に教えてくれる」(When you go to the shop, the familiar clerk carefully tells you which items are inexpensive or tasty), along with the face-to-face relationship「顔の見える関係」that helps ensure food safety. At the end, the author uses the pattern「～ばかりを求めるのではなく、～必要がある」(rather than seeking only..., it is necessary to...) in:「私たちは、安さや便利さばかりを求めるのではなく、食の安全のために、商店街の良さをもう一度見直してみる必要があるのかもしれない。」to emphasize the need to reconsider the merits of 商店街.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t14-q1.why.0: ✓ (a) Correct because the passage states that shopping streets have advantages that large supermarkets do not, such as staff who kindly recommend good, inexpensive products and ensure food safety through personal connections.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t14-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because the passage states that customers choose large supermarkets because they are inexpensive and convenient (「安くて便利だから」), not because they offer a wider variety of goods than shopping streets.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t14-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The passage states that when there is a face-to-face relationship, as in 商店街, shops naturally sell only safe, high-quality goods. It does not say that both places sell safe, high-quality goods.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t14-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) Incorrect because the passage only mentions the shopping-district staff kindly guiding customers (「いつもの店員が...丁寧に教えてくれる」); it does not mention the attitude of employees at a large supermarket.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t15-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 自分も、困っている旅行者の役に立つことができたから。
The author felt happy because they were able to help a traveler in difficulty, repaying the kindness and assistance they had received in the past.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t15-q1.explanation: Grammatically, the key expression「[Noun] の役に立つ」means “to be useful/helpful to someone or for something.” Combined with the potential expression「役に立つことができる」, it describes being able to perform an action that provides practical value to another person. The author also uses the polite respectful expression「お + V(stem) + です」in「お困りですか」to politely ask whether someone is having difficulty and offer assistance. The passage directly supports this with:「ガイドブックを片手に、とても不安そうな様子をみて、思わず「なにかお困りですか。」と英語で声をかけた。」The complete translation is: “Seeing someone holding a guidebook in one hand and looking very anxious, I instinctively spoke to them in English: ‘Are you having any trouble?’” As a test-taking tip, candidates may confuse this with choice (a) or (d) because the context mentions an earlier incident, but the keyword「自分も」(“I, too…”) in choice (c) signals the continuation of the theme of helping others: the greatest joy is being able to take the role of a person who helps someone else.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t15-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) This choice only refers to the past experience of being helped by someone else, not the direct reason for the author’s current feeling of happiness.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t15-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The passage is not intended to show pride in or flaunt the writer's ability to communicate in English.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t15-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) This is the correct answer because it fully reflects the author’s action: realizing that they themselves could be of help (役に立つ) to a confused tourist.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t15-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The memory of the kind Italian woman was only the initial motivation that prompted the author to speak up; it was not the fundamental reason for the joy felt after helping someone.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t16-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 自分の店の利用客を他の店にとられたくないから。
Facing intense competition from supermarkets that stay open late, some convenience stores began offering new services to retain their customers and prevent competitors from taking them away.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t16-q1.explanation: The key evidence is the sentence in paragraph 2: 「そこで、他店に客をとられないように、一部のコンビニが始めた ② 新サービスが「ご用聞きサービス」だ。」 (Therefore, to prevent other stores from taking their customers, the new service started by some convenience stores was the “order-taking service.”) Grammatically, the key structure 「V-ない + ように」 expresses a purpose aimed at preventing an unwanted state or event from occurring (“so that...not”), together with the passive form 「とられる」 (from 「とる」), which conveys having one's customers or benefits taken away by a competitor. The N3 reading comprehension test uses equivalent phrasing, changing the preventive purpose 「客をとられないように」 (so as not to lose customers) into the expression of desire 「客をとられたくないから」 (because they do not want to lose customers). To avoid the common trap in choice (b), note that the author merely lists supermarkets as one type of convenient store, 「スーパーなどの便利な店」, and does not use the comparative structure 「コンビニより」 at all. Finally, distinguish clearly between the original purpose of introducing the service and the customers' response after the service was launched, as in choice (c).
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t16-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The fact that neighborhood grocery stores once provided this service is mentioned only to explain the origin of the term 「ご用聞き」, not the reason convenience stores adopted it.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t16-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The passage only states that more convenience stores, such as supermarkets open late, are increasing; it does not claim that those places are more convenient than convenience stores (コンビニより便利).
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t16-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The fact that elderly people and busy homemakers favor the service is a result observed after its introduction, not the reason convenience stores began offering it.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t16-q1.why.3: ✓ (d) The passage clearly states that the purpose of launching the new service is 「他店に客をとられないように」, meaning “so that other stores do not take their customers away.”
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t17-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 自分 が 興味 を 持つ こと が で きる テー マ を 選ん で 作る こと
The passage advises people who find their days boring to choose a topic they like and are interested in, then make their own town map.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t17-q1.explanation: In the opening sentence, the author uses the pattern 「〜におすすめなのが、〜ことだ」(what is recommended for... is to...) in the quoted sentence: 「『毎日同じでつまらない。何か新しいことはないかな』という人におすすめなのが、好きなテーマを選んで自分の町の地図を作ってみることだ」. The author then compares this with taking photographs to clarify that the results differ depending on what each person is interested in (「きれいな花に興味がある人と、そこにある建物に興味がある人」). This highlights the idea of creating a map based on a theme that one personally likes and is interested in (「自分 が 興味 を 持つ こと が で きる テー マ」).
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t17-q1.why.0: ✓ (a) This is correct because the author recommends choosing a topic one likes and is interested in (好きなテーマ) when starting to make a mind map.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t17-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) Taking photos is only a comparison used for illustration; the passage does not require taking a large number of photos while making notes.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t17-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) This is incorrect because the passage emphasizes going outside to observe a subject of personal interest, not going outside to investigate many different things.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t17-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The passage is about discovering a new perspective on a familiar town, not about searching for many new things in the town.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t18-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) いろ いろ 書か れ て いる の で 、 予 定 が わか り に くい 。
Because too many different things are written down, the schedule becomes difficult to understand and follow.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t18-q1.explanation: The passage contains the quotation: 「正確にいうと、昨日までの過去にはいろいろ書かれているが、今日から先はまるで白紙。」(Strictly speaking, the past up to yesterday contains many things that have been written, but everything from today onward is completely blank.) The grammar pattern 「V-ます + にくい」(as in 「分かりにくい」) means that an action is difficult to perform, or that something is difficult to recognize or understand. When a notebook contains too much written content (「いろいろ書かれている」), managing and distinguishing the plans becomes more difficult. Therefore, choice (a) is correct.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t18-q1.why.0: ✓ (a) This is correct because the notebook contains too many intermingled notes, making the schedule difficult to follow.

default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t22-q4.verdict:

Likewise, choice (d) mentions 「日本文化」, but the passage only recommends taking an interest in it (「関心を持つ」), not studying hard (「一生懸命勉強する」). Recognizing the key phrase 「いちばん言いたいこと」 together with the emphasis pattern 「～よりも心配なのは…」 leads to the correct answer, (b).

default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-q4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) おじいさんにもう一度会いたいから
The author decided to continue visiting the nursing home because the old man's words of thanks moved them and made them genuinely want to see him again.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-q4.explanation: The decisive clue is: 「私はそれを聞いて、とてもうれしくなり、またこのおじいさんに会いに来たいと思いました。」(Hearing that, I felt very happy and thought that I would like to come and see this elderly man again.) Grammatically, the author uses the movement-purpose pattern V-masu stem + に来る together with the volitional ending「〜たい」in the past form「〜たいと思いました」to express a sincere wish at that moment. The phrase「また...会いに来たい」has the same meaning as choice (a),「もう一度会いたい」(want to meet again). Note that「またいらっしゃい」is a polite invitation to visit the nursing home again, not an invitation to the speaker's private home (choice b). Also,「いつも」describes the habit of playing games with friends on Saturdays, not visiting the elderly man every week (choices c and d).
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-q4.why.0: ✓ (a) This precisely matches the author’s wish to visit and meet the elderly man again after their warm conversation.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-q4.why.1: ✗ (b) The elderly man currently lives in a nursing home and politely says to visit again next time; he does not invite the visitor to his private home.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) Saturdays are usually when the author gets together with friends to play games; only this Saturday do they plan to visit their uncle.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) The author plans to bring a guitar so they can sing an old song with the elderly man; there is no intention of playing games.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-q4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 子どものころに、ダンスやランニングなどの骨を強くする運動をしておいた方がいい。
The author emphasizes that the skeleton develops and reaches maturity before the age of 30. Therefore, actively doing weight-bearing exercises such as running and dancing during childhood is essential for building strong bones.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-q4.explanation: The author's main message is most clearly summarized in the final two sentences: 「それを考えると、子どものころにより強い骨を作っておいた方がいいことがわかるだろう。」 and 「健康な骨を作るには、正しい時期に、効果のある運動をすることが大事なのだ。」 The completed sentence means: 'Considering that, you will understand that it is better to build stronger bones during childhood; to build healthy bones, it is important to do effective exercise at the right stage.' The key grammar pattern 「〜ておいた方がいい」 combines the preparatory form 「V-ておく」 with the advice pattern 「V-たほうがいい」. The past form 「V-た」 conveys advice to take action proactively, before the bones finish developing around age 30. For questions asking about the author's opinion, be wary of choices containing absolute wording such as 「どんな運動でも」 in (a), because the author rejects this idea with the partial negative pattern 「〜わけではない」 in 「どんな運動でもいいわけではない」.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-q4.why.0: ✗ (a) Incorrect because the passage states that not every type of exercise is beneficial; for example, swimming does little to strengthen bones. This contradicts the absolute expression “any kind of exercise” (どんな運動でも).
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-q4.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because the author only states that calcium and exercise are equally important, without mentioning any required sequence of taking calcium first and exercising afterward.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-q4.why.2: ✓ (c) Correct, because it accurately reflects the author's conclusion that people should choose weight-bearing exercises, such as dancing and jogging, to build strong bones from childhood.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) Incorrect, because the author points out that swimming has little effect on strengthening bones since the body floats in water. The article also never says that swimming as a child will prevent illness for life.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-q4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) もっと日本人と交流して、経験を積んでほしい。
The director emphasizes that what he is most concerned about and wants to tell the international students is that they lack practical experience interacting with Japanese people—something essential for working together in the future.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-q4.explanation: For questions asking what the author most wants to say (いちばん言いたいこと), pay attention to the sentence emphasizing the target audience and degree: 「特に留学生に言いたいんですが、敬語の知識とか言葉の量とかよりも心配なのは、日本人と交流する経験が足りないということです。」 (I especially want to say this to international students: more concerning than knowledge of honorific language or vocabulary size is the lack of experience interacting with Japanese people.) The sentence uses the comparison pattern 「A よりも B」(B is more than A) together with the desire pattern 「V-てほしい」(the te-form plus ほしい, expressing a wish for someone else to take an action) throughout the interview to emphasize the importance of gaining practical experience. The author further explains that only through real interaction can learners acquire the ability to choose topics, use backchannel responses (あいづち), and read the atmosphere so they can work well with others: 「...そういう力がないと、日本人と一緒に働くときに困ってしまうんですよ。」. Choice (a) is tempting because of the keyword 「旅行」, but in the passage 「旅行に行けるくらい」merely gives an extent using 〜くらい; it is not a recommended action. Choice (d) begins with the conjunction 「あとは」(in addition/as for the rest), so it is supplementary rather than the main point.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-q4.why.0: ✗ (a) Traveling is merely an illustrative example indicating the level of communication (旅行に行けるくらい); the author does not recommend that international students travel to many places with Japanese people.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-q4.why.1: ✓ (b) The author directly identifies the lack of experience interacting with Japanese people as his greatest concern regarding international students, and therefore hopes that they will actively interact with others and gain practical experience.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) The author emphasizes that lacking hands-on experience is the greater concern, rather than focusing on speaking fluently or choosing polished words.
default.q.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) Interest in culture is only an additional factor mentioned near the end (あとは), not the most important point the director wants to convey.

Change in reception hours

To: Arena
From: Yamada Takako

Now, on the 18th of next month, Angelina Moreau will give a piano concert at my university.

Adds an explanatory or emphatic tone to the writer’s statement about Japanese habits.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t4-p1.sentences.5.keys.0: Confirms that these expressions are used even when alone, matching the situation in option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t4-p1.sentences.5.keys.1: The two expressions correspond to before and after a meal: いただきます before eating and ごちそうさま afterward. Options 3 and 4 both match.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t4-p1.outline.0.label: The importance of greetings
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t4-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the value Japanese people place on greetings and the widespread practice of greeting familiar people.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t4-p1.outline.1.label: Polite expressions with strangers
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t4-p1.outline.1.note: Japanese people greet strangers in places such as the mountains and apologize when they nearly bump into them. Distinguish “nearly bump into” from “be bumped into” in option 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t4-p1.outline.2.label: Expressions before and after meals
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t4-p1.outline.2.note: Adds that even when alone, Japanese people say いただきます before a meal and ごちそうさま afterward.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t4-p1.vietnamese: Greetings are highly valued by Japanese people. People from any country would probably say “Hello” when they meet someone they know. However, in places such as the mountains, Japanese people also greet strangers when they meet them. They also say “Excuse me” when they nearly bump into a stranger. That is not all. Even when alone, Japanese people always say “Itadakimasu” before a meal and “Gochisousama” afterward to express gratitude.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.0.vi: Recently, importance has been placed on acquiring abilities that are immediately useful upon entering society, such as being able to use computers or speak foreign languages.
being able to use (in a list)
being able to speak (in a list)
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.0.gramma: Lists representative examples without making the list exhaustive. 使えたり and 話せたり come from the potential forms 使える and 話せる.
Indicates that something happens immediately after an action. 社会に出てすぐに means immediately upon entering adult or working life.
Nominalizes a verb phrase. 身につけること means the act of acquiring abilities.
Combines the passive with ～ている to describe something that is currently valued in society.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.1.vi: For this reason, classes in these subjects are being offered at many high schools.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.1.gramma: Connects the cause in the previous sentence to its result: because practical abilities are valued, many schools offer these classes.
The passive of 行う combined with ～ている describes an activity that is ongoing or regularly conducted.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.2.vi: On the other hand, reportedly, an increasing number of people say there is no need to study subjects such as classical literature and history because they are not useful.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.2.gramma: Introduces another aspect or a trend that contrasts with what has just been stated.
Gives examples within a broader group: classical literature, history, and similar subjects.
Gives a reason. Here, the claim that these subjects are useless is the reason offered by the people being described.
Follows a dictionary-form verb and means there is no need to do something.
Refers to people who say or hold the view expressed before と. This is a group's opinion, not the author's conclusion.
Follows a plain-form statement to report information heard from another source. Here it expresses hearsay, not an impression based on appearance.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.3.vi: However, the fact remains that other subjects are also important alongside computer and foreign language studies.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.3.gramma: Introduces a contrast. The author challenges the preceding view that other subjects need not be studied.
Means besides or in addition to something already mentioned; here it adds other subjects alongside computers and foreign languages.
Means also, emphasizing that other subjects matter too. It does not rank one subject above another.
Affirms that a fact remains unchanged. である is a formal equivalent of だ, and こと nominalizes the entire statement.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.3.keys.0: Marks the shift to the author's position, opposing the claim that other subjects are unnecessary.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.3.keys.1: Directly supports option 3: other subjects are important too, alongside immediately useful subjects; no ranking is given.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.4.vi: Schools probably need to devise ways to have students study these subjects in a balanced way.
well; evenly with バランス
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.4.gramma: The causative form of 学習する. In this educational context, it means having or arranging for students to study.
Softens a judgment. Here the author suggests that schools need ways to ensure balanced study.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.sentences.4.keys.0: The recommendation to balance both groups of subjects reinforces option 3: both immediately useful subjects and other subjects matter.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.outline.0.label: Emphasis on practical abilities
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.outline.0.note: Immediately useful abilities such as computer and foreign language skills are valued, so many high schools offer classes in them.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.outline.1.label: A view that dismisses other subjects
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.outline.1.note: The author reports that more people consider classical literature and history unnecessary because they see them as useless. This is a reported opinion.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.outline.2.label: Both groups of subjects matter
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.outline.2.note: The author affirms that other subjects also matter and recommends balanced study at school. This supports option 3 without ranking either group above the other.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.vietnamese: Recently, importance has been placed on acquiring abilities that are immediately useful upon entering society, such as being able to use computers or speak foreign languages. For this reason, classes in these subjects are being offered at many high schools. On the other hand, reportedly, an increasing number of people say there is no need to study subjects such as classical literature and history because they are not useful. However, the fact remains that other subjects are also important alongside computer and foreign language studies. Schools probably need to devise ways to have students study these subjects in a balanced way.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.sentences.0.vi: The letter below was sent by an elementary school to its students’ parents and guardians.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.sentences.0.gramma: A past-tense clause modifies もの, referring here to the letter the school sent.
A formal written equivalent of だ or です.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.sentences.6.vi: Thank you for your continued understanding and cooperation with Takada Elementary School.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.sentences.6.gramma: A humble form of ～をもらう, showing respect when receiving something from someone.
Expresses thanks for a benefit received; いただき is the formal connective form of いただく.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.sentences.7.vi: We are pleased to announce that Takada Elementary School will be holding an exhibition of student work.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.sentences.7.gramma: Marks a place or organization as the topic, here introducing the school’s activity.
Announces a decision or arrangement: the school will hold an exhibition.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.sentences.8.vi: We plan to show not only paintings, calligraphy, clay works, and similar creations, but also a photo exhibition capturing classroom activities and videos showing the students in their everyday school life.
be (humble; here used in a formal statement of plans)
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.sentences.8.gramma: Lists examples without making the list exhaustive.
Not only … but also …; the exhibition includes works, photographs, and videos.
A past-tense clause modifies a noun: おさめた modifies 写真展, and うつした modifies ビデオ.
A humble construction for the speaker’s action toward the listener; お見せする means to show.
A formal, humble way to state what one plans to do.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.sentences.8.keys.0: A photo exhibition capturing classroom activities supports option 1: displaying photographs featuring the students.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.sentences.9.vi: We sincerely hope you will come and see what the students’ life at school is like.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.sentences.9.gramma: Respectfully describes someone coming, used here to invite parents and guardians to attend.
Allows a location phrase to modify a noun: 学校での様子 means what life at school is like.
A respectful expression for having someone view something.
Expresses a very polite wish or request: we hope you could …; 存じます is the humble equivalent of 思います.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.outline.0.label: Context and letter details
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the school’s letter to parents and guardians, including the date, addressees, school, and principal.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.outline.1.label: Opening thanks
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.outline.1.note: The school thanks parents and guardians for their continued understanding and cooperation.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.outline.2.label: Exhibition announcement and contents
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.outline.2.note: The school will hold an exhibition featuring student work, classroom photographs, and videos of students. The photo exhibition supports option 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.outline.3.label: Invitation to attend
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.outline.3.note: Invites parents and guardians to attend and see the students’ activities at school.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t8-p1.vietnamese:
The letter below was sent by an elementary school to its students’ parents and guardians.

September 26, 20XX

To all parents and guardians

Takada Elementary School

Principal Yokota Kiichi

Dear Parents and Guardians,

Thank you for your continued understanding and cooperation with Takada Elementary School.

We are pleased to announce that Takada Elementary School will be holding an exhibition of student work. We plan to show not only paintings, calligraphy, clay works, and similar creations, but also a photo exhibition capturing classroom activities and videos showing the students in their everyday school life. We sincerely hope you will come and see what the students’ life at school is like.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.0.vi: People who are not good at tidying their rooms often have too many belongings.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.0.gramma: Be bad at doing something. の turns the action 片付ける into a noun phrase.
Describes an excessive state; here, having too many belongings.
Indicates that something often happens or is often the case.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.1.vi: The key to tidying up is to give belongings designated places.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.1.gramma: Identifies the main point: “the key is to…”. こと nominalizes the verb, and final だ or です is omitted.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.1.keys.0: Directly states what to do, matching “decide where to put things” in option 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.2.vi: If you make a habit of putting things back in their places immediately after use, they will no longer be scattered everywhere.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.2.gramma: Marks the time after an action is completed: “once you have used it…”.
If you make an effort or a habit of doing something; the conditional form of ～ようにする.
Something will no longer happen either. こと nominalizes 散らかる.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.3.vi: Also, to make room for those designated places, you need to throw away things you do not need.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.3.gramma: The following noun serves the purpose stated before ため; here, space for designated storage places.
Follows a dictionary-form verb to introduce a goal and what is needed to achieve it: “in order to…”.
It is also necessary to do something. も adds discarding unnecessary things to the preceding advice.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.3.keys.0: Matches “do not keep unnecessary things” in option 1. The advice is to discard unneeded items, not as many items as possible as in option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.4.vi: Store only as much as fits in your room, arranging things so they are easy to see and take out.
so as to be easy to see
so as to be easy to take out
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.4.gramma: Only the amount meeting the preceding condition; here, the amount that fits in the room.
The adverbial form of ～やすい, meaning “easy to do,” describing how items should be stored.
Placed after a dictionary-form verb at the end of a sentence to give an instruction.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.5.vi: If you do this, you will quickly see what you are missing and should also be able to avoid wasteful purchases, such as buying things similar to what you already own.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.sentences.5.gramma: Expresses a condition. こうすれば means “if you do this,” referring to the organizing method just described.
Lists benefits: recognizing missing items and avoiding wasteful purchases.
Modifies a noun to express similarity. 同じような物 means similar items.
Gives an action as a non-exhaustive example; here, buying items similar to those already owned.
Expresses the writer's prediction. 防げる is the potential form of 防ぐ, so 防げるだろう means “should be able to prevent.”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.outline.0.label: The problem: too many belongings
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the observation that people who struggle to tidy their rooms often own too many things.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.outline.1.label: Designate places for belongings
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.outline.1.note: States the key practice of assigning places to belongings and returning them after use. Sentence 1 supports the part of option 1 about deciding where things go.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.outline.2.label: Discard unneeded items and store what fits
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.outline.2.note: Explains the need to discard unnecessary things and store only what fits, keeping items visible and accessible. Sentence 3 supports the part of option 1 about not keeping unneeded items.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.outline.3.label: Benefits of organizing
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.outline.3.note: Organizing this way helps identify missing items and avoid wasteful purchases. These are outcomes, so option 2 does not answer how to tidy the room; option 4 adds cleaning, which the passage does not mention.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t9-p1.vietnamese: People who are not good at tidying their rooms often have too many belongings. The key to tidying up is to give belongings designated places. If you make a habit of putting things back in their places immediately after use, they will no longer be scattered everywhere. Also, to make room for those designated places, you need to throw away things you do not need. Store only as much as fits in your room, arranging things so they are easy to see and take out. If you do this, you will quickly see what you are missing and should also be able to avoid wasteful purchases, such as buying things similar to what you already own.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.0.vi: Take precautions to stay safe when living alone.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Expresses a purpose: for or for the sake of. Here, the purpose is safe living alone.
Makes an invitation or recommendation: let's do something.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.1.vi: ○ When you return home and open the door
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Connects actions in sequence: return home and then open the door.
Indicates when an action takes place.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.2.vi: It is dangerous if others realize that you live alone.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.2.vocab: are doing; live (with 一人暮らし)
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Describes an ongoing situation: living alone.
Nominalizes a clause: the fact that someone lives alone.
Links a condition to its consequence: if others find out, it is dangerous.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.3.vi: Make a habit of opening the door while saying “I'm home!”, as though your family were waiting for you.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Describes acting as if an imagined situation were true: as though family were waiting.
Describes an action in progress: waiting.
Attaches to the verb stem and expresses simultaneous actions: opening the door while speaking.
Advises making a conscious effort or habit of doing something.
Acting as though family were waiting means pretending someone else is inside, matching option 4.
This is the specific action used when entering to give the impression that someone is inside.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.4.vi: It is also effective to ring the bell before opening the door and act as though you have come to visit someone.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Introduces another method in addition to the one already mentioned.
Follows a dictionary-form verb to indicate doing something before another action.
押し is the connective stem of 押す, linking pressing the bell to the following action.
Here, indicates coming to a place to perform an action: coming to visit.
Here, means acting as though a situation were true: as though visiting someone.
の nominalizes the action, and も adds that this method is effective too.
Ringing the bell and pretending to visit someone also suggests someone is inside, supporting option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Introduces a hypothetical condition: if you encounter a burglar.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.6.vi: What would you do if there were a burglar in your room?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Emphasizes a hypothetical situation: supposing that…
Expresses the presence of a person or animal at a location.
Asks what action someone would take.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.7.vi: For example, in an apartment or flat, a burglar's only escape routes are the entrance door or a window.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Lists examples without necessarily being exhaustive.
Sets the location or scope under discussion: in apartments…
In 泥棒の逃げる道, の marks the subject of the noun-modifying clause, like が: the route the burglar uses to escape.
Uses a negative predicate to express limitation: only the entrance door or a window.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.8.vi: Make sure the burglar can escape quickly, and do not chase them.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.sentences.8.gramm: In 逃げられる, this is the potential form of 逃げる: can escape.
Take steps to make a situation possible: allow the burglar to escape.
Advises taking care not to do something: do not chase the burglar.
The person to be allowed to escape is the burglar. This rules out option 2 and directly contradicts option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.outline.0.label: Safety when living alone
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.outline.0.note: The title introduces precautions for staying safe when living alone.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.outline.1.label: Act as though someone is home
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.outline.1.note: When entering, greet an imagined waiting family or ring the bell as though visiting someone. This directly supports option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.outline.2.label: Let the burglar escape without pursuit
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.outline.2.note: If a burglar is in the room, allow them to escape quickly and do not pursue them. This rules out choices that misidentify who should escape or suggest blocking the burglar's escape.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.vietnamese:
～Take precautions to stay safe when living alone～

○ When you return home and open the door
It is dangerous if others realize that you live alone. Make a habit of opening the door while saying “I'm home!”, as though your family were waiting for you. It is also effective to ring the bell before opening the door and act as though you have come to visit someone.

○ If you encounter a burglar
What would you do if there were a burglar in your room? For example, in an apartment or flat, a burglar's only escape routes are the entrance door or a window. Make sure the burglar can escape quickly, and do not chase them.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.0.vi: This town was built about 40 years ago.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Passive voice: 作る -> 作られました (to be built / created).
Expresses an approximate quantity or amount (about 40 years).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.1.vi: It was a very beautiful town.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.2.vi: It is located about an hour by train from Tokyo, and about 20 minutes by bus from the station.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Particle で indicating the means of transportation (by train, by bus).
Expressing approximate time/quantity (about 1 hour, around 20 minutes).
Shows that transportation from Tokyo and the station was relatively convenient, supporting the description of a convenient town (便利) in question 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.3.vi: We got married 40 years ago and bought a house in this town.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Te-form used to link actions in chronological sequence: got married and then bought a house.
Evidence for identifying the author: Getting married 40 years ago proves the author is married (結婚している) and currently an elderly person (老人).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.4.vi: It is a large house with a spacious garden.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Noun modifying clause: 広い庭がある modifies 大きな家.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.5.vi: Many young couples also moved into neighboring houses.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Expressing action moving toward the speaker's location: 引っ越してくる (to move in).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.6.vi: It had plenty of greenery and was a very good place to raise children.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Verb dictionary form + のに indicating purpose or utility (good for raising children).
Direct evidence for question 2: Confirms that 40 years ago the town was rich in greenery (緑が多い町) and an excellent place to raise children.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.7.vi: Our daughter also grew up healthy and lively together with the neighborhood children.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Change of state with I-adjective: 大きい -> 大きくなる (to grow big / grow up).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.8.vi: Before long, the children of every household grew up and moved out of the town.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Noun + になる indicating transformation: to become an adult.
Te-form + 行く indicating movement away from the starting place: 出て行く (to leave/move out).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.9.vi: Most of the people living in the town now are 60 years old or older, and this town has become a town of elderly people.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.9.gramm: Noun + になる indicating becoming: become an elderly town.
Evidence for question 1 (the author living here for 40 years is also 60+, an elderly person) and question 3 (identifies the town today as an elderly town - 老人が住む町).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.10.vi: As one gets older, even pulling weeds in the garden becomes a tough task.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.10.gram: Conditional と expressing natural consequence or circumstance: when/as one grows older.
Nominalization of verb: 草をとるの (the act of weeding/pulling grass).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.11.vi: Because the hospital is far away, we worry if someone suddenly falls ill.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.11.gram: Expressing reason or cause objectively: because the hospital is far.
Conditional tara: if one suddenly gets sick.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.12.vi: Because of that, some people have moved to convenient apartments in Tokyo.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.13.vi: There are also houses where no one lives because family members got sick and ended up hospitalized.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.sentences.13.gram: Expressing an unfortunate or completed action: hospitalized unfortunately.
Nobody / no one + negative verb: nobody lives.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.outline.0.label: The town 40 years ago: A beautiful and ideal beginning
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.outline.0.note: Describes the town 40 years ago when newly built: green environment, convenient transport, attracting young couples to settle down and raise children.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.outline.1.label: Current state of the town: Aging population and loneliness
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.outline.1.note: Children grew up and left, current residents are mostly 60 or older; the town became inconvenient and deserted as residents moved away or were hospitalized.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.outline.2.label: Difficulties in daily life and the greatest worry about the bus service
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.outline.2.note: Daily life is inconvenient without nearby shops, relying on the husband's car; the author worries most about the bus service ceasing when old age prevents driving.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.vietnamese:
This town was built about 40 years ago. It was a very beautiful town. It is located about an hour by train from Tokyo and about 20 minutes by bus from the station. We got married 40 years ago and bought a house in this town. It is a large house with a spacious garden. Many young couples also moved into the neighboring houses. With abundant greenery, it was a wonderful place to raise children. Our daughter also grew up healthy and lively alongside the neighborhood children.

Eventually, the children of every household grew up and moved out of the town. Most of the people currently living in the town are 60 years old or older, turning it into a town of elderly residents. As people grow older, even weeding the garden becomes hard work. Since the hospital is far away, falling suddenly ill is a real concern. Because of that, some people have relocated to convenient apartments in Tokyo. There are also empty houses where no one lives because family members were hospitalized due to illness. The town suddenly became lonely and quiet. Because it is inconvenient, no young people are newly moving in.

Lately, I have come to feel that even daily life has become difficult. Since there are no shops nearby, I go shopping near the station by my husband's car. From here to the station takes about 15 minutes by car, but walking takes an entire hour. Right now, what worries me the most is how long the bus service will continue to operate. If the number of bus passengers declines, the buses will probably stop coming. When we grow older and can no longer drive, if there are no buses, what will happen to our lives? I am truly deeply concerned.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t20-p1.vietnamese:
This is an essay written by Tajima.

Last Saturday, I visited a facility called Hikari Home. Many elderly men and women who cannot live with their families live there. I did things such as listening to a 90-year-old man’s stories and having a meal with him.

Because the man could not walk, he remained seated in a chair the whole time. He told me all sorts of things, such as having as many as five children who had all graduated from good universities, and being a good singer when he was young.

At lunchtime, the man could not hold a spoon, so I helped him by bringing food to his mouth. He said “Thank you” to me many times. Then he said, “If you’d like, come again.” Hearing that made me very happy, and I thought I would like to come and see him again.

Tomorrow is Saturday. I usually spend the day doing things like playing games with friends, but tomorrow I plan to go and see the man. Next time, I hope to take a guitar along and sing together with him.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t21-p1.outline.4.label: Vocabulary notes
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t21-p1.outline.4.note: Defines osteoporosis and the verb meaning to maintain.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t21-p1.vietnamese:
Everyone knows that getting plenty of calcium is good for building healthy bones. However, it is not widely known that exercise is just as important. If people do not get enough exercise as children, their bones become more prone to fractures as they grow older, and they may develop osteoporosis.

Although exercise is important, that does not mean just any kind of exercise will do. Activities such as dancing, running, and jumping are effective for building healthy bones, while swimming is said to have little effect in this respect. This is because exercise that requires supporting one's own body weight helps strengthen bones, but the human body floats in water, so there is no need to support that weight underwater.

Exercise has various effects, and exercise suited to one's body makes bones thicker and stronger. Furthermore, the muscles around the bones also become stronger, and those muscles help maintain bone strength. Also, people who exercise regularly move quickly and can more easily avoid fractures and injuries caused by accidents and similar events than people who do not exercise at all.

Exercise for general health is beneficial regardless of the age at which one starts, but exercise for building strong bones is different. This is because bones finish forming during the period from birth to around age 30. Considering this, one can see that it is better to build stronger bones during childhood. To build healthy bones, it is important to do effective exercise at the right time.

(Note 1) Osteoporosis: a disease in which bones become weak.

(Note 2) Maintain: to preserve a certain state.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t22-p1.outline.1.label: Difficult job searches and a success rate of about 5%
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t22-p1.outline.1.note: The economic downturn makes good jobs difficult to find even for Japanese people, and harder still for foreign nationals. About 5% of registered applicants secure a placement.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t22-p1.outline.2.label: Prioritizing real interaction experience
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t22-p1.outline.2.note: Shifts to advice for people seeking work in Japan. The president particularly stresses international students' lack of interaction experience with Japanese people, a greater concern than honorific knowledge or vocabulary size.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t22-p1.outline.3.label: Skills needed to work with Japanese people
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t22-p1.outline.3.note: Minor language errors can be forgiven, and desu/masu forms avoid impoliteness. The crucial skills include selecting topics, responding as a listener, and sensing the atmosphere. Interest in Japanese culture is an additional suggestion.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t22-p1.outline.4.label: Vocabulary notes
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t22-p1.outline.4.note: Defines 不景気 and 就職.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t22-p1.vietnamese:
This time, we spoke with President Tanaka Mitsuaki, who founded a company that helps foreign nationals find jobs.

Q: What exactly does your company do?

— More than 1,400 foreign nationals have registered with us. Simply put, we try to refer them to their preferred companies as far as possible. In other words, we say to a company, “We have foreign candidates who can do this kind of work. Could you let them work for you?” Of course, companies also approach us and say, “We want foreign candidates who meet these requirements. Could you introduce someone suitable?” In short, we act as an intermediary between foreign job seekers and companies.

Q: I see. But with the recent economic downturn, ①isn't it difficult?

— Yes. Since even Japanese people find it difficult to get a good job, it is even harder for foreign nationals. Only ②about 5% of those who have registered actually secure a job, I would say.

Q: Please give some advice to foreign nationals who hope to find employment in Japan in the future.

— Well, let me think. I would like people who want to work in Japan to develop enough communication skills to be able to travel with Japanese people. What I especially want to tell international students is that, more than their knowledge of honorific language or vocabulary size, I am concerned about their lack of experience interacting with Japanese people. Even if they make a few language mistakes, those mistakes will be forgiven because they are foreign nationals. As for honorific language, speaking using “desu” and “masu” will not be considered impolite. But without skills such as choosing conversation topics, giving appropriate listener responses, and sensing the atmosphere of the situation, ③they will run into difficulties when working with Japanese people. Beyond that, I would also say it is important to take an active interest in Japanese culture.

(Note 1) Economic downturn: a situation in which the economy is in poor condition.

(Note 2) Finding employment: taking up a job.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t27-p1.sentences.4.vi: I ordered blue earphones (product code: EYH0025B), but the ones delivered were black.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t27-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Nominalizes the preceding clause and highlights what follows: what was ordered was blue earphones.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t27-p1.sentences.6.vi: Also, if blue is out of stock, white would be acceptable; however, if I cannot receive the item by next Friday, please cancel the order and issue a refund.
