default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.sentences.0.vi: Recently, more and more people have been listening to music or playing games on their mobile phones while walking.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Verb stem + ながら expresses two simultaneous actions: here, using a phone while walking.
Lists representative activities without implying an exhaustive list: listening to music and playing games.
In 増えている, indicates an ongoing trend of increasing numbers.
Introduces the growing group: people using their phones while walking. 数 in sentence 3 refers back to this group.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.sentences.1.vi: On roads where cars pass and on platforms where trains arrive and depart, doing so is truly dangerous.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.sentences.1.gramm: A clause precedes and modifies a noun: 車が通る modifies 道, and 電車が発着する modifies プラットホーム.
Gives examples from a broader set: roads with passing cars, train platforms, and similar places.
Combines the location marker で with は to frame the statement around those places.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.sentences.2.vi: In fact, accidents have already occurred.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Emphasizes that the danger has also led to actual accidents.
In 起きている, presents accidents as actual occurrences and an existing problem.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.sentences.3.vi: Throughout the city, posters, announcements, and other means are used to urge people to stop using their mobile phones while walking, but the number of people doing so does not seem to be going down.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.sentences.3.vocab: not readily; still not (with a negative)
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Expresses simultaneous actions: using a phone while walking.
こと turns the verb phrase into a noun phrase; は makes using a phone while walking the topic of the appeal.
ましょう expresses an appeal, and と marks its quoted content: let us stop that behavior.
Indicates a medium or means: here, posters and announcements.
Describes ongoing warnings, then uses が to introduce a result contrary to expectations.
Indicates that an expected change is slow or difficult to happen: the number still does not decrease.
Expresses an inference from the observed situation: it seems; it appears.
The appeal targets phone use while walking, identifying the group under discussion.
数 omits the already established referent: people using phones while walking. Their number remains unchanged despite the warnings, so option 4 is correct.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.sentences.4.vi: These days, it has become normal even for children to have mobile phones, so it seems the time has come to think of a better approach.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.sentences.4.gramm: In 子供も, emphasizes that even children have phones.
Nominalizes children having phones as the subject of 普通になっている.
Describes the resulting state of a change: this has become normal.
Gives the reason for the conclusion that a better approach is needed.
Expresses necessity or obligation: a better approach must be considered.
Indicates that the time or stage for the preceding action has arrived.
Expresses the writer's judgment: it seems the time to act has come.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.outline.1.note: Despite widespread posters and announcements, the number of people using phones while walking does not decrease. This is the referent of 数 in question 1.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.0.vi: As people grow older, their hair gradually turns white.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Expresses a natural consequence: hair turns white as people age.
An i-adjective changes to its -ku form before なる to express a change of state.
Describes a gradual change developing toward the present.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.1.vi: This is because the function that produces pigment for the hair gradually weakens.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Explains a cause: this is because…; it does not express purpose here.
Expresses a gradual change of state; 弱くなってくる means to gradually weaken.
作る modifies 働き: the function that produces pigment.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.2.vi: Before it grows out, hair is white, but the addition of melanin pigment makes it turn black or brown.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Before an action or event: before the hair grows out.
Provides explanatory background before a contrasting statement.
Passive form: 加えられる means to be added.
Nominalizes an event and expresses means or cause: through the addition of pigment.
Lists representative states or possibilities, such as turning black or brown.
Marks an explanation of how hair gets its color.
Question 3: rules out option 4; the passage says hair is white before it grows out.
Question 1: explains that melanin gives hair its color, clarifying the effect being discussed.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.3.vi: This melanin pigment is produced in cells called melanocytes, located at the roots of the hair.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Modifies a noun by its location: cells located at the hair roots.
Introduces a name: cells called melanocytes.
Polite passive form of 作る: is produced.
Question 1: identifies melanin production as the function of melanocytes, matching option 3. Their location at the roots also supports the inference for question 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.4.vi: These melanocytes can also be damaged by poor nutrition, lack of sleep, or illness, but as people age, their ability to produce melanin pigment steadily diminishes.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Gives a non-exhaustive list of examples: poor nutrition, lack of sleep, illness, and so on.
Here, causal で combines with も: also due to causes such as…
With a dictionary-form verb, expresses something that sometimes happens or may happen.
Links clauses while shifting the focus from causes of damage to the effects of aging.
Expresses a natural consequence of aging.
Describes an ongoing change over time: the ability to produce pigment gradually declines.
Question 3: the passage says pigment-producing ability declines, not that the number of melanocytes decreases as option 1 claims.
Question 3: this only says nutritional deficiency can cause damage; it does not claim that nutritious food increases melanin, as option 3 does.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.5.vi: Human hair comes in various colors, such as black, brown, and blond, depending on ethnicity. However, regardless of a group's hair color, aging causes hair to lose its ability to produce color and eventually turn white.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Expresses variation according to a factor: hair color varies by ethnicity.
Covers all possibilities: regardless of which ethnic group's hair color is involved.
Conditional form: 年を取れば means if or when people grow older.
To become unable to do something or lose the ability to do it.
Emphasizes an eventual result, with an undesirable nuance here: hair ends up turning white.
Question 3: directly supports option 2—hair turns white with age regardless of its original color.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.6.vi: Incidentally, because melanocytes are located at the roots of the hair, they cannot affect the portions that have not yet turned white.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Gives a reason: because melanocytes are located at the hair roots.
Expresses a change that has not happened yet: portions of hair that have not turned white.
に marks the target of the effect, while は highlights it: as for the portions that have not turned white.
Expresses inability: cannot exert an effect.
Question 1: in the explanation of melanocyte function, this effect refers to producing melanin pigment; choose option 3.
Question 2: according to the passage's reasoning, melanocytes at the roots cannot affect the portions that have not turned white, ruling out the story of all the hair turning white overnight.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.7.vi: Old tales include stories of hair turning completely white overnight because of a severe shock, but (　　　　).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Expresses a cause: because of a severe shock.
Indicates the time within which something occurs: 一晩で means in just one night.
Introduces the content of a story: a story saying that…
Signals a contrast; the blank should fit the argument rejecting the story of hair turning white overnight.
Question 2: が signals a rebuttal of the story just mentioned; together with the preceding sentence, it supports option 1: そんなことは、考えられません。
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.8.vi: (Note 1) Cell: here, a small structure within the body.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.8.gramm: A location clause modifies a noun: a structure located within the body.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.sentences.9.vi: (Note 2) Suffer damage: here, to become damaged.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.outline.0.label: Why hair turns white with age
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces hair whitening and its general cause: the weakening of pigment production.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.outline.1.label: How hair gets its color
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.outline.1.note: Melanin colors hair and is produced in melanocytes at the roots. Damage and aging affect pigment production. This explains the effect in question 1 and helps reject incorrect statements in question 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.outline.2.label: All hair colors turn white with age
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.outline.2.note: States that hair turns white with age regardless of ethnic differences in original hair color; directly supports option 2 in question 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.outline.3.label: Rejecting overnight whitening
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.outline.3.note: Shifts to the limits of the effects of melanocytes at the roots. This reasoning and the conjunction が require the blank to reject overnight whitening; question 2 takes option 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.outline.4.label: Vocabulary notes
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.outline.4.note: Explains the contextual meanings of 細胞 and ダメージを受ける.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.vietnamese:
As people grow older, their hair gradually turns white. This is because the function that produces pigment for the hair gradually weakens. Before it grows out, hair is white, but the addition of melanin pigment makes it turn black or brown. This melanin pigment is produced in cells called melanocytes, located at the roots of the hair. These melanocytes can also be damaged by poor nutrition, lack of sleep, or illness, but as people age, their ability to produce melanin pigment steadily diminishes.

Human hair comes in various colors, such as black, brown, and blond, depending on ethnicity. However, regardless of a group's hair color, aging causes hair to lose its ability to produce color and eventually turn white.

Incidentally, because melanocytes are located at the roots of the hair, they cannot affect the portions that have not yet turned white. Old tales include stories of hair turning completely white overnight because of a severe shock, but (　　　　).

(Note 1) Cell: here, a small structure within the body.

(Note 2) Suffer damage: here, to become damaged.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.0.vi: Bicycles are naturally used as a means of transportation, as well as for various purposes like dieting and sports, but it seems there are still few people who pay attention to bicycle safety.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Expresses 'not to mention A / of course A, but also B', establishing an obvious premise before adding further points.
Expresses subjective conjecture or impression based on observation ('it seems that / appears to be').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.1.vi: Before riding a bicycle, you should check the brakes and tires, and you should also wear a helmet just as when riding a motorcycle.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.1.vocab: in the same way, just like
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Used to give advice or suggest doing something ('should / had better do...').
Expresses similarity: 'just as...', 'in the same manner as...'.
Used to connect clauses to list parallel reasons or actions ('and..., as well as...').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.2.vi: Whether on a bicycle or a motorcycle, if you fall and hit your head you will suffer a severe injury, so it can be said that a helmet is like a seatbelt in a car.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Used to emphasize that the same applies regardless of which example is chosen ('whether A or B...').
Used for analogy: 'is like / something similar to...'.
Expresses a tentative conclusion: 'it could probably be said that...'.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.3.vi: Recently, accidents where cyclists become the perpetrators have been increasing, which is why bicycle insurance has been introduced.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Expresses an unintended action, regret, or an unfortunate outcome ('end up doing / unfortunately become').
Indicates an objective cause or reason ('because of / due to').
The phrase '自転車に乗っている人が加害者になってしまう事故' (accidents where the cyclist becomes the perpetrator) in sentence 3 is the direct antecedent of 'そんな事故' (such accidents) in sentence 4. Therefore, 'such accidents' refers specifically to accidents where the rider becomes the party at fault (加害者), explaining why option 2 (自分が加害者になってしまう事故) is correct. Other options describing injuries (option 1), lack of insurance (option 3), or financial strain (option 4) are merely accompanying circumstances or outcomes, not the antecedent of 'そんな事故'.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.4.vi: If you cause such an accident, depending on the circumstances you may end up suffering from a financial burden, so it is probably necessary to enroll in insurance in case of an emergency.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Expresses 'depending on the circumstances / in some cases'.
Indicates a resulting outcome or consequence ('end up having to / result in').
Expresses doing something in advance as preparation ('do beforehand').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.5.vi: Another thing is that for people who ride with children on their bicycles, I would also like them to pay attention to child seats.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Expresses a desire or request for someone else to do something ('want someone to do...').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.6.vi: Choosing a size that fits the child's body is of course essential, but while riding, children may also play pranks, move their bodies around, or fall asleep, so I would like riders to consider various situations and choose one that is both safe and good.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.6.vocab: there are times when, may also
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.6.gramm: States that something is obvious before emphasizing a further important point ('it goes without saying that..., but...').
Used to list representative actions or states ('doing things like... and...').
Expresses that something happens occasionally ('there are times when / sometimes...').
Expresses a desire or hope for someone to do something ('want/hope someone to do...').
The author explains that riders must be careful with child seats (②気をつけてほしい) because while riding, children are mischievous, move their bodies around ('あちこち体を動かしたり', meaning they do not stay still 'じっとしていない'), and may fall asleep ('眠ってしまうこともある', matching '寝てしまうこともある'). This explains why option 4 is correct. Option 1 merely restates carrying a child, option 2 is not mentioned in the text, and option 3 (children grow quickly) is not the stated reason.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.7.vi: Bicycles are convenient vehicles, but if not used properly, they become dangerous vehicles.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Negative conditional construction: 'if not..., then bad consequence'.
Expresses an unfortunate or undesirable outcome ('ends up becoming').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.8.vi: However, if each and every user thought of bicycles as being the same as motorcycles and the same as cars, I think they would immediately realize that all of them are necessary.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Indicates equivalence or similarity: 'the same as / identical to...'.
Used for explanatory emphasis, expressing personal thoughts or longing.
'③どれも全部' (all of them) summarizes all the bicycle safety precautions presented sequentially in the text: checking brakes and tires before riding, wearing helmets (para 1), obtaining bicycle insurance (para 2), and selecting safe child seats (para 3). Seatbelts in sentence 2 were only an analogy to illustrate the protective importance of helmets; bicycles do not have seatbelts, which invalidates option 4 and confirms option 3 as correct. Options 1 and 2 incorrectly list vehicles rather than safety measures.

In the concluding sentence, the author summarizes their central point: if every cyclist realizes that bicycles carry risks and responsibilities comparable to motorcycles or cars, they will immediately grasp the necessity of all safety precautions. This conveys the primary message that riders should treat bicycles like motor vehicles and prioritize safety, explaining why option 1 is correct. Option 2 focuses vaguely on skilled driving, option 3 misinterprets the text as watching out for cars/motorcycles on the road, and option 4 contradicts the opening sentence which acknowledges using bicycles for exercise and weight loss.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.sentences.9.vi: (Note) Suffer from financial burden: here, it means facing monetary difficulties (trouble with money due to compensation).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.0.label: Purposes of bicycle use and basic safety precautions
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.0.note: Bicycles are used for various purposes yet safety is often overlooked; riders should inspect brakes and tires and wear helmets like motorcyclists, as helmets protect lives similarly to car seatbelts.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.1.label: Liability in accidents and bicycle insurance
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.1.note: Accidents where cyclists cause harm to others are increasing, and causing one leads to heavy financial burdens, making bicycle insurance an essential precaution.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.2.label: Safety precautions when carrying children on child seats
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.2.note: Riders carrying children must carefully select an appropriate child seat because young children are active, fidgety, and prone to falling asleep during the ride.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.3.label: Treating bicycles like motor vehicles for comprehensive safety
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.3.note: Bicycles are convenient but dangerous if misused; if riders view bicycles like motorcycles or cars, they will understand that all mentioned safety precautions are truly necessary.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.4.label: Explanation of vocabulary in the text
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.4.note: Clarifies that 'suffering from financial burden' (経済的負担に苦しむ) means encountering financial hardship due to compensation liabilities.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.vietnamese:
Bicycles are naturally used as a means of transportation, as well as for various purposes such as dieting and sports; however, it seems that there are still few people who pay attention to bicycle safety. Before riding a bicycle, you should check the brakes and tires, and you should also wear a helmet just as when riding a motorcycle. Whether on a bicycle or a motorcycle, if you fall and hit your head you will suffer a severe injury, so it can be said that a helmet is like a seatbelt in a car.

Recently, accidents in which cyclists become the perpetrators have been increasing, which is why bicycle insurance has been introduced. If you were to cause such an accident, depending on the situation you might end up struggling with a financial burden, so enrolling in insurance in advance for emergencies is likely necessary as well.

Furthermore, for people who ride bicycles carrying children, I would also like them to pay attention to child seats. Choosing a size that fits the child's body is of course essential, but while riding, children may play pranks, move their bodies around, or fall asleep, so I want riders to consider various situations and choose a seat that is both safe and good.

A bicycle is a convenient vehicle, but if not used properly, it turns into a dangerous one. However, if each individual user thought of bicycles as being the same as motorcycles and the same as cars, I believe they would immediately realize that all of these measures are necessary.

(Note) Suffer from financial burden: here, it means facing monetary hardship.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.0.vi: This is a text message sent by mobile phone.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.0.gramm: A formal written equivalent of ～だ／～です, meaning “is.”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.2.vi: The sample from the Kawasaki factory was finished late last night.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Expresses that a product is completed; the completed item is marked by が.
Polite past form, indicating that completion of the sample has already occurred.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.3.vi: Someone from the factory will bring us the sample by 10 a.m. today.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Marks a deadline: “by”; here, the sample will be delivered by 10 a.m.
A verb’s ます-stem + に来る expresses coming to do something; 届けに来る means coming to deliver.
Indicates that someone performs an action benefiting the speaker or the speaker’s group.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.4.vi: I am heading to the Shizuoka factory by Shinkansen, so please check the sample when it arrives and, if there are no problems, place the order right away.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Marks the means of transport: 新幹線で means “by Shinkansen.”
Expresses an action in progress: the sender is on the way to the Shizuoka factory.
Gives the reason for the following request: the sender is traveling and asks the recipient to handle the sample.
Marks a condition or a future occasion; 届いたら here means “when the sample arrives.”
Links actions in sequence: check the sample, then order if it is satisfactory.
Conditional form of ない: “if there is no…”; 問題がなければ means “if there are no problems.”
Requests that an action be done in preparation for what follows; here, placing the order once the sample is confirmed to be satisfactory.
This is the main request to Yamashita: check the Kawasaki sample and order immediately if there are no problems. It matches option 4; the other details provide context or concern a later discussion.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.5.vi: I am concerned because the Shizuoka bags look likely to be delayed, but I think I can be back at the office by 4 p.m., so let’s discuss after I return whether to start sales with just the Kawasaki bags.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Singles out one side in contrast with another: here, the Shizuoka bags as compared with the Kawasaki bags.
A verb’s ます-stem + そうだ expresses an apparent likelihood: the bags look likely to be delayed.
Gives reasons: the likely delay causes concern, and the expected return by 4 p.m. allows a later discussion.
Connects clauses with a mild contrast or transition: the sender is concerned but expects to return for a discussion.
に marks a time and は emphasizes it; here, the sender expects to be back by 4 p.m.
戻れる is the potential form of 戻る: “can return.”
Expresses the speaker’s opinion or expectation rather than certainty.
Expresses a restriction: with only the Kawasaki bags.
Makes an embedded question the topic: whether to begin sales.
Expresses sequence: discuss the matter after returning.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.6.vi: Thank you for taking care of this.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.sentences.6.gramm: A conventional expression concluding a request; お願いします is omitted in this message.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.outline.0.label: Message type and recipient
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.outline.0.note: Identifies the text as an SMS and opens with a greeting to Yamashita.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.outline.1.label: Kawasaki sample completed
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.outline.1.note: The sample was completed last night and will arrive by 10 a.m. today.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.outline.2.label: Check the sample and order
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.outline.2.note: As Morita is traveling to the Shizuoka factory, Yamashita is asked to check the sample and order immediately if it is satisfactory. This is the main purpose of the message and matches option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.outline.3.label: Discuss the sales launch after returning
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.outline.3.note: The Shizuoka bags look likely to be delayed. Morita expects to return by 4 p.m. and then discuss whether to launch sales with only the Kawasaki bags.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.outline.4.label: Closing and signature
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.outline.4.note: Closes with a request for cooperation and Morita’s signature.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t44-p1.vietnamese:
This is a text message sent by mobile phone.

Good morning, Yamashita.

The sample from the Kawasaki factory was finished late last night. Someone from the factory will bring us the sample by 10 a.m. today. I am heading to the Shizuoka factory by Shinkansen, so please check the sample when it arrives and, if there are no problems, place the order right away. I am concerned because the Shizuoka bags look likely to be delayed, but I think I can be back at the office by 4 p.m., so let’s discuss after I return whether to start sales with just the Kawasaki bags. Thank you for taking care of this.

Morita
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.0.vi: This notice is posted in the lobby of the Japanese language school.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.0.gramm: States where something has been posted and remains. ～てある describes the resulting state of an intentional action.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.2.vi: A Christmas party will be held on Saturday, December 20, in Room 503.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Hold an activity at a location; で marks where the activity takes place.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.3.vi: The party runs from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., but you may join after it has started.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Indicates a time span from a starting point to an ending point.
Connects mildly contrasting statements: the hours are fixed, but arriving later is allowed.
Expresses permission: it is fine to do something.
Joining after the party starts is allowed, so arriving by 11 a.m. is not required; this rules out option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.4.vi: The participation fee is 500 yen, and drinks and light refreshments will be served.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.4.gramm: で is the connective form of です, linking the fee information to the next statement.
When referring to food and drinks at an event, this means they are served.
Participants must pay a 500-yen fee; this is the common requirement in option 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.5.vi: There will be a gift exchange that day, so please prepare and bring one gift worth about 1,000 yen.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.5.gramm: As; here, the gift exchange is held as one of the party activities.
Gives the reason for the following request: a gift is needed because there will be a gift exchange.
Approximately; modifies the following noun, here a gift worth about 1,000 yen.
Links actions in sequence and makes a request: please prepare and bring.
Participants are asked to bring one gift worth about 1,000 yen; the next sentence allows singing instead.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.6.vi: Anyone who finds preparing a gift troublesome may sing a song instead.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.6.gramm: A phrase modifying 人: a person who finds something troublesome. 面倒 is a な-adjective.
Permits an alternative: participants may sing instead of preparing a gift.
A gift and a song are alternatives, so bringing a gift is not compulsory for everyone. Together with the fee requirement, this supports option 1 and rules out option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.7.vi: We hope to make this an enjoyable party where many students can get to know one another, so please do join us.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Expresses ability or possibility; 交流できる means being able to interact.
Expresses a desire to create a certain state: hoping to make the party enjoyable.
Gives the reason for the invitation to participate.
An enthusiastic invitation or request: please do something.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.8.vi: We are also looking for three volunteers to help prepare for the party.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Describes someone doing something for the speaker’s benefit; here, helping the organizers prepare.
Indicates ongoing recruitment or a current call for people to fill a role.
Preparation help is a separately recruited volunteer role, not a requirement for all participants; this rules out option 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.9.vi: Anyone interested should contact Sugiyama at the first-floor reception desk.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.sentences.9.gramm: An abbreviated notice-style expression omitting a request such as ‘please contact.’ まで marks the contact person or destination.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.outline.0.label: Christmas party notice
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the notice posted in the school lobby and its title.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.outline.1.label: Time, location, and fee
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.outline.1.note: The party takes place on December 20 in Room 503 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.; joining later is allowed. The fee is 500 yen, with drinks and light refreshments provided.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.outline.2.label: Prepare a gift or a song
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.outline.2.note: Participants should prepare a gift worth about 1,000 yen or sing instead if preparing a gift is troublesome. The organizers encourage students to join and socialize.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.outline.3.label: Volunteer recruitment
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.outline.3.note: Three volunteers are being recruited separately to help with preparations; interested students should contact Sugiyama at the first-floor reception desk.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t45-p1.vietnamese:
This notice is posted in the lobby of the Japanese language school.

Christmas Party Notice

A Christmas party will be held on Saturday, December 20, in Room 503. The party runs from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., but you may join after it has started. The participation fee is 500 yen, and drinks and light refreshments will be served. There will be a gift exchange that day, so please prepare and bring one gift worth about 1,000 yen. Anyone who finds preparing a gift troublesome may sing a song instead. We hope to make this an enjoyable party where many students can get to know one another, so please do join us.

We are also looking for three volunteers to help prepare for the party. Anyone interested should contact Sugiyama at the first-floor reception desk.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.0.vi: While we were eating dinner, Dad said, “Shall we get a dog?”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.0.gramm: While doing something; here, while the family is eating dinner.
The volitional form plus か suggests doing something together: “Shall we…?”
Reports what someone said, with the quoted content before と.
The suggestion of getting a dog prompts the siblings’ smiles in the next sentence, supporting the inference that they had wanted one (Question 1).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.1.vi: My younger sister and I looked at each other and smiled happily.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Links actions in sequence: looking at each other and then smiling.
Their shared delight immediately after Dad’s suggestion implies that they had wanted a dog. The prior wish is inferred from the situation, not stated explicitly (Question 1, answer 3).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.2.vi: Seeing that, Mom said, “Wait a moment. If we get a dog, make sure you take proper care of it.”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Sets a condition based on the preceding suggestion: if we are going to get a dog…
A sentence-final て-form can express an informal request, as in 待って.
Expresses a request with an insistent reminder and an expectation of agreement.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.3.vi: When Dad asked, “Do you think you can do it?”, we replied, “Yes.”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Expresses wondering or a gentle question: “I wonder if…”
A clause quoting a question modifies a noun: the father who asks whether they can do it.
Answers someone with quoted words; に marks the recipient and と marks the response.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.4.vi: A week later, Dad brought a puppy home.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Follows a period of time to mean “later,” here one week later.
Brings a person or animal back to the speaker’s location.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.5.vi: The puppy had white fur, but Dad looked at its big black eyes and said, “Let’s name it ‘Kuro.’”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Connects contrasting ideas: the fur is white, but Dad chooses クロ, a name suggesting black.
Links い-adjectives: 大きい becomes 大きくて; the eyes are both big and black.
Indicates simultaneous actions by the same subject: Dad speaks while looking at the puppy’s eyes.
Proposes a choice or decision: “Let’s choose…,” here choosing a name.
Establishes that the puppy’s fur is white, ruling out options 1 and 2 (Question 2).
Both 大きくて and 黒い describe the eyes: they are big and black, confirming answer 4 rather than small eyes (Question 2).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.6.vi: Our lives changed after Kuro arrived.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Links an event with a subsequent change: Kuro arrives and the family’s life changes.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.7.vi: To give Kuro two walks a day and feed him, the four of us divided up the tasks and assigned responsibilities.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.7.gramm: The causative of する: have or let someone do something; here, have the dog take walks.
Expresses purpose: to provide walks and food.
After a group, indicates who acts together: all four family members.
Continuative forms such as させ and 分け link actions, similarly to させて and 分けて.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.8.vi: My younger sister and I began getting up early, and Dad also began coming home early to walk Kuro.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Expresses a change in habit: beginning to get up early or come home early regularly.
A noun plus のために expresses purpose: for Kuro’s walks.
Only the younger sister and narrator are said to start getting up early, not the whole family, ruling out option 1 in Question 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.9.vi: There were difficulties, such as walks on rainy days and early-morning feeding, but after Kuro arrived, the family also talked more.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.9.gramm: Gives a non-exhaustive list of examples: rainy-day walks, early feeding, and so on.
Acknowledges that difficulties existed before introducing a positive aspect.
Marks an additional change: family conversation increased too.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.10.vi: Whenever the person in charge could not care for Kuro, we made sure someone else took over.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.10.gram: A clause modifies a noun: 係になった者 means the person assigned responsibility.
Cannot do something, whether due to ability or circumstances; here, cannot care for the dog.
Sets the situation in which the following response applies: when the assigned person is unavailable.
Describes making arrangements or adopting a practice to ensure something happens: someone else takes over.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.10.keys: Taking over for one another illustrates mutual support and consideration, reinforcing answer 4 in Question 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.11.vi: Our family’s life came to revolve around Kuro.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.11.gram: Becomes the center; here, the family’s routine is organized around Kuro.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.11.keys: Kuro becoming central to daily life does not mean everyone thinks only about Kuro. The final sentence rules out option 2 in Question 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.12.vi: And everyone in the family began thinking about one another, rather than just themselves.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.12.gram: Not only…; indicates that their concern extends beyond themselves.
Describes an established change: they began considering one another.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.sentences.12.keys: Rejects the idea of thinking only about oneself, ruling out option 3 in Question 3.
Directly states the key change: everyone began considering one another, matching answer 4 in Question 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.outline.0.label: The suggestion to get a dog
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.outline.0.note: Dad suggests getting a dog, delighting the siblings. Mom reminds them to care for it properly, and they agree.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.outline.1.label: The puppy and the name Kuro
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.outline.1.note: A week later, Dad brings home a puppy with white fur and big black eyes. Looking at its eyes, he chooses the name Kuro.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.outline.2.label: Changes in daily routines
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.outline.2.note: The family shares the care duties. The siblings get up early and Dad comes home early. Despite the work involved, the family talks more.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.outline.3.label: Learning to consider one another
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.outline.3.note: Family members take over when the assigned person is unavailable. Life revolves around Kuro, and everyone begins considering others as well as themselves.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t47-p1.vietnamese:
While we were eating dinner, Dad said, “Shall we get a dog?” My younger sister and I looked at each other and smiled happily. Seeing that, Mom said, “Wait a moment. If we get a dog, make sure you take proper care of it.” When Dad asked, “Do you think you can do it?”, we replied, “Yes.”

A week later, Dad brought a puppy home. The puppy had white fur, but Dad looked at its big black eyes and said, “Let’s name it ‘Kuro.’”

Our lives changed after Kuro arrived. To give Kuro two walks a day and feed him, the four of us divided up the tasks and assigned responsibilities. My younger sister and I began getting up early, and Dad also began coming home early to walk Kuro. There were difficulties, such as walks on rainy days and early-morning feeding, but after Kuro arrived, the family also talked more. Whenever the person in charge could not care for Kuro, we made sure someone else took over. Our family’s life came to revolve around Kuro. And everyone in the family began thinking about one another, rather than just themselves.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.0.vi: For 16 years, I have kept lying to my husband.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Verb stem + 続けている describes an action continuing up to the present.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.1.vi: That is because I keep saying I love strawberry cake, even though I dislike it.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.1.gramm: と marks the content of what is said: saying that one loves something.
Expresses an action repeated or continued up to the present.
Explains the reason for the preceding statement: that is because…
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.2.vi: It happened when we were going out for a drive on our first date.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Means to go out for an activity; ドライブに出かける means to go out for a drive.
Sets the scene for a recollection: it was when…
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.3.vi: When I got into my husband's car, I noticed a wonderful smell.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Introduces something noticed upon performing an action: when I got into the car…
Used for sensory impressions such as smells and sounds; 匂いがする means there is a smell.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.4.vi: When I said, “Wow, that smells nice,” my husband pointed to a cake box on the back seat.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Means when someone said…, then…; the first と quotes speech, and the second introduces the response.
A relative clause modifying a noun: the box that was on the back seat.
Marks a means or instrument: 指で means with a finger.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.5.vi: When I looked inside, I saw that the box was full of strawberry cake.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Introduces a discovery made after an action: upon looking, the narrator found…
Expresses filling a space or container completely: filling the whole box.
Here it describes a past state: the cake was already in the box.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.6.vi: “I didn't know what kind you liked,” my husband said anxiously, and his face in profile looked as adorable as a young boy's.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.6.gramm: In どういうの, の stands in for the noun referring to a kind of cake.
An embedded question: not knowing what kind someone likes.
Gives a reason; the resulting action is left unstated in the husband's speech.
Describes apparent emotion accompanying an action: speaking with a worried look.
Makes a comparison: as adorable as a young boy.
His concern about her preferences supports the view that he is thoughtful in Question 3.
His worried, endearing appearance makes her reluctant to disappoint him; together with the next sentence, this supports option 2 in Question 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.7.vi: Seeing him like that, I blurted out, “①Thank you! I love strawberry cake!”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Links seeing her husband's appearance to her subsequent verbal reaction.
A conversational topic marker similar to は: as for strawberry cake…
An informal explanatory ending after a noun or な-adjective, here conveying warm emphasis.
Expresses an unintended action, here blurting out something that did not reflect her real preference.
Adds an explanatory tone to the account of how the lie began.
そんな姿 refers to her husband's worried, endearing appearance in the preceding sentence, indicating that she wanted to avoid disappointing him rather than reacting to the smell or quantity of cake.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.8.vi: Looking back now, perhaps I should have told the truth.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.8.gramm: In 今思えば, it introduces a present reflection: looking back now…
Expresses regret over an action not taken: I should have told the truth.
Softens a judgment by expressing uncertainty: perhaps that was the case.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.9.vi: Even now, whenever there is an occasion, my husband always brings home strawberry cake.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.9.gramm: In 今でも, it emphasizes continuation into the present: even now; still.
Describes a condition regularly followed by the same action: whenever there is an occasion, he buys cake.
Here it means doing something and returning with the result: buying cake and bringing it back.
He remembers what he believes she likes and brings it home whenever there is an occasion, supporting option 1 in Question 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.10.vi: Strawberry cake is a token of my husband's love.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.10.gram: Noun + なのだ explains the significance of the husband's cake purchases.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.10.keys: She regards the cake as an expression of his love, showing that she sees him as caring and thoughtful; this is the clearest evidence for Question 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.11.vi: Many times afterward, I tried to tell him the truth, but even now I remain unable to say it.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.11.gram: Volitional verb + とする means to try or intend to act; 言おうとした means tried or intended to say.
Emphasizes that there were many occasions when the action occurred.
Links contrasting ideas: she repeatedly tried to speak but still could not.
Means remaining in a state of not doing or being unable to do something; 言えない is the negative potential form of 言う.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.12.gram: Means to notice or realize something; に marks what is noticed.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.13.vi: Wouldn't it be enough to turn the lie into the truth?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.13.voca: if I were to turn it into
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.13.gram: Means to make something into something else: turning a lie into the truth.
Here it emphasizes carrying an action through completely, rather than doing it accidentally.
A tentative suggestion phrased as a self-directed question, with an ending such as ないか omitted: wouldn't it be enough to…?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.13.keys: Introduces her new solution: making her claim to love strawberry cake true; the next sentence specifies this for Question 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.14.vi: Wouldn't it be enough to actually come to like strawberry cake?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.14.gram: Means to come to like something; を marks the object of affection in this construction.
Suggests a solution to oneself: wouldn't it be enough to…?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.14.keys: This is what そうしよう in the next sentence refers to: deciding to come to like strawberry cake, option 2 in Question 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.15.vi: Resolving in my heart, “②That's it, I'll do that,” I have started eating strawberry cake instead of lunch every day.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.15.gram: Means to resolve inwardly to do something; しよう is the volitional form of する.
Means instead of…; here, strawberry cake replaces lunch.
Verb stem + はじめている indicates an action that has begun and is continuing.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.15.keys: そう refers back to actually coming to like the cake. Her central decision is to like it; eating it daily is the means of doing so.
This may tempt readers toward option 1 in Question 2, but it describes the action taken to achieve the goal stated in the preceding sentence.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.16.vi: It is curious how everything tastes good when you are hungry.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.16.voca: if it becomes empty; if hungry
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.16.gram: Marks a condition: if or when one is hungry.
With a question word, expresses an unrestricted range: 何でも means anything.
The く-form of an い-adjective + なる expresses change: おいしくなる means to become delicious.
Gives the reason for finding it curious: everything tastes good when one is hungry.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.17.vi: The day when my lie becomes the truth is drawing near.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.sentences.17.gram: Noun + になる means to become…; here, the lie becomes the truth.
The preceding clause modifies 日: the day when the lie becomes the truth.
Expresses an ongoing process: that day is drawing nearer.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.outline.0.label: A lie lasting 16 years
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.outline.0.note: The narrator admits that she has kept claiming to love strawberry cake despite disliking it.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.outline.1.label: A lie born from his thoughtfulness
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.outline.1.note: On their first date, her husband brought cake but worried about her preferences. Seeing his anxious, endearing expression, she said she loved it to avoid disappointing him.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.outline.2.label: Strawberry cake as a token of love
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.outline.2.note: Her husband still buys the cake whenever there is an occasion. She sees it as an expression of his love and remains unable to tell the truth despite repeated attempts.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.outline.3.label: An idea for making the lie true
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.outline.3.note: She finds a new solution: actually coming to like strawberry cake. This is the idea referred to by そうしよう.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.outline.4.label: Eating the cake to learn to like it
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.outline.4.note: She starts eating the cake instead of lunch every day to carry out her resolution. Since hunger makes everything taste good, she believes the day she truly likes it is approaching.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t48-p1.vietnamese:
For 16 years, I have kept lying to my husband. That is because I keep saying I love strawberry cake, even though I dislike it.

It happened when we were going out for a drive on our first date. When I got into my husband's car, I noticed a wonderful smell. When I said, “Wow, that smells nice,” he pointed to a cake box on the back seat. I looked inside and saw that the box was full of strawberry cake. “I didn't know what kind you liked,” he said anxiously, and his face in profile looked as adorable as a young boy's. Seeing him like that, I blurted out, “①Thank you! I love strawberry cake!”

Looking back now, perhaps I should have told the truth. Even now, whenever there is an occasion, my husband always brings home strawberry cake. Strawberry cake is a token of his love. Many times afterward, I tried to tell him the truth, but even now I remain unable to say it.

Recently, however, I realized something. Wouldn't it be enough to turn the lie into the truth? Wouldn't it be enough to actually come to like strawberry cake? Resolving in my heart, “②That's it, I'll do that,” I have started eating strawberry cake instead of lunch every day. It is curious how everything tastes good when you are hungry. The day when my lie becomes the truth is drawing near.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.0.vi: Benches on station platforms in Japan normally face the train doors, but on the platforms at Shin-Osaka Station, they face the direction in which trains travel.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.0.gramm: A conversational contraction of ～ている; 向かい合ってる means 向かい合っている.
Doing something is normal; の nominalizes the preceding clause.
Presents background before a contrast: normally…, but…
Facing or heading in a particular direction.
The passive with ～ている describes the resulting state of being placed.
Introduces the bench arrangement referred to by これ in sentence 2; sentence 1 clarifies it.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.1.vi: In other words, the benches are positioned at a right angle of 90 degrees to the platform rather than parallel to it.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Marks a reference point for a relationship or comparison; here, the benches' angle relative to the platform.
Not…, but…; contrasts two bench arrangements.
Describes an existing state or arrangement.
Direct evidence for question 1: これ refers to placing the benches perpendicular to the platform, matching option 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.2.vi: ① This is to protect passengers who are drunk from accidents.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Protect someone or something from a danger.
Explains a purpose: it is in order to…
これ refers back to the arrangement described in the previous two sentences, not to adding benches.
States the safety purpose, supporting the reason asked for in question 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.3.vi: ② According to a recent survey, accidents involving falls from platforms are increasing year by year.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.3.gramm: According to…; identifies the source of information.
With 増える, expresses an ongoing upward trend.
A survey finding; it says accidents increase annually, not that every year has over 100 cases as option 2 of question 2 claims.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.4.vi: Of those accidents, reportedly as many as 132 this year involved passengers who were drunk.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Modifies a noun to indicate a cause or the party responsible.
After a quantity, emphasizes that it is surprisingly large: as many as 132 cases.
Follows a plain form to report information heard from another source.
Identifies a subset of accidents; it does not support option 1 of question 2, which attributes all accidents to drunkenness.
The figure 132 applies to this year, not every year, helping eliminate option 2 of question 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.5.vi: Furthermore, an investigation into the behavior of drunk passengers revealed that 60% of those who fell had stood up from a bench, walked straight ahead, and continued straight off the platform.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Here, marks a factual discovery made after investigating.
Among…; specifies the group to which a proportion applies.
Links actions in sequence: standing up, walking straight, and falling.
It was discovered that…; こと nominalizes the finding.
Decisive evidence for question 2, option 4: 60% is more than half, and the stated behavior is standing up and walking straight, not sleeping on a bench.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.6.vi: At Shin-Osaka Station, staff considered what they could do to reduce accidents.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Expresses a condition; どうしたら asks what action would achieve the desired result.
Embeds a question: consider how or whether…
減らせる is the potential form of 減らす: can reduce.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.7.vi: They also considered installing doors between the platform and the trains to keep passengers from falling, but that would cost hundreds of millions of yen.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.7.gramm: So that…does not happen; expresses a preventive purpose.
Also considered doing…, but…; こと nominalizes the action.
After a quantity, emphasizes its large size: costs reaching hundreds of millions of yen.
Here, conveys an undesirable result: incurring a very large cost.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.8.vi: Various other ideas were proposed, but they decided to change the direction of the benches.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Connects contrasting clauses: several ideas arose, but this option was chosen.
Expresses a deliberate decision to do something.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.9.vi: With this arrangement, even if passengers stand up from a bench and walk straight ahead, they will not fall off the platform, and it costs nothing.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.9.gramm: If this arrangement is used…; takes the bench reorientation as the condition.
Even if…; walking straight still does not lead to the described fall.
Here, denies that an event will occur: they will not fall. It does not mean 'there is no need to'.
Lists advantages or reasons: improved safety and no expense.
Main evidence for question 3, option 2: the arrangement improves safety at no cost. It addresses walking straight from a bench, not the elimination of every kind of accident.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.10.vi: Recently, it is reported that this is no longer limited to Shin-Osaka Station: ③ more and more stations have been changing the orientation of their benches.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.10.gram: Not only…; extends the scope beyond Shin-Osaka Station.
Describes a change that has developed up to the present and is continuing.
Reports information from another source: reportedly…
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.11.vi: As this example shows, a slight change in how we look at things often leads to good ideas.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.11.gram: Expresses a condition: changing one's perspective can produce good ideas.
It is not uncommon for…; negates 'few' to indicate that something happens fairly often.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.11.keys: States the general message for question 4, option 3: changing one's perspective can generate good ideas; the station benches are an example.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.12.vi: If we take an interest in and ask questions about the various things we use in our lives, might our everyday lives become better?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.12.gram: Take an interest in and have questions about…; や gives a non-exhaustive list.
States a condition under which life could improve.
An い-adjective changes to ～く before なる to express a change of state.
Offers a tentative opinion and invites agreement: might it not be that…?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.sentences.12.keys: Completes the main message in question 4: curiosity, questioning, and a change of perspective can improve life, rather than improvement in life first producing ideas.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.outline.0.label: An unusual bench arrangement
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces benches positioned perpendicular to the platform at Shin-Osaka Station to protect drunk passengers. これ refers to this arrangement.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.outline.1.label: Survey findings on accidents
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.outline.1.note: Accidents are increasing annually. Investigation of drunk passengers' behavior revealed that 60% of those who fell had stood up from a bench and walked straight ahead.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.outline.2.label: A simple, inexpensive solution
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.outline.2.note: Installing doors would be expensive, so the station chose to reorient its benches. This prevents the described type of fall at no cost, explaining its adoption by more stations.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.outline.3.label: A new perspective can improve life
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.outline.3.note: From the bench example, the author concludes that changing our perspective and taking an inquisitive interest in everyday objects can generate good ideas and improve life.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t49-p1.vietnamese:
Benches on station platforms in Japan normally face the train doors, but on the platforms at Shin-Osaka Station, they face the direction in which trains travel. In other words, the benches are positioned at a right angle of 90 degrees to the platform rather than parallel to it. ① This is to protect passengers who are drunk from accidents. ② According to a recent survey, accidents involving falls from platforms are increasing year by year. Of those accidents, reportedly as many as 132 this year involved passengers who were drunk. Furthermore, an investigation into the behavior of drunk passengers revealed that 60% of those who fell had stood up from a bench, walked straight ahead, and continued straight off the platform.

At Shin-Osaka Station, staff considered what they could do to reduce accidents. They also considered installing doors between the platform and the trains to keep passengers from falling, but that would cost hundreds of millions of yen. Various other ideas were proposed, but they decided to change the direction of the benches. With this arrangement, even if passengers stand up from a bench and walk straight ahead, they will not fall off the platform, and it costs nothing. Recently, it is reported that this is no longer limited to Shin-Osaka Station: ③ more and more stations have been changing the orientation of their benches.

As this example shows, a slight change in how we look at things often leads to good ideas. If we take an interest in and ask questions about the various things we use in our lives, might our everyday lives become better?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.1.vi: Sometimes I plan carefully and travel abroad; other times, I casually board a train and try getting off at a station whose name appeals to me.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Sometimes one does one thing, and at other times another; presents different possible behaviors.
Try doing something to experience it or see what happens; here, getting off the train.
A preceding clause modifies a noun: 気に入った modifies 名前.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.2.vi: There, I enjoy the town’s scents and scenery and try wandering around while listening closely to the sounds that reach me.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.2.gramm: In 聞こえてくる, indicates sounds reaching the listener.
Expresses two simultaneous actions: listening while walking.
Try doing something; here, walking around to explore.
Question 2: illustrates experiencing a destination through smell, sight, and hearing.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.3.vi: In the towns I reach in this way, there is something I always do.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Here, expresses a repeated or habitual action.
Here, means “there is something that…,” rather than the experience pattern ～たことがある.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.4.vi: That is to photograph the dishes that catch my attention there and try tasting them.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Record or preserve something in a photograph.
Try performing an action; 味見をしてみる means to try tasting.
Nominalizes an action with こと to explain “it is doing…”; である is a formal written equivalent of だ.
Question 2: tasting local dishes is part of experiencing a destination through the senses.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.5.vi: Even if it is yakisoba that I regularly eat, when I taste it in a town I am visiting for the first time, it (　　　　).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Even assuming…; introduces a concessive hypothetical condition. だったとしても means “even if it were…”.
食べている describes a regular eating habit, rather than eating at this moment.
初めて行った modifies 街, and 口にした modifies それ.
Question 1: even though the dish is familiar, the following clause must express an experience different from the usual one.
Question 1: tasting the dish in a new town makes the experience distinctive, supporting option 1, “certainly not the usual taste.”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.6.vi: In this way, wherever I travel, I make a point of using all five senses to experience and enjoy the place.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.6.gramm: In 五感を使って, indicates the means: by using the five senses.
Make a conscious effort to maintain a practice or habit.
Question 2: this is the direct referent of そんなこと in the next sentence, matching option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.7.vi: As I repeated these experiences, I began to suddenly remember those towns while doing something else.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.7.gramm: While repeatedly doing something, a change gradually occurs, often unintentionally.
While an action is in progress.
Expresses the emergence of a new state or pattern; here, spontaneously recalling places visited.
Question 2: refers to using the senses to experience and enjoy destinations, as stated in the preceding sentence.
Question 3: memories arise suddenly, rather than through deliberate efforts to avoid forgetting as in option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.8.vi: This invariably happens when I eat something, smell a scent, or hear music playing in the streets.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Lists representative actions; they need not all happen together.
When an action occurs or has occurred; here, identifies when memories are triggered.
Question 3: hearing music in the streets triggers memories and supports option 3; prior familiarity is inferred from the recollection context.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.9.vi: When I eat curry rice full of large chunks, or catch the smell of wind that suggests rain is about to fall, I suddenly recall a town I visited long ago and feel an indescribable nostalgia.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.sentences.9.gramm: In a noun-modifying clause, の can replace が as the subject marker, as in 具の…入った and 雨の降りだしそうな.
Attaches to a verb stem to express the start of an action; 降りだす means to start raining or falling.
Seems about to…; そうな is used before a noun. Here, the wind suggests imminent rain.
A fixed expression for a feeling that is difficult to put into words.
Come to experience a particular feeling.
Question 3: the trigger is smelling rain-bearing wind, rather than merely seeing dark skies or impending rain as in option 2.
Question 3: confirms that nostalgia arises when sensory impressions spontaneously bring back a previously visited town.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.outline.0.label: Enjoying travel and exploration
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.outline.0.note: The writer enjoys both planned and spontaneous trips, taking in each destination’s scenery, scents, and sounds.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.outline.1.label: Tasting food in a new place
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.outline.1.note: The writer always photographs and tastes dishes that attract attention. Even familiar food feels different when eaten somewhere new.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.outline.2.label: Experiencing places with all five senses
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.outline.2.note: This sentence summarizes the writer’s approach to travel and supplies the referent of そんなこと in the following sentence.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.outline.3.label: Sensory triggers for memories and nostalgia
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.outline.3.note: Repeated sensory experiences allow tastes, smells, and music to later trigger spontaneous memories of visited places and feelings of nostalgia.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t59-p1.vietnamese:
I like traveling. Sometimes I plan carefully and travel abroad; other times, I casually board a train and try getting off at a station whose name appeals to me. There, I enjoy the town’s scents and scenery and try wandering around while listening closely to the sounds that reach me.

In the towns I reach in this way, there is something I always do. That is to photograph the dishes that catch my attention there and try tasting them. Even if it is yakisoba that I regularly eat, when I taste it in a town I am visiting for the first time, it (　　　　).

In this way, wherever I travel, I make a point of using all five senses to experience and enjoy the place.

As I repeated these experiences, I began to suddenly remember those towns while doing something else. This invariably happens when I eat something, smell a scent, or hear music playing in the streets. When I eat curry rice full of large chunks, or catch the smell of wind that suggests rain is about to fall, I suddenly recall a town I visited long ago and feel an indescribable nostalgia.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.0.vi: It has been five years since the law stipulated that seat belts must also be worn in the rear seats when driving on expressways.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Indicates a time or situation: when driving on expressways.
Emphasizes inclusion: even in the rear seats.
Be required to do something by a rule; 決められる is the passive of 決める.
A certain amount of time has passed since an event.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.1.vi: If you happen to be caught by the police without wearing a seat belt, only points are deducted from your driver's license; there is no fine.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Do something without doing another action; する becomes せずに.
Introduces a hypothetical case: if caught by the police.
Limits the consequence to one thing: only losing points.
Direct evidence for Question 1, option 1: even if caught, people do not have to pay a fine.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.2.vi: Perhaps because of that, people who wear seat belts in the rear seats on ordinary roads reportedly ①still account for only 33 percent of the total.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Perhaps because of…; suggests a possible cause of an undesirable result.
A formal equivalent of で, indicating a place or context.
Only…; emphasizes a smaller quantity than expected.
Reportedly; presents information obtained from another source.
その refers to the absence of a fine in the preceding sentence, linking it to the low usage rate; evidence for Question 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.3.vi: However, just because there is no fine does not mean there is a valid reason to go without a seat belt.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Just because… does not mean…; rejects the inference that no fine means no need for a seat belt.
Do not have to do something; it is acceptable not to do it.
Does not constitute a valid reason for something.
Evidence for Question 3, option 2: the need to wear a seat belt rests on its value, regardless of whether a fine applies.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.4.vi: If an accident is caused while seat belts are not being worn, the fatality rate in the rear seats rises to a striking 4.8 times as high.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Without doing something before or during another event.
In the event that…; sets up an accident scenario.
Reach as much as…; も emphasizes a surprisingly large figure.
Adds explanatory emphasis or supports the preceding argument.
Supports Questions 2 and 3: the consequence of not wearing a belt demonstrates its value in protecting life.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.5.vi: In contrast, if you are wearing a seat belt, the possibility of dying is almost eliminated, even if you suffer an injury such as a broken bone.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.5.vocab: in relation to; in contrast to
even if it becomes; even if one ends up
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.5.gramm: In contrast to…; それに対して shifts from not wearing a belt to wearing one.
If in a certain state; here, the state of wearing a seat belt.
Even if a situation such as… occurs; a broken bone is an example of an injury.
Something almost ceases to happen; this does not claim it can never happen.
Direct evidence for Question 2, option 2: wearing a belt reduces the possibility of dying in an accident.
Rules out Question 2, option 3: injuries such as broken bones can still occur while wearing a belt.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.6.vi: This fact alone should be a sufficient reason to ②wear a seat belt on ordinary roads.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Even just…; emphasizes that a single piece of evidence is sufficient.
A sufficient reason to do…; の nominalizes the verb, and に marks the action for which the reason is sufficient.
Expresses a considered judgment and invites the reader's agreement.
このこと refers to the greatly reduced possibility of death in the preceding sentence, identifying the reason asked about in Question 2.
Supports Question 3: the author advocates wearing belts on ordinary roads because they protect life.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.7.vi: Of course, some people cannot wear seat belts because of various circumstances.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Marks a cause: because of various circumstances.
Cannot do something; here, cannot wear a seat belt.
There are also people who…; acknowledges exceptions.
Rules out Question 3, option 3: the author acknowledges people who cannot wear belts because of their circumstances.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.8.vi: However, if you do not wear a seat belt because it is a hassle or simply because you dislike being unable to move freely, you should probably reconsider.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Dislike doing or experiencing…; の nominalizes the preceding clause.
For the reason that…; specifies the content of a reason.
If it is the case that…; sets a condition for the advice.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t60-p1.vietnamese:
It has been five years since the law stipulated that seat belts must also be worn in the rear seats when driving on expressways. If you happen to be caught by the police without wearing a seat belt, only points are deducted from your driver's license; there is no fine. Perhaps because of that, people who wear seat belts in the rear seats on ordinary roads reportedly ①still account for only 33 percent of the total.

However, just because there is no fine does not mean there is a valid reason to go without a seat belt. If an accident is caused while seat belts are not being worn, the fatality rate in the rear seats rises to a striking 4.8 times as high.

In contrast, if you are wearing a seat belt, the possibility of dying is almost eliminated, even if you suffer an injury such as a broken bone. This fact alone should be a sufficient reason to ②wear a seat belt on ordinary roads.

Of course, some people cannot wear seat belts because of various circumstances. However, if you do not wear a seat belt because it is a hassle or simply because you dislike being unable to move freely, you should probably reconsider. What you gain in return for that inconvenience is immeasurably valuable.

(Note 1) Fine: money paid for failing to follow the rules.

(Note 2) Immeasurable: beyond what one can imagine.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t61-p1.vietnamese:
Heating appliances are indispensable for getting through the cold winter. What kind of heating appliance really suits our daily lives? First, a typical example is the air conditioner. Air conditioners warm a room quickly, so their advantages are comfort and low electricity costs.

However, even air conditioners are ① not an all-purpose solution. Airflow from air conditioners lowers the humidity in the air, causing various viruses to emerge. Air with humidity below 40 percent provides an environment in which viruses can easily live. For this reason, quite a few people use a humidifier together with their air conditioner.

Next, there are gas and electric heaters. Gas costs are relatively low compared with electricity costs, but using a gas heater poses a risk of the humidity rising too high. It is said that humidity above 60 percent can also cause mold to develop. In that respect, electric heaters pose no humidity concerns, but if you leave one on continuously just because it is cold, you will end up ② being shocked when you see the next month's electricity bill.

Finally, there is the kotatsu, a heated table that has been used since long ago. Since a kotatsu warms only the feet and legs, it can truly be called a good heating appliance that keeps the head cool and the feet warm. That said, it also has a weakness. The weakness is that once you get under it, you cannot move around. Since only the space under the table is warm, it may not suit active people.

As described above, each heating appliance has its own advantages and disadvantages. It is said that the proportion of people using air conditioners reaches 60 percent or more, but that does not necessarily mean an air conditioner suits you too. We should choose the most suitable heating appliance according to the local climate, household composition, lifestyle, and similar factors.
