default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.0.vi: Today, we live in an age when we can easily look up anything on a smartphone or computer, but it goes without saying that reading newspapers, books, and similar materials is important.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Lists representative examples rather than an exhaustive set: newspapers, books, and so on.
Marks the means used for an action; here, looking things up using a smartphone or computer.
The potential form of an ichidan verb: 調べる → 調べられる, meaning can look up.
Connects contrasting ideas: although digital research is easy, reading books and newspapers remains important.
Nominalizes a verb or clause: 読むこと means reading, while 大事であること means the fact that it is important.
A formal written equivalent of だ, used to make an assertion.
Expresses that there is no need to do something. 言うまでもない means it goes without saying.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.1.vi: Reading words written on paper can stimulate the brain not only through the eyes but also through the hands, helping the mind function better.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.1.gramm: 書かれた is the past passive form of 書く and modifies 字: characters written on paper.
Means by doing something, indicating the means or cause of the following result.
Means not only… but also…, extending the statement from the eyes to the hands.
Means through a medium or intermediary; here, through the hands.
Expresses ability. でき is the connective form leading into the result that the mind functions better.
Changes an i-adjective into an expression of becoming: 良い → 良くなる, become better.
Adds an explanatory tone, clarifying the benefit of reading words on paper.
Directly identifies the action: reading words written on paper. This supports the reading part of option 3.
States the exact result asked about: improving how the mind functions.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.2.vi: Of course, writing with a pen is also important.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Indicates using a tool to do something; here, using a pen to write.
Nominalizes an action and adds も: writing is also important, alongside reading.
Adds writing to the previous sentence's point about reading, completing the support for option 3. It does not mention making notes in books or newspapers as option 2 does.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.3.vi: Carrying a planner around is by no means uncool.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.3.vocab: by no means; never (with a negative)
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Nominalizes an action and makes it the topic: carrying a planner around.
Emphasizes a negative statement: by no means; absolutely not.
Negates a characterization of an action: it is not something uncool.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.4.vi: Japan reportedly has the second-highest proportion of people who read print newspapers in the world.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.4.gramm: A clause placed before 人 modifies it: people who read print newspapers.
Expresses the second-highest degree within a stated scope; here, the world's second-highest proportion.
Follows a plain form to report information: reportedly; I hear that. 多いそうだ expresses hearsay, not appearance.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.5.vi: The volume of paperwork used in companies is also much greater than in other developed countries.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.5.gramm: で marks where the action occurs; 会社で使用する modifies 書類: documents used in companies.
Adds another example of paper use in Japan: company documents alongside print newspapers.
Means compared with…, identifying other developed countries as the comparison.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.6.vi: Although recycling and related tasks are indeed demanding, the benefits of paper probably outweigh those difficulties.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Gives a representative example and implies other similar things.
Concedes a point before presenting a contrast: it is indeed demanding, but…
Means more than…; それ以上に indicates that the benefits exceed the difficulties just mentioned.
Here it means an aspect or respect rather than a physical place: beneficial aspects.
Expresses the writer's judgment or conjecture: probably.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.7.vi: According to the passage, what should one do to help the mind function better?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Means in order to achieve…, presenting a goal before asking how to reach it.
Expresses what would be advisable; どうしたらいい asks what one should do.
Means it is written that…; と marks the written content, while ～てある describes the resulting state of writing.
Marks a question. The required method must come from the passage rather than personal inference.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.outline.0.label: Reading still matters
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the convenience of digital research, then affirms the importance of reading books and newspapers. This provides context rather than evidence for how to improve mental functioning.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.outline.1.label: Benefits of reading and writing on paper
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.outline.1.note: Sentence 1 states that reading words on paper helps the mind function better; sentence 2 adds the importance of writing with a pen. Together, they support option 3. Sentence 3 further encourages carrying a planner.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.outline.2.label: Paper use and its value
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.outline.2.note: Describes the prevalence of print newspapers and company paperwork in Japan, then suggests that paper's benefits outweigh the difficulties of recycling.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.outline.3.label: Question about improving mental functioning
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.outline.3.note: The question asks which actions help the mind function better according to the passage. The supporting evidence is in sentences 1 and 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t63-p1.vietnamese:
Today, we live in an age when we can easily look up anything on a smartphone or computer, but it goes without saying that reading newspapers, books, and similar materials is important.

Reading words written on paper can stimulate the brain not only through the eyes but also through the hands, helping the mind function better.

Of course, writing with a pen is also important.

Carrying a planner around is by no means uncool.

Japan reportedly has the second-highest proportion of people who read print newspapers in the world.

The volume of paperwork used in companies is also much greater than in other developed countries.

Although recycling and related tasks are indeed demanding, the benefits of paper probably outweigh those difficulties.

According to the passage, what should one do to help the mind function better?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.0.vi: This is an email that Tanaka received from Suzuki.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Arrive from someone to someone; から marks the sender and に the recipient.
The clause ending in 届いた modifies メール: an email that arrived.
A formal written copula equivalent to だ or です.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.4.gramm: A polite suffix attached to a person's name.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.5.vi: Thank you for your hard work.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.5.vocab: a workplace greeting acknowledging someone's efforts
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.5.gramm: A standard polite workplace greeting; it does not necessarily mean the recipient is tired.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.6.vi: I said I would return to the office in the afternoon, but the work here is not finished, so it looks like I will not be able to return.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Said that…; と marks the content of the statement.
Gives background and gently introduces a contrast with expectations.
A negative connective equivalent to ～ないで or ～なくて; here it gives the reason for being unable to return.
Does not seem likely to…; with the potential stem 戻れ, it means being unlikely to be able to return.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.7.vi: I am sorry to ask, but please take care of the following tasks this afternoon.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Uses an apology as a polite lead-in to a request.
Asks the listener to carry out or handle the stated task.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.8.gramm: A counter for copies of documents and publications.
Identifies the required task as printing 100 brochure copies.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.9.gramm: A polite statement specifying the required printing method.
Printing must be double-sided; option 2 incorrectly specifies single-sided printing.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.10.vi: Please ask Kato how to do it.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.10.gram: Attaches to a verb's ます-stem to express how to do it: やる → やり方.
Ask someone; に marks the person being asked.
Politely asks the listener to do something.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.10.keys: Directly supports option 1: get instructions from Kato before printing. It does not request entering data together with Kato.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.11.vi: Once the printing is finished, please put the brochures in a cardboard box and leave them there.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.11.gram: When or once…; here できたら means once the printing is finished, rather than if possible.
Asks someone to do something and leave the result ready for later.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.13.vi: There is a memo on my desk.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.13.gram: States that an object exists at a location marked by に.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.14.vi: Please enter the contents of the memo into the file.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.14.gram: Enter the content marked by を into the destination marked by に.
Asks someone to complete a task in preparation for later use.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.14.keys: Tanaka is asked to enter the memo's contents; there is no instruction to do so with Kato as option 3 claims.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.15.vi: After entering the data, please leave the memo as it is on the desk without throwing it away.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.15.gram: After an activity; 入力後 means after entering the data.
Do something without doing another action; 捨てずに means without throwing it away.
Asks someone to perform an action and maintain the resulting state; here, leave the memo on the desk.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.15.keys: The memo must remain as it is on the desk, rather than be tidied away as option 4 suggests.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.16.vi: If you still have time after finishing those tasks, please help Kato with their work.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.16.gram: Even if or even after…; here it refers to time still remaining after the tasks are finished.
If…; 時間があれば sets the condition that time remains.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.sentences.16.keys: Helping Kato is conditional on finishing and having time left; it does not mean entering data together with Kato.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.outline.0.label: Email details and greeting
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces Suzuki's email to Tanaka, including the recipient, subject, sending time, and greeting.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.outline.1.label: Reason for requesting afternoon help
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.outline.1.note: Suzuki is unlikely to return to the office because the work elsewhere is unfinished, so asks Tanaka to handle the listed tasks.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.outline.2.label: Print brochures following instructions
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.outline.2.note: Ask Kato how to print, produce 100 double-sided copies, and put them in a cardboard box. This supports option 1 and rules out option 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.outline.3.label: Enter data and retain the memo
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.outline.3.note: Enter the contents of the memo on Suzuki's desk into the file, then leave the memo where it is. There is no request to enter data with Kato or tidy the memo away.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.outline.4.label: Additional help if time remains
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.outline.4.note: Help Kato only after completing the listed tasks and if time remains; the email ends with a closing and Suzuki's signature.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t64-p1.vietnamese:
This is an email that Tanaka received from Suzuki.

To: s.tanaka@nnn.co.jp
Subject: Afternoon work
Sent: December 10, 20XX, at 11:12 a.m.

Dear Tanaka,

Thank you for your hard work.

I said I would return to the office in the afternoon, but the work here is not finished, so it looks like I will not be able to return.

I am sorry to ask, but please take care of the following tasks this afternoon.

1. Printing brochures (100 copies): Print on both sides. Please ask Kato how to do it. Once the printing is finished, put the brochures in a cardboard box and leave them there.

2. Data entry: There is a memo on my desk. Please enter its contents into the file. After entering the data, leave the memo as it is on the desk without throwing it away.

If you still have time after finishing those tasks, please help Kato with their work.

Best,

Suzuki
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.1.vi: At Aomidori CD & Books, an indoor classical concert is held on the third Sunday of every month.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.1.gramm: To hold or conduct an event or activity.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.2.vi: Please come and enjoy a relaxing moment with the beautiful melodies of the piano, violin, and cello...
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Used to politely invite someone to enjoy or accept something.
Confirms the concert features three instruments: piano, violin, and cello. This detail combines with sentence 8 (the CD contains the performed pieces) to prove option 4 is correct.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.3.vi: Location: 1st floor, the cafe next to the CD sales section
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.4.vi: Date and time: Third Sunday of every month, 2:00 PM – 3:00 PM
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Indicates a time span from one hour to another.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.6.vi: Performers: Aoi Mizuno, Kaoruko Wada, Akiko Jojima
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.7.vi: ※ Please kindly refrain from eating and drinking inside the cafe during the performance.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Attached to a noun to mean 'in the middle of' or 'during'.
A formal polite business expression used to request customers to refrain from doing something.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.8.vi: ※ Customers who purchase the CD "Classic Freak" containing the concert's musical program will receive autographs from all three performers.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Humble / respectful expression indicating receiving an action favorably done by someone (here: customer purchasing).
Humble form of します, used to politely state one's own or the store's action.
The CD 'Classic Freak' contains pieces performed in the concert (which consist of piano, violin, and cello melodies per sentence 2), meaning the CD includes performances of these three instruments -> Option 4 is correct. Additionally, 'お買い上げいただいた方' indicates customers must buy the CD to get autographs, rather than receiving a free CD upon arrival (refuting option 1).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.outline.0.label: Introduction to the Weekend Classical Concert
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.outline.0.note: Announcement of the regular monthly classical concert featuring melodies played on piano, violin, and cello.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.outline.1.label: Concert Details and Performer Information
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.outline.1.note: Provides specific details on location (1st floor next to the CD section), time (third Sunday, 2:00 PM - 3:00 PM), admission (free), and the three performers.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.outline.2.label: Notices for Attendees and CD Promotion
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.outline.2.note: Rules requesting attendees to refrain from eating or drinking during the performance, and a bonus offer of three performers' autographs when purchasing the concert CD.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t65-p1.vietnamese:
WEEKEND CLASSICAL CONCERT

At Aomidori CD & Books, we hold an indoor classical concert on the third Sunday of every month.

Please come and enjoy a relaxing moment with the beautiful melodies of the piano, violin, and cello...

Location: 1st floor, the cafe next to the CD sales section
Date & Time: Third Sunday of every month, 2:00 PM – 3:00 PM
Admission: Free
Performers: Aoi Mizuno, Kaoruko Wada, Akiko Jojima

※ Please kindly refrain from eating and drinking inside the cafe during the performance.
※ Customers who purchase the CD "Classic Freak" containing the concert's musical program will receive autographs from all three performers.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.0.vi: At some point in history, straight lines came to be considered beautiful in women's kimono.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.0.gramm: After an interrogative expression, か marks uncertainty; いつの時代からか means “from some unspecified era.”
To be considered or regarded as; expresses a generally accepted judgment.
Expresses a change into a new state or practice.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.1.vi: As a result, putting on a kimono became a great hardship.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Marks a cause: “because of; as a result of.” それ refers to the preceding preference for straight lines in kimono.
Nominalizes a verb phrase: 着物を着ること means “putting on a kimono.”
Means “became”; presents the result of a change in a somewhat formal style.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.2.vi: People began placing cloth against the chest and waist, hiding all the curves of the body that should naturally express its beauty.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.2.gramm: に marks the surface something is placed against. 当て is the connective stem of 当てる, linking actions in written language.
Modifies a noun with an expectation: “curves that should express beauty.”
Describes an emerging practice: people began concealing the body's curves.
A formal explanatory ending; this sentence explains the hardship mentioned previously.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.3.vi: Finally, the body is tightly bound with an obi sash stretched straight.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.3.gramm: In 最後には, に marks the stage and は emphasizes the final step.
A preceding clause modifies a noun: まっすぐ伸びた describes the state of the sash.
Marks the means used: the body is bound with an obi sash.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.4.vi: Someone unfamiliar with this would probably wonder why anyone wears such an uncomfortable, straight-lined garment.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Connects an い-adjective to another description: uncomfortable and straight-lined.
Expresses purpose; 何のために means “for what purpose.”
Embeds a question within a thought, expressing “wonder why/whether…”
Expresses the author's conjecture about what an unfamiliar observer would think.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.5.vi: Yet human psychology is curious: just when everything seems concealed, the hands and the area around the neck, visible only slightly, appear extraordinarily beautiful.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Introduces a general, mildly exclamatory observation: “human psychology is a curious thing.” で connects it to the explanation that follows.
In 隠れている, marks the resulting state of being concealed rather than an ongoing act of hiding.
Here it means “just when one thinks…, …,” introducing an unexpected contrast between concealment and the beauty of what remains visible.
Limits the extent: 少しだけ means “only a little.”
Gives non-exhaustive examples: the hands and the area around the neck.
An い-adjective takes its ～く form before 見える to mean “look/appear…”
Direct support for option 3: small glimpses of the body are perceived as exceptionally beautiful.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.6.vi: The beauty that Japanese people perceive is precisely the beauty created by this concealment.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.sentences.6.gramm: In a noun-modifying clause, の can replace が as the subject marker: 日本人の感じる美しさ means “the beauty Japanese people perceive.”
隠された is the past passive form of 隠す: “was concealed.”
こと nominalizes an event and による marks its causal role: “beauty resulting from concealment.”
An emphatic explanatory ending; here it states the author's central conclusion.
States the main idea: concealment makes the small visible parts stand out as beautiful. Together with the preceding sentence, this supports option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.outline.0.label: A preference for straight lines
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the view that straight lines are beautiful in women's kimono. This is background, so option 2 does not express the main point.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.outline.1.label: The hardship of wearing kimono
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.outline.1.note: Describes placing cloth against the body, hiding curves, and tightening the sash, leading outsiders to question the purpose of wearing kimono. Option 1 only restates this supporting discussion.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.outline.2.label: Beauty in what remains visible
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.outline.2.note: ところが marks a turn: when nearly everything is concealed, small glimpses of the hands and neck appear especially beautiful. This directly supports option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.outline.3.label: Beauty created by concealment
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.outline.3.note: The author concludes that Japanese people perceive beauty created by concealment. Together with sentence 5, this establishes option 3. Option 4 is incorrect because the passage concerns hidden curves and perceived beauty.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t66-p1.vietnamese: At some point in history, straight lines came to be considered beautiful in women's kimono. As a result, putting on a kimono became a great hardship. People began placing cloth against the chest and waist, hiding all the curves of the body that should naturally express its beauty. Finally, the body is tightly bound with an obi sash stretched straight. Someone unfamiliar with this would probably wonder why anyone wears such an uncomfortable, straight-lined garment. Yet human psychology is curious: just when everything seems concealed, the hands and the area around the neck, visible only slightly, appear extraordinarily beautiful. The beauty that Japanese people perceive is precisely the beauty created by this concealment.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.1.vi: Sometimes I carefully plan a trip abroad; other times, I casually board a train and try getting off at a station whose name appeals to me.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Sometimes… and other times…; presents different actions on different occasions.
Try doing something as an experience; here, getting off at a station.
A clause modifies a noun: 気に入った名前 means a name one found appealing.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.2.vi: There, I enjoy the town’s scents and scenery, wandering around while listening closely to the sounds that reach me.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Lists examples without implying an exhaustive list.
In 聞こえてくる, describes sounds coming toward the perceiver.
While doing…; listening and walking happen simultaneously.
Try an action to experience it.
Question 2: a concrete example of experiencing a destination through smell and sight.
Question 2: adds hearing, showing that the experience extends beyond food.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.3.vi: In the towns I end up in this way, there is something I always do.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Here, expresses a repeated habit rather than an action in progress.
Here, means “there is something…”; こと is modified by 私が必ずしている, rather than forming the experience pattern ～たことがある.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.4.vi: That is to photograph a dish that catches my attention there and try tasting it.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Preserve a visual record of something in a photograph.
Try doing; 味見をしてみる means to try tasting a dish.
Nominalizes an action with こと and explains it using the formal written copula である: “it is to…”.
Question 2: tasting food is one part of the sensory experience; merely photographing and eating food does not cover all of そんなこと.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.5.vi: Even if it is the yakisoba I regularly eat, when I taste it in a town I am visiting for the first time, it (　　　).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Even assuming…; the outcome goes against what the condition might lead one to expect.
Describes an established habit in everyday life.
初めて行った modifies 街, and 口にした modifies それ.
Question 1: although the dish is familiar, the following clause should express a different experience from usual.
Question 1: eating in a new place makes the flavor feel different, supporting option 1: 決していつもの味ではない。
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.6.vi: In this way, when traveling, I make a point of using all five senses to experience and enjoy each place.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Summarizes the preceding examples: “in this way”.
Make a conscious effort to maintain a practice or habit.
Indicates the means used to perform an action: using…
Question 1: shows that flavor is part of the overall experience of a place. Question 2: this is the direct referent of そんなこと in the next sentence, matching option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.7.vi: As I repeated these experiences, I began to find myself suddenly remembering those towns while doing something else.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.7.gramm: While continuing an activity, a change gradually occurs.
While an action is in progress.
Expresses a change: a new behavior or state begins to occur.
Question 2: points back to using the five senses to experience and enjoy a destination in the preceding sentence.
Question 3: the memories arise spontaneously, rather than through deliberate recall to avoid forgetting as in option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.8.vi: It invariably happens when I eat something, smell a scent, or hear a tune playing in the streets.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Lists representative actions without implying that they all occur together or in sequence.
When an event occurs; here, identifies occasions that trigger memories.
Question 3: hearing music in the streets is explicitly listed as a memory trigger; together with the nostalgia in the next sentence, this supports option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.9.vi: When I eat curry and rice filled with large chunks of ingredients, or catch the smell of wind that suggests rain is about to fall, I suddenly remember a town I visited long ago and feel an indescribable nostalgia.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.sentences.9.gramm: In noun-modifying clauses, の can replace が as the subject marker, as in 具の…入った and 雨の降りだしそうな.
Attaches to a verb stem to mark the start of an action: 降りだす means to start raining.
Seems about to…; そうな modifies a noun based on perceived signs.
Describes a feeling that cannot easily be put into words.
Come to experience a particular feeling.
Question 3: the trigger is smelling the wind, rather than merely seeing a dark sky or noticing approaching rain as in option 2.
Question 3: confirms that nostalgia arises when sensory experiences spontaneously recall a previously visited place; together with the preceding sentence, this supports option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.outline.0.label: A love of travel and different ways to travel
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.outline.0.note: The author enjoys traveling, sometimes with careful planning and sometimes spontaneously.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.outline.1.label: Experiencing destinations through the senses
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.outline.1.note: The author enjoys scenery, scents, sounds, and food. Even a familiar dish feels different when eaten somewhere new; option 1 completes the blank.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.outline.2.label: A habit of using all five senses
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.outline.2.note: This sentence summarizes the preceding experiences and supplies the main referent of そんなこと in the next sentence. Question 2 takes option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.outline.3.label: Sensory triggers of memory and nostalgia
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.outline.3.note: The passage shifts from experiences during travel to memories that return unexpectedly later. Food, smells, and music recall past destinations; hearing music in the streets supports option 3 for question 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t67-p1.vietnamese:
I like traveling.

Sometimes I carefully plan a trip abroad; other times, I casually board a train and try getting off at a station whose name appeals to me.

There, I enjoy the town’s scents and scenery, wandering around while listening closely to the sounds that reach me.

In the towns I end up in this way, there is something I always do.

That is to photograph a dish that catches my attention there and try tasting it.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t68-p1.vietnamese:
It has been five years since the law required seat belts to be worn even in the rear seats when driving on expressways.

If someone happens to be caught by the police without wearing a seat belt, only points are deducted from their driver's license; there is no fine.

Perhaps because of that, it is reported that the proportion of people who wear seat belts in the rear seats on ordinary roads is still only 33%.

However, the absence of a fine does not justify not wearing a seat belt.

If an accident occurs while a seat belt is not being worn, the death rate for rear-seat occupants rises to a startling 4.8 times as high.

By contrast, if a seat belt is worn, death becomes extremely rare even if injuries such as broken bones occur.

This fact alone should be reason enough to wear a seat belt on ordinary roads.

Of course, some people are unable to wear a seat belt due to various circumstances.

However, if someone does not wear a seat belt because it is a nuisance or simply because they dislike being unable to move freely, they should probably reconsider.

For what one gains in return is immeasurably valuable.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t69-p1.vietnamese:
Heating appliances are essential for getting through the cold winter. What kind of heating appliance really suits our lives?

First, a typical example is the air conditioner. An air conditioner warms the room quickly, so its advantages are comfort and low electricity costs. However, even the air conditioner ①cannot do everything. Because its airflow lowers humidity in the air, it becomes a cause of various viruses emerging. Air with humidity below 40 percent provides an environment in which viruses can easily live. For that reason, quite a few people use an air conditioner together with a humidifier.

Next, there are gas and electric heaters. Gas costs are relatively low compared with electricity costs, but using a gas heater brings a risk of humidity in the air rising too high. It is said that humidity above 60 percent can also cause mold to develop. In that respect, electric heaters pose no humidity concerns, but if you leave one on continuously just because it is cold, you will ②be shocked when you see the following month's electricity bill.

Finally, there is the kotatsu, a heated table that has been used since long ago. Since a kotatsu warms only the feet and legs, it can be called a good heating appliance that truly keeps the head cool and the feet warm. Nevertheless, it also has a drawback. Once you get under it, you cannot move around. Since it is warm only underneath the table, it may not suit active people.

As discussed above, each heating appliance has its own advantages and disadvantages. The proportion of people using air conditioners is said to reach 60 percent or more, but that does not necessarily mean an air conditioner suits you. We should choose the most suitable heating appliance based on the temperature where we live, our household composition, our lifestyle, and similar factors.

④ Korean Restaurant

Usage fee: 5,000 yen

Number of users: 30 to 50 people

Cuisine: Korean course meal, free all-you-can-drink soft drinks and alcohol (beer, Japanese sake, makgeolli)

Format: Seated buffet

Other: Bringing in cakes, wine, etc., is permitted (no bring-in fee)
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.0.vi: This is a notice posted at a supermarket.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Describes a state resulting from an intentional action: the notice has been posted and remains there. に marks the location.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.1.vi: For three days starting tomorrow, the supermarket “X-Mart” will hold a “Special Thank-You Sale.”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Marks a starting point: あしたから means “starting tomorrow.”
で marks where an activity takes place, while は presents that location as the topic.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.2.vi: Juice normally costs 500 yen per set of three bottles; during the sale, each set comes with two extra bottles for the same price.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Follows a quantity to indicate the contents: ３本入り means “containing three bottles.”
Marks juice as the topic. The phrase before ジュース describes the normal price and number of bottles per set.
Connects actions: include two extra bottles and sell the set at the original price.
で marks the selling price: 同じねだんで means “at the same price.”
One set of juice costs 500 yen, so three sets cost 3 × 500 = 1,500 yen.
Each set includes two extra bottles but still costs 500 yen; the extra bottles do not add to the price.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.3.vi: Also, milk normally priced at 120 yen per bottle will be reduced to 100 yen.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Expresses a change to a new amount or state; here, the price of milk becomes 100 yen.
Use the sale price of 100 yen per bottle: three bottles cost 300 yen. Using the old price would give the incorrect answer of 1,660 yen after the 200-yen discount.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.4.vi: Furthermore, customers who spend at least 1,000 yen will receive 200 yen off their total bill.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Sets an inclusive minimum: 1,000円以上 means 1,000 yen or more, including exactly 1,000 yen.
A humble expression for receiving an action from someone. Here, the store uses 買っていただいた to respectfully refer to customers making purchases.
A clause ending in the past form modifies a following noun: 買っていただいた modifies おきゃくさま, and 合計した modifies ねだん.
Indicates a price reduction from an original amount. Here, 200 yen is subtracted from the total bill.
Replace the final い of an i-adjective with くなります to express a change: 安い → 安くなります means “become cheaper.”
The juice and milk total 1,800 yen, meeting the minimum purchase requirement of 1,000 yen.
Subtract 200 yen once from the total bill: 1,500 + 300 − 200 = 1,600 yen, so option 2 is correct.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.5.vi: Please take advantage of this sale.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.sentences.5.gramm: A polite invitation or request formed with ご, an action noun, and ください. Here, ごりようください invites customers to shop at the store.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.outline.0.label: Notice and sale dates
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the supermarket notice and X-Mart’s special sale, which lasts three days starting tomorrow.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.outline.1.label: Juice and milk offers
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.outline.1.note: Each juice set includes two extra bottles and remains 500 yen; milk drops to 100 yen per bottle. Three juice sets and three milk bottles total 1,800 yen before the bill discount.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.outline.2.label: Additional discount on the total
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.outline.2.note: Purchases of at least 1,000 yen receive 200 yen off the total. The amount due is therefore 1,800 − 200 = 1,600 yen, corresponding to option 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.outline.3.label: Invitation to shop
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.outline.3.note: Closes the notice with a polite invitation to customers.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t71-p1.vietnamese:
This is a notice posted at a supermarket.

For three days starting tomorrow, the supermarket “X-Mart” will hold a “Special Thank-You Sale.”

Juice normally costs 500 yen per set of three bottles; during the sale, each set comes with two extra bottles for the same price.

Also, milk normally priced at 120 yen per bottle will be reduced to 100 yen.

Furthermore, customers who spend at least 1,000 yen will receive 200 yen off their total bill.

Please take advantage of this sale.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.0.vi: This is a notice posted at a hospital.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Describes a state resulting from an intentional action: the notice has been posted and remains there.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.1.gramm: States what will change; が marks the subject undergoing the change.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.2.vi: From September, the hospital's reception hours will change.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Marks a starting point in time: from September.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.3.vi: On Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, reception will begin 30 minutes earlier, at 8:30 a.m.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Replace the final い of an i-adjective with くなる to express a change. 30分早くなる means to become 30 minutes earlier.
なり is the linking form of なる, used in writing to connect to the following clause.
A formal way to announce the specified starting time.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.4.vi: The closing time will remain unchanged at 5 p.m.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.4.gramm: A plain-form verb modifies a noun: 終わる時間 means the time when something ends.
Marks the ending point: reception continues until 5 p.m.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.5.vi: On Thursdays, the hospital will continue to accept patients only in the morning, as before.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Expresses following an existing pattern or state. 今までどおり means as before.
Limits the scope: patients are accepted only in the morning.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.6.vi: The hours will also remain the same, from 9 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Means also: the specific hours remain unchanged as well.
Means the same as; で connects this statement to the explanation of the hours.
States a time interval from its starting point to its ending point.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.7.vi: In addition, the hospital is currently closed on Saturdays, but from September it will also open on the second and fourth Saturdays of each month.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Connects contrasting facts: currently closed on Saturdays, but adding Saturday openings from September.
Marks a starting point and highlights a contrast with the period before it.
に marks the days of the activity, while も means also: the specified Saturdays are additional opening days.
第 before a number forms an ordinal. 第2、第4土曜日 refers to the second and fourth occurrences of Saturday in a month.
The new schedule adds only the second and fourth Saturdays. The question identifies September 5 as the first Saturday, so the hospital remains closed; choose option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.8.vi: However, please note that reception hours on those days will be from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Adds a condition or limitation to the preceding statement: the open Saturdays have their own hours.
Marks the interval from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Gives the reason for the following reminder: these are the hours, so readers should take note.
A polite request pattern. ご注意ください means “please take note.”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.outline.0.label: Changes starting in September
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the hospital notice and when the new reception hours take effect.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.outline.1.label: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday hours
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.outline.1.note: Reception starts 30 minutes earlier at 8:30 a.m. and still ends at 5 p.m.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.outline.2.label: Thursday hours remain unchanged
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.outline.2.note: Thursday reception remains limited to the morning, from 9 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.outline.3.label: Two additional Saturday openings each month
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.outline.3.note: From September, the hospital opens on the second and fourth Saturdays from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. The first Saturday is not an opening day, supporting option 4. The notice ends with the hospital's name.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t72-p1.vietnamese:
This is a notice posted at a hospital.

Changes to reception hours

From September, the hospital's reception hours will change.

On Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, reception will begin 30 minutes earlier, at 8:30 a.m. The closing time will remain unchanged at 5 p.m.

On Thursdays, the hospital will continue to accept patients only in the morning, as before. The hours will also remain the same, from 9 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.

In addition, the hospital is currently closed on Saturdays, but from September it will also open on the second and fourth Saturdays of each month. However, please note that reception hours on those days will be from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m.

Harukaze Hospital
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.0.vi: The following is an email Yamada sent to Alena.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.0.gramm: The preceding clause modifies メール: an email that someone sent to another person.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.2.vi: It's hot every day, isn't it?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Offers an observation and invites agreement: “isn't it?”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.3.vi: Now then, on the 18th of next month, Angelina Moreau will give a piano concert at my university.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.3.gramm: で marks where an activity takes place; here, giving a concert at a university.
The concert date is already fixed, so Alena does not need to arrange a date with Yamada; this rules out option 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.4.vi: Alena, you like this performer, right, if I remember correctly?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Checks information the speaker remembers. Here, it does not imply that Alena no longer likes the performer.
Expresses liking someone or something. In casual speech, が can be omitted, as in この人好き.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.5.vi: Students at my university can buy tickets at half price, so if you'd like to go, I'll buy them and send them to you.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.5.gramm: States a condition: if someone is a student at the speaker's university.
で marks the price; 買える is the potential form of 買う, meaning “can buy.”
Gives the reason for the following offer: access to half-price tickets motivates the offer to buy them.
The conditional form of ～たい: “if you want to….” 行きたい becomes 行きたければ.
Links actions in sequence: buy the tickets, then send them.
Yamada offers to buy and send tickets if Alena wants to go. Alena should reply to Yamada about whether to buy tickets, matching option 2; contacting the university as in option 3 is unnecessary.
The email already explains eligibility for half-price tickets, so there is no need to email the university to ask, as in option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.6.vi: I wish I could go with you too, but I have something to do that day and can't go.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Here, expresses a wish: “It would be nice if I could go with you.”
Introduces the speaker's feelings before a contrasting fact: wishing to go together but being unable to.
The て form expresses a reason: having a commitment prevents the speaker from going.
Negates ability. 行けません means “cannot go,” from 行く → 行ける.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.7.vi: If your friends are going with you too, please let me know how many tickets you want.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.7.vocab: how many tickets or flat objects
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Sets a condition based on the recipient's plans: if friends are also going.
Embeds a question in a request for information. なんまいほしいか means “how many tickets you want.”
Makes a polite request: please let me know.
Yamada asks Alena to report the number of tickets wanted if friends are joining, reinforcing the need to reply to the email's sender.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.sentences.8.gramm: States a unit price in yen per ticket. まい is the counter for thin, flat objects such as tickets.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.outline.0.label: Email introduction and greeting
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.outline.0.note: Identifies Yamada as the sender and Alena as the recipient, followed by a greeting and a comment about the weather.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.outline.1.label: Concert information
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.outline.1.note: Introduces the performer, venue, and fixed concert date, and recalls Alena's interest in the performer.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.outline.2.label: Offer to buy tickets
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.outline.2.note: Students at Yamada's university can buy half-price tickets. Yamada offers to buy and send tickets if Alena wants to go, but cannot join because of another commitment.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.outline.3.label: Ticket quantity and price
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.outline.3.note: If friends are joining, Alena should tell Yamada how many tickets are wanted. The stated price is 2,500 yen per ticket.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t73-p1.vietnamese:
The following is an email Yamada sent to Alena.

Hello. It's hot every day, isn't it?

Now then, on the 18th of next month, Angelina Moreau will give a piano concert at my university.

Alena, you like this performer, right, if I remember correctly?

Students at my university can buy tickets at half price, so if you'd like to go, I'll buy them and send them to you.

I wish I could go with you too, but I have something to do that day and can't go.

If your friends are going with you too, please let me know how many tickets you want.

Tickets cost 2,500 yen each.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.0.vi: Greetings are highly valued by Japanese people.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.0.gramm: The passive of 大切にする (to value), combined with ～ている to describe a state. 日本人に identifies the people who value greetings.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.1.vi: People from any country probably say hello when they meet someone they know.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Used with a question word to express unrestricted inclusion: people from any country.
In 知っている, expresses the state of knowing someone, rather than an action in progress.
Introduces a time or situation: when meeting someone familiar. The ～た form does not make the whole sentence a past narrative.
と marks the quoted greeting; 「こんにちは」 is what is said.
Expresses a supposition or an expectation the reader will likely share: probably; presumably.
Option 1 matches the passage: people say hello to someone they know, so it is not the answer to the question asking for the unmatched statement.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.2.vi: However, in places such as the mountains, Japanese people also greet strangers they meet.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.2.gramm: など gives examples, で marks the location of an action, and は highlights the setting. 山などでは means in places such as the mountains.
A negative verb modifies 人: 知らない人 means someone one does not know, or a stranger.
Means also when. も adds encounters with strangers to the previously mentioned encounters with familiar people.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.3.vi: They also say “excuse me” when they nearly bump into a stranger.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Attaches to a verb's masu-stem to express that something nearly happened. ぶつかりそうになった means nearly bumped into someone, without asserting that a collision occurred.
Means also when, adding another situation in which Japanese people use a social expression.
と marks the words being spoken: say “すみません.”
This supports answer 2: the passage says nearly bumping into a stranger, whereas option 2 uses ぶつかられた, meaning being bumped into by a stranger. These are different situations, so option 2 does not match the passage.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.4.vocab: does not exist; here: is not
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Means it is not only that, signaling that another example or point will follow.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.5.vi: Even when they are alone, Japanese people always say “itadakimasu” before a meal and “gochisousama” afterward to express gratitude.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.5.vocab: expression of gratitude before a meal
expression of thanks after a meal
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.sentences.5.gramm: で indicates the circumstances or manner of an action; 一人で means alone.
Expresses concession: even if or even when. 一人でいても means even when alone.
Indicates the times before and after an event. The two expressions that follow correspond to before and after the meal, respectively.
Adds an explanatory tone and emphasizes the information the writer is conveying.
Confirms that these mealtime expressions are used even when alone, supporting option 3.
“いただきます” corresponds to before a meal and “ごちそうさま” to afterward. Options 3 and 4 both match the passage, so neither is the required answer.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.outline.0.label: The importance of greetings
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the importance of greetings to Japanese people and the widespread custom of greeting acquaintances. Sentence 1 supports option 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.outline.1.label: Expressions used with strangers
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.outline.1.note: Describes greeting strangers in places such as the mountains and apologizing when nearly bumping into them. Distinguish nearly bumping into someone in the passage from being bumped into in option 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.outline.2.label: Expressions before and after meals
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.outline.2.note: Adds that even when alone, Japanese people say “itadakimasu” before meals and “gochisousama” afterward, supporting options 3 and 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t74-p1.vietnamese:
Greetings are highly valued by Japanese people.

People from any country probably say hello when they meet someone they know.

However, in places such as the mountains, Japanese people also greet strangers they meet.

They also say “excuse me” when they nearly bump into a stranger.

That is not all.

Even when they are alone, Japanese people always say “itadakimasu” before a meal and “gochisousama” afterward to express gratitude.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.0.vi: This winter is particularly dry compared with other years.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Compared with…; marks the reference for a comparison. Here, this winter is compared with other years.
Describes an ongoing state, here the dry conditions.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.1.vi: Fires can start easily when the air is dry, so take great care around sources of fire.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.1.gramm: When…; introduces the circumstances in which the advice applies.
Attaches to a verb's masu-stem to indicate ease or likelihood. 起こりやすい means “likely to occur.”
Because…; gives the reason for the advice that follows.
Let us…; expresses a polite encouragement or reminder.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.2.vi: Gas stoves, cigarettes, and heaters can be listed as common causes of fires.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Likely to become…; here, things likely to become causes of fires.
As…; identifies the category to which the following examples belong.
Examples include…; a common expression for listing examples. Here, あげられます is the passive form of あげる.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.3.vi: For gas stoves in particular, accidents occur most often during cooking, so make sure you do not leave the flame unattended while cooking.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Regarding…; は highlights gas stoves among the fire sources just mentioned.
Added to an activity noun and read ちゅう, meaning “during…”. 料理中 means “during cooking.”
… is the most frequent; 一番 marks the highest degree.
Because…; links the frequency of cooking accidents to the advice to stay by the stove.
While doing…; specifies the time when an activity is in progress.
Leave…; を marks the place being left, here 火のそば, “the area beside the flame.”
Make sure not to…; advises the reader to avoid an action, here leaving the flame unattended while cooking.
Direct evidence for option 4: stay by the flame while cooking. Option 4 restates this advice as その場をはなれてはいけない, meaning that you must not leave that spot.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.4.vi: As for cigarettes, smoking in bed and carelessly discarding cigarette butts cause fires.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Lists representative examples without implying that the list is exhaustive.
Cause or trigger…; often used with undesirable events or consequences, such as accidents or fires.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.5.vi: Forgetting to turn off heaters is also a major cause of fires.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Added to a verb's masu-stem to form a noun meaning “forgetting to do something.” 消し忘れ means “forgetting to turn off.”
Also…; adds forgetting to turn off heaters to the causes already mentioned.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.6.vi: Pay close attention to these points and make every effort to prevent fires.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Pay attention to…; に marks what requires attention. これら refers to the fire risks described above.
Connects paying attention with working to prevent fires; the first action contributes to the following goal.
Make an effort toward…; here, the goal is fire prevention.
Let us…; ends the passage with an appeal for action.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.outline.0.label: Dry weather increases fire risk
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.outline.0.note: This winter is unusually dry. Dry air makes fires more likely, so sources of fire require particular care.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.outline.1.label: Fire sources and cooking precautions
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.outline.1.note: Lists gas stoves, cigarettes, and heaters as likely fire sources. The instruction to stay by the flame while cooking directly supports option 4 for question 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.outline.2.label: Risks from cigarettes and heaters
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.outline.2.note: Identifies smoking in bed, carelessly discarding cigarette butts, and forgetting to turn off heaters as causes of fires.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.outline.3.label: A call for fire prevention
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.outline.3.note: Concludes by urging readers to pay attention to these risks and work to prevent fires.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t75-p1.vietnamese:
This winter is particularly dry compared with other years.

Fires can start easily when the air is dry, so take great care around sources of fire.

Gas stoves, cigarettes, and heaters can be listed as common causes of fires.

For gas stoves in particular, accidents occur most often during cooking, so make sure you do not leave the flame unattended while cooking.

As for cigarettes, smoking in bed and carelessly discarding cigarette butts cause fires.

Forgetting to turn off heaters is also a major cause of fires.

Pay close attention to these points and make every effort to prevent fires.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.0.vi: Recently, acquiring abilities that are immediately useful upon entering society, such as being able to use computers or speak foreign languages, has been considered important.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.0.vocab: being able to use (in a list)
being able to speak (in a list)
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.0.gramm: The potential forms of 使う and 話す express the ability to use or speak. が marks what someone can use or speak.
Lists representative examples without making an exhaustive list. Here, computer use and foreign-language ability illustrate useful abilities.
Indicates that something happens immediately after an action or transition: immediately upon entering society.
こと nominalizes an action. 大事にされている combines the passive with ～ている to indicate that the action is currently valued.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.1.vi: For this reason, classes in these areas are being offered at many high schools.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.1.vocab: are being held; are being conducted
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Connects the preceding cause to its result: because practical abilities are valued, many schools offer classes in them.
で marks the location of an activity. 行われている is the passive of 行う with ～ている, describing an activity currently being conducted.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.2.vi: On the other hand, the number of people who say there is no need to study subjects such as classical literature or history because they are not useful is reportedly also increasing.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Introduces a contrasting trend: practical subjects are valued, while some other subjects are being dismissed.
Gives a non-exhaustive list of examples, such as classical literature, history, and similar subjects.
Marks a reason. Within the reported opinion, the claim that these subjects are not useful is the reason given for not needing to study them.
Expresses that there is no need to do something; it does not express a prohibition.
The clause before と gives what is said, and 言う modifies 人. も indicates that there are also people who say this.
In 増えている, this expresses an ongoing trend: the number of such people is increasing.
Follows a plain form to report information heard from elsewhere. The writer is reporting an opinion and a trend, rather than endorsing that opinion.
The claim that these subjects need not be studied is attributed to other people, not endorsed by the writer, so option 4 is incorrect.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.3.vi: However, it remains true that other subjects are also important alongside the study of computers and foreign languages.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Introduces a contrast with the preceding opinion. Here, the writer asserts that other subjects remain important.
Means besides or in addition to. Together with the following も, it adds other subjects to the areas of study considered important.
Means also: other subjects are important too. It does not express a ranking.
である is a formal written equivalent of だ, and こと nominalizes the statement. The pattern emphasizes that a fact remains unchanged.
Marks the shift from other people's opinion to the writer's opposing position.
Directly supports option 3: other subjects are important too. It does not rank subjects as options 1 and 2 do.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.4.vi: Schools probably need to devise ways to have students study these subjects in a balanced way.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.sentences.4.gramm: で marks the setting, while は makes that setting the topic: as for what happens at schools.
The causative form of 学習する means to have students study. The students are understood and omitted from the sentence.
The clause before 工夫 describes the goal of the approach to be devised. だろう softens the judgment or recommendation: such an approach is probably needed.
これら includes computers, foreign languages, and other subjects. The recommendation to balance them supports option 3 without privileging one group.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.outline.0.label: Emphasis on practical abilities
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.outline.0.note: Abilities that are immediately useful upon entering society are valued, leading many high schools to offer computer and foreign-language classes.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.outline.1.label: Views dismissing other subjects
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.outline.1.note: The writer reports that more people consider classical literature and history unnecessary because they are not useful. Distinguishing this reported view from the writer's position rules out option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.outline.2.label: Other subjects matter too
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.outline.2.note: After しかし, the writer affirms that other subjects remain important and recommends balanced learning. This supports option 3; the passage does not rank one group above another.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t76-p1.vietnamese:
Recently, acquiring abilities that are immediately useful upon entering society, such as being able to use computers or speak foreign languages, has been considered important.

For this reason, classes in these areas are being offered at many high schools.

On the other hand, the number of people who say there is no need to study subjects such as classical literature or history because they are not useful is reportedly also increasing.

However, it remains true that other subjects are also important alongside the study of computers and foreign languages.

Schools probably need to devise ways to have students study these subjects in a balanced way.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.0.vi: Call for Participants: Sakura Ward Resident Marathon
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.1.vi: The date and time is Sunday, November 7, 20XX, and the start and meeting location will be Sakura Park.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Indicates a designated state, official decision, or result; used formally instead of ～になる/～です.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.2.vi: As for the courses: adults (university students and above) have 20km, 10km, 5km, and 3km; junior high and high school students have 10km, 5km, and 3km; and elementary school students have 5km and 3km.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Indicates 'and above' or 'or more' (inclusive of the threshold mentioned).
Specifies that adults (university students and above) are eligible for the 20km, 10km, 5km, and 3km courses; the 65-year-old man in option 3 is an adult and therefore fully eligible to apply for the 20km course.

Specifies that elementary school students can only join the 5km and 3km courses; the 10-year-old boy in option 4 is an elementary school student and cannot participate in the 10km course, making option 4 incorrect.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.3.vi: Open to both men and women (gender does not matter).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Pattern expressing 'regardless of / without distinction of' (here used in the formal polite form ～は問いません).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.4.vi: When applying, please write your desired course, full name, address, telephone number, and age on a postcard, and send it to the address below.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Expresses 'when, at the time of...' in formal contexts and public instructions.
Expresses 'after doing..., upon doing...' before proceeding to the next action (here in honorific form お書きの上).
Polite honorific request: お + Verb stem + ください.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.5.vi: * Please note that applications are limited to a maximum of one person per postcard.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.5.vocab: we take the liberty of doing / we will do (humble)
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Indicates an upper limit: 'up to, at most'.
Humble polite expression indicating the speaker's action, expressing polite notification with the recipient's permission or understanding.
Specifies that each postcard is limited to at most one person. Therefore, option 1 (2 people sharing 1 postcard) and option 2 (3 people sharing 1 postcard) are incorrect, while option 3 (2 people applying on separate postcards '別々のはがき') is completely correct.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.6.vi: * The application deadline is Friday, October 1 (postmarked on that day is valid).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.6.vocab: valid if postmarked on the day
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Fixed administrative phrase: an application is valid as long as the postmark is stamped on or before the deadline day.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.outline.0.label: Title, Date, Time, and Venue
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.outline.0.note: Announces recruitment for the Sakura Ward Resident Marathon, specifying the date (November 7, 20XX) and the meeting/starting location at Sakura Park.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.outline.1.label: Course Categories and Participant Eligibility
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.outline.1.note: Details race courses for each age group (adults/college students and above, junior/senior high students, and elementary school students), and notes that both men and women are welcome.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.outline.2.label: Application Procedures and Important Notes
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.outline.2.note: Provides instructions for postcard application, strictly limits one applicant per postcard, and gives the deadline of October 1 (postmarked valid).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t77-p1.vietnamese:
Sakura Ward Resident Marathon: Call for Participants

The marathon will be held on Sunday, November 7, 20XX. The starting and meeting place will be Sakura Park.

Available courses: for adults (university students and above), 20km, 10km, 5km, and 3km; for junior high and high school students, 10km, 5km, and 3km; for elementary school students, 5km and 3km.

Open to all genders.

To apply, please write your desired course, full name, address, telephone number, and age on a postcard, and send it to the address listed below.

* Please note: each postcard is strictly limited to one applicant only.

* Application deadline: Friday, October 1 (postmarked on that day is valid).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.sentences.0.vi: The letter below was sent by an elementary school to its students’ parents or guardians.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.sentences.0.gramm: が marks the sender, and に marks the recipient. Here, the school sends the letter to parents or guardians.
A clause ending in a past-tense verb modifies もの: something that someone did something to. Here, it refers to the letter the school sent.
A formal written affirmative ending equivalent to だ or です.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.sentences.2.vi: Thank you for your continued understanding and cooperation with Takada Elementary School.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.sentences.2.gramm: ご before nouns such as 理解 and 協力 expresses respect for the recipients’ understanding and cooperation.
いただく is the humble form of もらう. いただき connects it to an expression of thanks: thank you for giving us…
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.sentences.3.vi: We are pleased to announce that Takada Elementary School will be holding an exhibition of students’ work.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.sentences.3.vocab: now; turning to the main subject
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.sentences.3.gramm: で combines with は to present a place or organization as the topic, here Takada Elementary School.
Follows a dictionary-form verb to announce an established decision or arrangement: it has been decided that…
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.sentences.4.vi: In addition to works such as paintings, calligraphy, and clay creations, we plan to present a photo exhibition capturing classroom activities, as well as videos showing the students in their everyday school life.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Lists representative examples without implying an exhaustive list. Here, it lists types of work and material to be shown.
Not only… but also… The second part adds the photo exhibition and videos to the creative works.
A modifying clause precedes its noun: おさめた modifies 写真展, while うつした modifies ビデオ, specifying what the photographs and videos capture.
A humble pattern for the speaker’s action directed toward someone respected. お見せする means that the school will show something to the parents or guardians.
A formal, humble version of ～予定でいます: we plan to… The verb before 予定 is in the dictionary form.
A photo exhibition capturing classroom activities supports option 1: displaying photographs featuring the students.
The school plans to show videos of the students, rather than have parents and students film together. The sentence also mentions neither selling works nor making them together.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.sentences.5.vi: We sincerely hope you will attend and see what the students’ life at school is like.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.sentences.5.gramm: A polite expression for having someone come: お越し honors the parents’ visit, while いただく humbly presents the school as receiving that favor.
で marks where an activity takes place, and の connects it to a noun. 学校での様子 means what the students’ activities or life at school are like.
A polite, humble expression for having someone view what one presents. ご覧 is an honorific expression associated with 見る.
Expresses a very polite wish or invitation: we hope you could… いただけたら is the conditional form of いただける, and 存じます is the humble form of 思います.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.outline.0.label: Sender and recipients
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.outline.0.note: Identifies the text as a letter from an elementary school to parents or guardians, followed by the salutation.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.outline.1.label: Opening thanks
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.outline.1.note: Thanks parents and guardians for their continued understanding and cooperation.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.outline.2.label: Exhibition announcement and contents
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.outline.2.note: Announces the exhibition, which will include creative works, photographs of classroom activities, and videos of students. Sentence 4 provides the evidence for option 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.outline.3.label: Invitation to attend
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.outline.3.note: Invites parents and guardians to attend and see what the students’ life at school is like.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t78-p1.vietnamese:
The letter below was sent by an elementary school to its students’ parents or guardians.

Dear Parents and Guardians,

Thank you for your continued understanding and cooperation with Takada Elementary School.

We are pleased to announce that Takada Elementary School will be holding an exhibition of students’ work.

In addition to works such as paintings, calligraphy, and clay creations, we plan to present a photo exhibition capturing classroom activities, as well as videos showing the students in their everyday school life.

We sincerely hope you will attend and see what the students’ life at school is like.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.0.vi: People who are not good at tidying their rooms often have too many things.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Be bad at doing something; の nominalizes the verb phrase.
Describes an ongoing excessive state; here, having too many possessions.
Indicates that something often happens or is often the case.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.1.vi: The key to tidying up is to give things a designated place.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Identifies the essential action: “The key is to…”. こと nominalizes the action, and the final だ is omitted.
States the main method: designate places for things, matching the instruction to decide where things go in option 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.2.vi: If you make a habit of putting things back in that place immediately after using them, they will no longer be scattered everywhere.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Here, marks the time after an action is completed: once you have used something.
If you make a point or habit of doing something; the conditional form of ～ようにする.
Something will also stop happening; here, things being scattered around.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.3.vi: Also, to make room for that designated place, you need to throw away things you do not need.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.3.gramm: The following noun serves the preceding purpose: space for that designated place.
Follows a dictionary-form verb to introduce a goal and what is needed to achieve it.
It is also necessary to do something; も adds discarding unnecessary things to the method already given.
Supports not keeping unnecessary things in option 1. Only unneeded items should be discarded, rather than as many items as possible as in option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.4.vi: Store only as much as fits in your room, arranging things so they are easy to see and take out.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.4.vocab: so as to be easy to see
so as to be easy to take out
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Only the amount that…; 部屋に入る modifies 分, limiting possessions to what fits in the room.
The adverbial form of ～やすい, meaning easy to do; describes storing things so they are easy to see and retrieve.
Placed after a dictionary-form verb at the end of a sentence to give an instruction. Here, しまう means “put away,” rather than forming ～てしまう.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.5.vi: If you do this, you will immediately know what you are missing and will probably also avoid wasteful purchases, such as buying similar items.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Expresses a condition. こうすれば means if you follow the methods just described.
Links benefits: identifying missing items and avoiding wasteful purchases.
Modifies a noun to express similarity; 同じような物 means similar items.
Gives an example of an action; buying similar items is one example of wasteful shopping.
Expresses the writer’s prediction. 防げる is the potential form of 防ぐ, meaning can prevent.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.outline.0.label: The problem: too many things
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.outline.0.note: Opens with the observation that people who struggle to tidy their rooms often have too many possessions.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.outline.1.label: Give things a designated place
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.outline.1.note: Gives the key method: designate a place and return things there after use. This supports deciding where things go in option 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.outline.2.label: Discard unneeded items and store what fits
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.outline.2.note: Make space by discarding unneeded items, keep only what fits, and arrange it for easy viewing and retrieval. Discarding unneeded items provides the other basis for option 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.outline.3.label: Benefits of organizing
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.outline.3.note: Identifying missing items and avoiding wasteful purchases are results of organizing this way, rather than the main tidying method asked about.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t79-p1.vietnamese:
People who are not good at tidying their rooms often have too many things.

The key to tidying up is to give things a designated place.

If you make a habit of putting things back in that place immediately after using them, they will no longer be scattered everywhere.

Also, to make room for that designated place, you need to throw away things you do not need.

Store only as much as fits in your room, arranging things so they are easy to see and take out.

If you do this, you will immediately know what you are missing and will probably also avoid wasteful purchases, such as buying similar items.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.sentences.0.vi: Modern people who cannot eat at home tend to lack the nutrients necessary to sustain life.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.sentences.0.gramm: In a clause modifying a noun, の can replace が as the subject marker. 食事のとれない modifies 現代人: people who cannot have meals.
Expresses purpose: in order to…; here, to sustain life.
Attaches to a verb stem to express a tendency, usually an undesirable one. 不足しがち means tending to be deficient.
A formal written equivalent of the copula だ.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.sentences.1.vi: Supplements were created to make up for those nutritional deficiencies.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Expresses the purpose of creating supplements: to make up for missing nutrients.
The past passive form of 作る: 作られた means were created.
Nominalizes the preceding clause with の and identifies its referent with …だ: what was created for that purpose was supplements.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.sentences.2.vi: Supplements are easy to use and convenient, but quite a few people mistakenly believe that simply taking them is enough.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.sentences.2.gramm: で links two な-adjectives, and が introduces a contrast: easy to use and convenient, but…
Introduces a subset of a group: among them, there are also people who…
Means all one needs to do is…. Here, ただ飲めばいい is the belief the author identifies as mistaken.
Means mistakenly believe that…. と marks the mistaken belief, while ～ている describes the current mental state.
Uses a negative expression to emphasize a substantial number: quite a few also…
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.sentences.3.vi: Taking too many supplements can destroy other nutrients; even taking a large amount may have little effect unless they are taken with certain other foods.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.sentences.3.vocab: do not take; do not consume
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Attaches to a verb stem to express excess: 飲みすぎる means taking too much.
Links a condition to its consequence: if too much is taken…; if not taken with other foods…
Expresses an undesirable result: 壊してしまう means ending up destroying something.
Lists representative situations: destroying other nutrients or having little effect. The ～た form within this pattern does not itself indicate past time.
Expresses concession: even if a large amount is taken, the result may still be disappointing.
Means if…not or unless; states a necessary condition for avoiding an undesirable outcome.
Means together with…; here, taking supplements with certain other foods.
Means not very much or not significantly. たいして効果がない means having little effect.
Describes a harmful consequence of excessive intake, showing that how supplements are taken affects the outcome.
