Shows that even a large intake may have little effect when taken improperly, supporting option 2 for question 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.sentences.4.vi: However, the current reality is that many people are taking supplements in vain because they are taking them incorrectly.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Attaches to a verb stem to describe how to do something: 飲み方 means the way of taking or drinking.
Here it expresses a cause: because of incorrect intake. This differs from the purpose expressed by ために in the first two sentences.
Describes ongoing or habitual behavior: taking supplements in vain.
Nominalizes the entire clause with の to state the current reality: the current situation is that…
An explanatory, emphatic ending after a noun; here it stresses the reality the author wants readers to notice.
Directly states the cause: incorrect intake makes taking supplements ineffective, preventing their intended benefit. Question 1 therefore takes option 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.outline.0.label: Nutritional deficiencies and the purpose of supplements
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces nutritional deficiencies among modern people who cannot eat at home and explains that supplements were created to address those deficiencies.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.outline.1.label: Misunderstanding how to take supplements
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.outline.1.note: Shifts from convenience to the mistaken belief that simply taking supplements is enough. The examples show that excessive intake or missing accompanying foods may cause harm or limit effectiveness.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.outline.2.label: Incorrect intake leads to wasted use
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.outline.2.note: Concludes that many people take supplements in vain because they take them incorrectly. This directly supports option 2; the stated cause is not daily intake, expense and effort, or inevitable nutritional deficiency regardless of intake.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t80-p1.vietnamese:
Modern people who cannot eat at home tend to lack the nutrients necessary to sustain life.

Supplements were created to make up for those nutritional deficiencies.

Supplements are easy to use and convenient, but quite a few people mistakenly believe that simply taking them is enough.

Taking too many supplements can destroy other nutrients; even taking a large amount may have little effect unless they are taken with certain other foods.

However, the current reality is that many people are taking supplements in vain because they are taking them incorrectly.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.0.vi: Take precautions to live safely on your own.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Expresses a purpose: for, in order to; here, to live safely alone.
Makes a suggestion or encourages an action.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.1.vi: When you return home and open the door
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Links actions in sequence: return home, then open the door.
Indicates when an action takes place.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.2.vi: It is dangerous if others find out that you live alone.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Describes an ongoing state: currently living alone.
Nominalizes the clause 一人暮らしをしている: the fact that someone lives alone.
Links a condition to its consequence: if living alone becomes known, there is danger.
Explains why one should create the impression that someone else is home, supporting option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.3.vi: Make a point of saying “I'm home!” as you open the door, as though your family were waiting for you.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Expresses resemblance or appearance: as though…; it does not assert that the family is actually waiting.
Describes an action in progress: waiting.
Two actions performed simultaneously by the same person: speaking while opening the door.
Encourages a deliberate action: make a point of doing…
Directly supports option 4: act as if someone is home; it does not mean asking family to actually wait, as in option 1.
Gives a concrete way to suggest that someone else is inside when entering.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.4.vi: Another effective approach is to ring the bell before opening the door, acting as though you have come to visit someone.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Introduces an additional method: besides that, also…
Dictionary-form verb + 前に: before doing…
押し is the continuative stem of 押す, linking actions in writing much like 押して.
Here, indicates having come to visit someone.
Here, means making it appear that one has come to visit someone.
の nominalizes the action, and も adds the meaning “doing… also.”
Pretending to visit someone also implies that someone is inside, reinforcing option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Introduces a hypothetical situation: if you encounter a burglar.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.6.vi: What would you do if there were a burglar in your room?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Expresses the presence of a person or animal at a location.
Asks how someone would respond: what would you do?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.7.vi: For example, in condominium or apartment buildings, a burglar's only escape routes are the entrance door or a window.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Lists examples without necessarily being exhaustive.
Sets the location or context under discussion.
In 泥棒の逃げる道, の replaces が as the subject marker in a noun-modifying clause: the route by which the burglar escapes.
Uses a negative predicate to mean “only”: only the entrance door or a window.
The escape routes here are for the burglar, not for the resident as option 2 assumes.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.8.vi: Let the burglar escape quickly, and do not chase them.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.sentences.8.gramm: 逃げられる is the potential form of 逃げる: can escape; it is not passive here.
Arranges for a desired state: enabling the burglar to escape quickly. し is the linking stem of する.
Advises avoiding an action: make sure not to chase.
Rules out option 3: the passage advises allowing a quick escape, the opposite of closing the door to trap the burglar.
The advice is not to chase the burglar; the passage does not recommend keeping doors open as in option 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.outline.0.label: Safety when living alone
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the purpose: encouraging people who live alone to take safety precautions.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.outline.1.label: Make it seem someone is home
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.outline.1.note: To avoid revealing that you live alone, greet an imagined person when opening the door or ring the bell as if visiting someone. This supports option 4; family members do not need to actually wait inside as in option 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.outline.2.label: What to do when encountering a burglar
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.outline.2.note: If a burglar is in the room, allow them to escape quickly and do not pursue them. The escape routes discussed belong to the burglar; this section rules out options 2 and 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t81-p1.vietnamese:
～Take precautions to live safely on your own～

○ When you return home and open the door

It is dangerous if others find out that you live alone.

Make a point of saying “I'm home!” as you open the door, as though your family were waiting for you.

Another effective approach is to ring the bell before opening the door, acting as though you have come to visit someone.

○ If you encounter a burglar

What would you do if there were a burglar in your room?

For example, in condominium or apartment buildings, a burglar's only escape routes are the entrance door or a window.

Let the burglar escape quickly, and do not chase them.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.0.vi: When we develop a fever from catching a cold, for example, we take medicine.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Gives an action as one example among possible situations: catching a cold, for example.
Indicates the time when a situation has occurred: when a fever develops.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.1.vi: But what if we could lower a fever through food alone, without taking medicine?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Expresses doing something without doing another action. 飲まずに means without taking medicine.
Means using only a particular means: here, food alone.
Expresses the ability or possibility of performing an action.
Poses a hypothetical situation for the reader to consider: what if…?
Introduces lowering fever through food, supporting option 2 in question 1; this is a hypothesis, while the recommendation appears in the final sentence.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.2.vi: The best-known food for helping with a fever is, above all, rice porridge.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Means to be effective against a symptom or problem.
Emphasizes the most notable example within a topic: when it comes to…, above all it is….
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.3.vi: Rice porridge is easy to digest, and you can add ingredients you like, such as vegetables and eggs, so it is good for replenishing missing nutrients.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.3.gramm: The connective form of an い-adjective: 良い becomes 良く, linking the first property to the next clause.
Lists non-exhaustive examples: vegetables, eggs, and similar ingredients.
入れられる is the potential form of 入れる: can add.
Gives the reason for the statement that follows.
Dictionary-form verb + のにいい means good or suitable for doing something. Here のに expresses purpose, not concession.
Direct evidence for question 2, option 4: porridge is good for replenishing missing nutrients.
Means porridge is easy to digest; it does not state that porridge improves digestive function, as option 2 in question 2 claims.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.4.vi: Next, miso soup with green onions is also very effective against a fever.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Means also works well against…. も adds green onion miso soup to the list of foods.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.5.vi: Green onions help lower a fever because they promote sweating, and miso can replace the salt lost through sweating.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.5.gramm: The causative form: かく becomes かかせる. 汗をかかせる means to cause sweating.
Expresses a cause: because green onions promote sweating.
Presents an action as beneficial to the speaker or people generally; 下げてくれ is the connective form.
Identifies an event that causes a result: salt is lost as a result of sweating.
失われた is the past passive form of 失う, modifying 塩分: the salt that was lost.
Means can replenish using…; で marks the means, and ことができる expresses possibility.
States the effect of green onions, supporting the first part of option 1 in question 3; it also rules out option 1 in question 2 because this effect is not attributed to porridge.
States that miso replaces lost salt, corresponding to the nutrient-replenishment part of option 1 in question 3. The passage specifically refers to salt.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.6.vi: Dandelion roots that have been dried are also said to help lower a fever.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.6.gramm: もの is modified by a sequence of actions: material that has been exposed to dry. させた is a past causative form.
Expresses a beneficial effect: helping lower a fever.
At the end of the sentence, reports what is said or heard: it is said that….
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.7.vi: Then there is matcha ice cream.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.7.gramm: The plain affirmative copula after a noun. The topic is omitted, continuing the preceding list of foods.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.8.vi: Because it melts quickly and is easy to eat, it would probably be good to start with this when you have no appetite.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.8.vocab: this, referring to matcha ice cream
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Attaches to a verb's ます-stem to express ease: 食べやすい means easy to eat.
Gives the reason: because it melts quickly and is easy to eat.
In the clause modifying とき, の can replace が: 食欲のない is equivalent to 食欲がない.
Means to start eating with…; これ refers to the matcha ice cream in the preceding sentence.
Offers a tentative recommendation: it would probably be good to….
Being easy to eat when appetite is poor describes matcha ice cream, ruling out option 3 in question 3 about green onion miso soup.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.9.vi: As described above, there is indeed a wide variety of foods that are effective in lowering a fever.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.9.gramm: 以上のように means as described above and introduces a summary of the examples.
Means to be effective for doing…. In this sentence, 効果のある modifies 食べ物, with の replacing が.
Introduces a topic and states what exists within it: there are many kinds of fever-lowering foods.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.10.vi: When you have a fever, rather than relying only on medicine, why not first try foods like these?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.10.gram: Means to rely only or excessively on…. ばかり restricts what one relies on.
Rejects one approach in favor of another: instead of relying only on medicine, try food first.
Marks a starting point or priority: begin with the foods mentioned.
Means to try doing something to see the result.
Offers a gentle suggestion: why not try…?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.sentences.10.keys: Main evidence for question 1, option 2: the author advises against relying only on medicine, without saying to abandon it completely.
The recommendation to try these foods first supports option 2 in question 1; it does not discuss taking medicine after meals or waiting until the fever falls.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.outline.0.label: Introducing food as a way to lower fever
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.outline.0.note: The author moves from the usual practice of taking medicine for fever to the possibility of lowering it through food alone.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.outline.1.label: Porridge and replenishing nutrients
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.outline.1.note: Porridge is presented as a typical choice that is easy to digest and allows added ingredients to replenish missing nutrients.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.outline.2.label: Two benefits of green onion miso soup
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.outline.2.note: According to the passage, green onions promote sweating to help lower fever, while miso replaces salt lost through sweating.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.outline.3.label: Dandelion roots and matcha ice cream
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.outline.3.note: The passage adds dried dandelion roots and matcha ice cream; being easy to eat with poor appetite describes the ice cream, distinguishing it from green onion miso soup.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.outline.4.label: The recommendation to try foods first
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.outline.4.note: The author summarizes the variety of foods and recommends trying them first rather than relying only on medicine. This is the main evidence for the author's position.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t82-p1.vietnamese:
When we develop a fever from catching a cold, for example, we take medicine.

But what if we could lower a fever through food alone, without taking medicine?

The best-known food for helping with a fever is, above all, rice porridge.

Rice porridge is easy to digest, and you can add ingredients you like, such as vegetables and eggs, so it is good for replenishing missing nutrients.

Next, miso soup with green onions is also very effective against a fever.

Green onions help lower a fever because they promote sweating, and miso can replace the salt lost through sweating.

Dandelion roots that have been dried are also said to help lower a fever.

Then there is matcha ice cream.

Because it melts quickly and is easy to eat, it would probably be good to start with this when you have no appetite.

As described above, there is indeed a wide variety of foods that are effective in lowering a fever.

When you have a fever, rather than relying only on medicine, why not first try foods like these?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.0.vi: Recently, the number of people shopping at large supermarkets rather than shopping streets has been increasing.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Not A, but B (used to negate the former and affirm the latter).
Expresses a trend or change that has been continuing from the past up to the present.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.1.vi: At large supermarkets, above all, the prices are very low.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Adverb emphasizing the most prominent aspect ("in any case", "above all").
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.2.vi: In addition, it is convenient because payments for various products, such as groceries and daily necessities, can be completed at a single cash register.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Gives representative examples ("such as...", "and the like").
Direct evidence for Question 1: The text states supermarkets are convenient because payments for various products can be completed at a single register, which matches Option 3 (paying for various foods takes only one time, making it convenient). Option 1 is incorrect because the text says prices are cheap overall rather than depending on the item; Option 2 is not mentioned; Option 4 describes shopping streets, not supermarkets.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.3.vi: Although shopping streets are inconvenient because you have to pay at each individual shop, when you go there, the familiar clerk will kindly tell you about cheap or delicious items.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Expresses obligation or necessity ("must do / have to do").
Someone does something favorably for the speaker.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.4.vi: Each has its good and bad points, but a great many people choose large supermarkets because they are "cheap and convenient."
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Lists multiple items meaning "both A and B".
Quotative particle expressing reasoning or motivation ("with the reason that...").
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.5.vi: However, it is said that to prevent food-related accidents, having a "face-to-face relationship" where the shop and the buyer know each other is vital.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.5.vocab: in order to / for the sake of
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Indicates purpose or objective ("in order to...", "for the purpose of...").
Reports hearsay or acknowledged general opinion ("it is said that...").
Central evidence for Question 2: The author highlights that establishing a 'face-to-face relationship' between shop and buyer is essential for preventing food accidents. This concept is clarified in the next sentence as shops caring for their customers by selling only safe goods, aligning with Option 2 (shops sell food while keeping customers in mind).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.6.vi: When they know who the buyers are, shops naturally come to sell only safe, high-quality goods.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Conditional conjunction indicating a natural, inevitable consequence ("when / if...").
Indicates a gradual change in habit or state ("come to do...", "reach a point where...").
Provides an explanatory nuance to clarify a reason or reality.
Supporting evidence for Question 2: This explains the practical meaning of a 'face-to-face relationship': knowing the customer leads the shopkeeper to naturally sell only good and safe goods out of care for them (confirming Option 2). Options 1 (not trading imported food), 3 (befriending the cashier), and 4 (prioritizing freshness over price) are not stated in the text.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.7.vi: Does this not mean that the shopping streets, which have been disappearing recently, might actually be ideal for food safety?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Conjunction used to draw an inference from the preceding context ("That means...", "In other words...").
Rhetorical question expressing a modest or cautious opinion ("Isn't it likely that...?").
Comparative evidence for Question 3: The author argues that shopping streets, where personal relationships exist, are actually ideal for food safety—a distinctive merit that supermarkets lack despite their affordability and convenience. This confirms Option 1 (shopping streets possess good qualities that supermarkets lack). Options 2, 3, and 4 are unsupported or contradict the text's comparisons.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.8.vi: Perhaps instead of merely seeking cheapness and convenience, we need to reconsider the virtues of shopping streets for the sake of food safety.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Not merely doing A, but... (advising against one-sided pursuit).
Try doing something to see the result.
Expresses a necessity to do something ("need to...").
Expresses cautious conjecture or deduction ("perhaps / might be").
Direct concluding evidence for Question 3: The author balances 'cheapness and convenience' (the supermarket's strengths) against 'food safety' (the distinctive virtue of shopping streets), concluding that we should re-evaluate shopping streets. This directly demonstrates that shopping streets hold merits not found in large supermarkets (Option 1).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.outline.0.label: Current shopping trends and supermarket advantages
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the growing trend of consumers choosing large supermarkets due to cheap prices and convenient single-counter checkout.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.outline.1.label: Shopping street characteristics and consumer habits
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.outline.1.note: Discusses the inconvenience yet friendliness of shopping streets, noting that most consumers still prefer supermarkets for price and ease.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.outline.2.label: Importance of buyer-seller relationships for food safety
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.outline.2.note: Shifts focus: To prevent food scandals, a face-to-face relationship between shopkeeper and customer is crucial in ensuring food quality.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.outline.3.label: Value of shopping streets and a call for reconsideration
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.outline.3.note: Concludes that traditional shopping streets are ideal for food safety and urges people to re-evaluate their worth beyond cheapness and convenience.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t83-p1.vietnamese:
Recently, the number of people shopping at large supermarkets rather than traditional shopping streets has been increasing.

At large supermarkets, prices are very low above all else.

Furthermore, it is convenient because payments for various items, such as groceries and daily necessities, can be completed at a single cash register.

Shopping streets are somewhat inconvenient since you have to pay at each individual store, but when you visit, the familiar staff will kindly tell you about cheap or delicious items.

While both have their advantages and disadvantages, a great many people choose large supermarkets because they are "cheap and convenient."

However, it is said that to prevent food-related incidents, having a "face-to-face relationship" where the shop and the customer know each other is vital.

When a shop knows who the buyers are, it naturally comes to sell only safe and good products.

Doesn't this mean that the traditional shopping streets disappearing in recent years might actually be ideal for food safety?

Perhaps instead of merely seeking cheapness and convenience, we need to reconsider the virtues of shopping streets for the sake of food safety.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.0.vi: At a station bustling with people coming and going, I noticed a traveler from overseas carrying a large bag.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.0.gramm: A preceding clause modifies a noun: たくさんの人が行き来する modifies 駅.
持った modifies 旅行者 and describes the traveler as carrying a bag, rather than having finished carrying it.
Indicates origin: 海外からの旅行者 means a traveler from overseas.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.1.vi: Seeing the traveler with a guidebook in one hand and looking very anxious, I instinctively spoke to them in English: “Are you having any trouble?”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.1.gramm: With something in one hand; here it describes the traveler's posture.
Describes an observed appearance: 不安そうな様子 means an anxious-looking demeanor.
Connects noticing the anxious appearance with subsequently speaking to the traveler.
A respectful question about the listener's state: お困りですか means “Are you having trouble?”
と marks the words spoken when initiating contact with someone.
Q1: The anxious appearance prompts the writer to approach; the writer does not yet know the traveler needs a platform.
Q1, option 3: The question shows that the writer's purpose is to help the traveler with a difficulty.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.2.vi: “How do I get to the platform for trains to Kyoto?”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.2.gramm: A clause modifies a noun. In context, 京都へ行くホーム means the platform for trains going to Kyoto.
Asks for an appropriate course of action; どう行ったらいい means “How should I get there?”
An informal question ending seeking an explanation or guidance.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.3.vi: “Oh, in that case, I think it's platform eight.”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Uses the information just given as the basis for a response: “in that case.”
Expresses uncertainty or a tentative judgment: “I think…” or “perhaps…”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.4.vi: As I said this, I thought, “Will they be all right? They're in an unfamiliar country and cannot speak Japanese. It's crowded here, too, so they might get lost.” With that in mind, I said, ①“Then please follow me.”
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Two actions occur simultaneously: the writer speaks while thinking.
Expresses an uncertain self-directed question; here it conveys concern for the traveler.
Emphasizes an additional inability: the traveler cannot speak Japanese either.
Adds one reason among others: the station is also crowded.
Expresses an undesirable outcome: ending up lost.
Expresses a possibility rather than certainty.
Makes a polite request: ついて来てください means “please follow me.”
Q2, option 4: The writer worries that the traveler may not reach platform eight alone because the country is unfamiliar, they cannot speak Japanese, and they may get lost in the crowd.
そう思って directly links the concern about getting lost to the decision to lead the traveler.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.5.vi: I can manage this much English.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Indicates degree: このくらいの英語 refers to the amount or level of English just used.
Limits the statement to a condition: if only this much English is needed, the writer can manage.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.6.vi: It feels good to receive kindness when you are in trouble.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Indicates a time or situation: 困ったとき means when in trouble and does not necessarily refer only to the past.
Describes receiving a beneficial action from someone, from the recipient's perspective.
の nominalizes the preceding action so that a feeling about it can be stated.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.7.vi: I have had that kind of experience myself.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.7.gramm: States that the speaker also has what was just mentioned; も emphasizes the shared experience.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.8.vi: I fondly miss the woman who was kind to me when I got lost in rural Italy, could find neither a bus nor a taxi, and did not even understand the language.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.8.gramm: A linking form common in writing: 迷い connects to the next event, similarly to 迷って.
Negates both items: neither a bus nor a taxi could be found.
言葉もわからない emphasizes that the writer did not even understand the local language.
Someone performed an action benefiting the writer; this conveys gratitude toward the woman.
親切にしてくれた modifies おばさん; the main statement expresses fond longing for that woman.
Q3: Identifies the woman who once helped the writer, providing the background for the comparison in the final sentence; this is not itself the immediate reason for the happy return home.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.9.vi: Thinking that perhaps I, too, had managed to do a little good, just as that woman had done for me, I returned home ②feeling happy.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.sentences.9.gramm: に marks the person who performed a beneficial action: that woman previously helped the writer.
Expresses similarity: doing good just as the woman had done for the writer.
少しは emphasizes a modest minimum, “at least a little”; 私も means “I, too,” connecting the former recipient with the present helper.
Expresses a tentative, modest reflection: “perhaps I, too, have…”
The writer reflects on the good deed while returning home.
Indicates the mood accompanying an action: returning in a happy mood.
帰ってきた describes coming back to the reference point, home.
Q3, option 3: The writer is happy to have helped someone in difficulty, just as someone once helped them; the focus is the good deed, rather than English ability or merely remembering the woman.
The mood asked about in Q3 is directly linked to the immediately preceding thought about having done some good.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.outline.0.label: Noticing an anxious traveler and offering help
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.outline.0.note: The writer notices a traveler at the station and approaches because the traveler looks anxious. The initial purpose is to help; the writer does not yet know what specific help is needed.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.outline.1.label: Leading the traveler out of concern
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.outline.1.note: The traveler asks for the platform for Kyoto. After answering, the writer worries that the traveler might get lost and offers to lead the way. The comment about English merely shows that the writer can handle the communication needed.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.outline.2.label: Recalling kindness received
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.outline.2.note: Reflecting on the happiness of receiving help in difficulty, the writer recalls a woman who helped when they were lost in Italy. This memory provides the background for the comparison in the final sentence.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.outline.3.label: Happy to have helped someone else
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.outline.3.note: The writer returns home happy because they feel they have done some good by helping someone in difficulty, just as the woman once helped them.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t84-p1.vietnamese:
At a station bustling with people coming and going, I noticed a traveler from overseas carrying a large bag.

Seeing the traveler with a guidebook in one hand and looking very anxious, I instinctively spoke to them in English: “Are you having any trouble?”

“How do I get to the platform for trains to Kyoto?”

“Oh, in that case, I think it's platform eight.”

As I said this, I thought, “Will they be all right? They're in an unfamiliar country and cannot speak Japanese. It's crowded here, too, so they might get lost.” With that in mind, I said, ①“Then please follow me.”

I can manage this much English.

It feels good to receive kindness when you are in trouble. I have had that kind of experience myself.

I fondly miss the woman who was kind to me when I got lost in rural Italy, could find neither a bus nor a taxi, and did not even understand the language.

Thinking that perhaps I, too, had managed to do a little good, just as that woman had done for me, I returned home ②feeling happy.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.0.vi: Since Japan’s first convenience store opened in 1974, convenient stores operating around the clock have attracted more and more customers.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.0.gramm: After or since an event; the opening of the first store sets the starting point.
Connects descriptions: operating 24 hours and being convenient.
Expresses a change continuing from the past to the present: growing customer numbers.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.1.vi: Not only the new products released one after another but also the wide range of services account for their popularity.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.1.gramm: Not only A but also B; identifies both new products and services as reasons for popularity without comparing quantities.
A preceding clause modifies a noun: 次々に出る describes 新商品.
Question 1: establishes that stores offer many services in addition to selling products.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.2.vi: At convenience stores, people can do various things, such as reserve concert tickets, drop off parcels for delivery, and pay utility bills.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Lists representative examples rather than an exhaustive set of services.
Sets a location as the topic or context: at convenience stores.
Expresses what is possible; いろいろなことができる means that various things can be done.
Question 1: concrete examples show that stores provide services beyond selling goods.
Question 1: directly supports option 3, which says that many services are available.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.3.vi: Convenience stores are now more than just places that sell goods.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Not merely something that does one thing; denies the limitation to selling goods, not the act of selling itself.
No longer; emphasizes that the role of convenience stores has changed.
Presents an explanation or conclusion drawn from the preceding examples.
Question 1: stores do more than sell goods; they also offer many services, supporting option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.4.vi: Recently, however, convenient shopping options such as supermarkets open late at night have increased, and competition between convenience stores and these shops has grown fiercer.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Marks a time limit: remaining open until late at night.
In 開いている, expresses the continuing state of being open.
An i-adjective takes ～く＋なる to express change: becoming fiercer.
A change has developed up to the present: competition has grown fiercer.
Question 3: gives the background to the new service; the direct purpose appears in the next sentence.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.5.vi: Therefore, to avoid losing customers to other stores, some convenience stores introduced a new service called “goyōkiki,” an order-taking and home-delivery service.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.5.gramm: An adverse passive construction: having customers taken by another store; に marks the competing store.
So that something does not happen; expresses the aim of avoiding customer loss.
A relative clause modifies a noun: the new service that some convenience stores introduced.
Question 3: directly states the aim of retaining customers, matching option 4.
Question 2: identifies the service being asked about; sentences 7–8 explain how it works.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.6.vi: “Goyōkiki” means shop staff going from house to house to take orders and deliver goods, a practice followed by local shops in the past.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Defines a term: ご用聞き involves taking orders at people’s homes and delivering goods; ことで connects the definition to the next clause.
を marks the places visited in succession: making rounds of houses.
Describes a practice regularly carried out in the past.
Question 2: this is the traditional method; confusing it with the convenience-store service would lead to option 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.7.vi: Convenience stores do not visit houses to take orders; they receive orders by phone or over the Internet and deliver the ordered goods to customers’ homes.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.7.gramm: A negative connective equivalent to ～ないで; 回らず means without going from house to house.
In 家は, は highlights a contrast with the traditional method: visiting houses is not part of this service.
Marks the means: taking orders by phone or over the Internet.
に marks the delivery destination: delivering to a home.
Question 2: rules out option 2 because convenience stores do not visit homes to take orders.
Question 2: includes both remote ordering and home delivery, matching option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.8.vi: The service is not only frequently used by older people who cannot go shopping; it has also become popular among busy housewives.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Go to do an activity: 買い物に行く means to go shopping.
Negates ability: 行けない means cannot go, whereas 行かない means do not go.
Not only…but also among…; extends the service’s appeal to busy housewives.
Become popular among a group; に marks that group.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.9.vi: What services will appear next? There is much to look forward to from convenience stores in the future.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.9.vocab: from now on; in the future
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.sentences.9.gramm: Introduces an embedded question or something the writer wonders about: what service will appear next.
Here it means to emerge or come into existence, rather than ability to perform an action.
Also something to look forward to; expresses the writer’s positive expectations for the future.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.outline.0.label: More than a place to shop
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the growth of convenience stores and their varied services. Ticket reservations, parcel acceptance, and bill payments explain statement ① and support option 3 for question 1.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.outline.1.label: Competition prompts a new service
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.outline.1.note: ところが introduces fiercer competition, and そこで leads to the response: a new service. The explicit aim is to prevent other stores from taking customers, so question 3 takes option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.outline.2.label: How orders and delivery work
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.outline.2.note: Contrasts traditional house-to-house order taking with convenience stores’ phone or Internet orders followed by home delivery. This supports option 4 for question 2. The service appeals to older people and busy housewives.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.outline.3.label: Looking forward to future services
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.outline.3.note: The writer closes with positive anticipation of the services convenience stores will develop in the future.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t85-p1.vietnamese:
Since Japan’s first convenience store opened in 1974, convenient stores operating around the clock have attracted more and more customers. Not only the new products released one after another but also the wide range of services account for their popularity. At convenience stores, people can do various things, such as reserve concert tickets, drop off parcels for delivery, and pay utility bills. Convenience stores are now more than just places that sell goods.

Recently, however, convenient shopping options such as supermarkets open late at night have increased, and competition between convenience stores and these shops has grown fiercer. Therefore, to avoid losing customers to other stores, some convenience stores introduced a new service called “goyōkiki,” an order-taking and home-delivery service.

“Goyōkiki” means shop staff going from house to house to take orders and deliver goods, a practice followed by local shops in the past. Convenience stores do not visit houses to take orders; they receive orders by phone or over the Internet and deliver the ordered goods to customers’ homes. The service is not only frequently used by older people who cannot go shopping; it has also become popular among busy housewives.

What services will appear next? There is much to look forward to from convenience stores in the future.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.0.vi: Some people feel uneasy when they have no plans.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Expresses a condition with a habitual result: having no plans causes uneasiness.
Expresses a change into a state: becoming uneasy.
Question 1: Defines the type of person illustrated by the woman in the next sentence, supporting option 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.1.vi: The woman I saw at a café the other day was just such a person.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.1.gramm: 見かけた modifies 女性: the woman whom the narrator saw.
Past form of だ, identifying the woman as the type just described.
Question 1: そう refers back to feeling uneasy without plans in sentence 0 and directly attributes that trait to the woman.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.2.vi: She took a red planner out of her bag and gazed at it for a while.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Links successive actions: taking out the planner and then looking at it.
Describes an action continuing at a past point in time.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.3.vi: Then she suddenly started making phone calls, arranging drinks, meals, and dates one after another and adding the plans to her planner.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Attaches to a verb stem to mean starting an action; かけ始め is the connective form.
Lists examples without necessarily giving an exhaustive list.
Shows an action progressing over time, here entering successive plans into the planner.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.4.vi: However, there seemed to be one day she simply could not fill with plans.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Emphasizes that something cannot be achieved despite all efforts.
Expresses an inference based on the narrator's observations: it seemed that.
Within the clause modifying 一日, の replaces subject-marking が: 予定の埋まらない means 予定が埋まらない.
Question 2: Introduces the remaining gap in her schedule, establishing what she wants to resolve before feeling satisfied.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.5.gramm: A noun-ending fragment omits the predicate to emphasize the empty Thursday.
Question 2: Identifies Thursday as the gap that needs filling.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.6.vi: Apparently, she could not bear that.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Marks and emphasizes the person concerned: for her.
Past negative of the potential expression: could not.
Marks the narrator's inference from observed behavior.
Questions 1 and 2: それ refers to the empty Thursday; she cannot tolerate a gap in her schedule.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.7.vi: Finally, she called her regular hair salon and insisted that she wanted her perm redone because she did not like the one she had recently had, and that they should book her for Thursday because that was her only free day the following week. At last, she had a plan for Thursday.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.7.gramm: いつも行っている describes regularly visiting that salon.
Introduce the two reasons she gives: disliking the perm and being free only on Thursday.
Attaches to a verb stem to mean doing something again or redoing it; かけ直す means redoing a perm.
Expresses wanting another person to do something: redo the perm and make an appointment.
Means only, with all other possibilities excluded; 木曜日しか空いていない means being free only on Thursday.
と marks the content of the statement or request she insists on.
Question 2: The salon appointment fills the remaining empty day; booking the salon is the means, while eliminating the gap is what satisfies her.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.8.vi: She gazed at the page, now black with entries, and smiled with apparent satisfaction.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Past passive of 埋める: the page had been filled with entries.
Describes the apparent manner of an action: smiling as though satisfied.
Question 2: The page is completely filled with entries, leaving no gaps; this is the main evidence for option 3.
Question 2: She smiles while looking at the fully scheduled page, revealing the source of her satisfaction.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.9.vi: My planner, on the other hand, is completely white.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.9.gramm: Introduces a contrast, shifting from her full planner to the narrator's blank one.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.10.vi: To be precise, all sorts of things are written in the section covering the past up to yesterday, but from today onward it is as blank as an empty sheet.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.10.gram: Introduces a precise clarification of the preceding general statement.
Contrasts two time spans: up to yesterday and from today onward.
Combines the passive with ている to describe the resulting state of entries being present.
Links contrasting clauses: past dates contain entries, while dates from today onward are blank.
Emphasizes resemblance: looking just like blank paper.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.10.keys: Question 3: Past dates contain entries, so option 4's claim that the entire planner is blank is incorrect.
Question 3: The section from today onward is blank, supporting option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.11.vi: Nothing is written in the section for the future.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.11.gram: Expresses total negation: not a single thing is written.
Negative passive state: no entries have been written.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.11.keys: Question 3: Directly states that nothing is written for the future, confirming option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.12.vi: Like her, I too opened my planner.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.12.gram: Expresses doing something like someone else: opening the planner as she did.
Marks the narrator as doing the same thing: I too opened my planner.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.13.vi: But no matter how long I stared at it, no plans came to mind.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.sentences.13.gram: Repeats the same verb to emphasize that continued effort does not change the outcome.
Expresses total negation in the past: no plans at all came to mind.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.outline.0.label: Uneasy without plans
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces people who feel uneasy without plans and identifies the woman at the café as one of them.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.outline.1.label: The empty Thursday
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.outline.1.note: She repeatedly calls to arrange activities, but Thursday remains empty, which she apparently cannot bear.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.outline.2.label: Satisfied with a full schedule
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.outline.2.note: She books a salon appointment to fill Thursday and smiles at the densely filled page. Her satisfaction comes from eliminating the gap in her schedule.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.outline.3.label: The narrator's blank future
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.outline.3.note: Contrasts the narrator's planner with hers: past dates contain many entries, but nothing is written from today onward. The entire planner is not blank.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.outline.4.label: No plans come to mind
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.outline.4.note: The narrator opens the planner as she did but cannot think of any plans, completing the contrast between them.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t87-p1.vietnamese:
Some people feel uneasy when they have no plans.

The woman I saw at a café the other day was just such a person.

She took a red planner out of her bag and gazed at it for a while.

Then she suddenly started making phone calls, arranging drinks, meals, and dates one after another and adding the plans to her planner.

However, there seemed to be one day she simply could not fill with plans.

A blank Thursday. Apparently, she could not bear that.

Finally, she called her regular hair salon and insisted that she wanted her perm redone because she did not like the one she had recently had, and that they should book her for Thursday because that was her only free day the following week. At last, she had a plan for Thursday.

She gazed at the page, now black with entries, and smiled with apparent satisfaction.

My planner, on the other hand, is completely white.

To be precise, all sorts of things are written in the section covering the past up to yesterday, but from today onward it is as blank as an empty sheet.

Nothing is written in the section for the future.

Like her, I too opened my planner. But no matter how long I stared at it, no plans came to mind.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.0.vi: This town was built about 40 years ago.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Follows a quantity to express approximation ('about', 'around').
Clue for Q2: The town was constructed about 40 years ago, indicating it was a newly built town (新しい町) back then.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.1.vi: It was a very beautiful town.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.2.vi: It is located about 1 hour by train from Tokyo, and about 20 minutes by bus from the station.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.2.gramm: Indicates the means of transportation (by train, by bus).
Clue for Q2: Taking 1 hour from Tokyo plus a 20-minute bus ride shows it was inconvenient (不便), ruling out the convenient town option.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.3.vi: We got married 40 years ago and bought a house in this town.
Clue for Q1: The author married 40 years ago, indicating along with later clues that they are a married elderly person (結婚している老人).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.4.vi: It is a large house with a spacious garden.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Noun-modifying relative clause ('広い庭がある' modifies '大きな家').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.5.vi: Many young married couples also moved into the neighboring houses.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.5.gramm: Indicates movement toward the speaker's location (moved here).
Clue for Q2: Many young couples moved in 40 years ago, ruling out the option that it was inhabited by elderly people back then.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.6.vi: There was plenty of greenery here, making it a very good place to raise children.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Indicates purpose or context of evaluation ('for raising children').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.7.vi: Our daughter also grew up healthy and lively together with the neighborhood children.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Indicates change of state ('became big, grew up').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.8.vi: Eventually, the children of every household grew up into adults and left the town.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Indicates movement away from the current perspective (went out and away).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.9.vi: Most people currently living in the town are over 60 years old, and this town has become a town of elderly people.
Clue for Q1 and Q3: Current inhabitants (including the author) are mostly over 60 (elderly), making it a town where old people live (老人が住む町).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.10.vi: As one gets older, weeding the garden also becomes difficult work.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.10.gram: Conditional expressing natural consequence ('as/when one ages...').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.11.vi: Because the hospital is far away, it is worrying if one suddenly falls ill.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.11.gram: Expresses objective reason ('because the hospital is far').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.12.vi: Because of that, some people have moved to convenient apartments in Tokyo.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.12.gram: Expresses the existence of people who did something ('some people have moved').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.13.vi: There are also houses where no one lives because family members were hospitalized due to illness.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.13.gram: Expresses an unintentional or regrettable occurrence.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.14.vi: The town suddenly became lonely and quiet.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.14.gram: Indicates a change of state ('became lonely/deserted').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.14.keys: Clue for Q3: Confirms the current state of the town as having become lonely and quiet (さびしい町).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.15.vi: Because it is an inconvenient town, no young people are newly moving in.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.15.gram: Expresses cause/reason after na-adjective ('because it is inconvenient').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.15.keys: Clue for Q2 & Q3: Shows the town's inconvenient nature (不便な町) and that no young people move in, confirming it is now a lonely town of elderly residents.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.16.vi: Lately, I have come to feel that daily life is also tough.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.16.gram: Indicates a gradual shift in habit or perception ('have come to think/feel').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.17.vi: Since there are no stores nearby, I go shopping near the station in my husband's car.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.17.gram: Indicates the purpose of movement (go to do shopping).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.17.keys: Clue for Q1: The author mentions 'my husband' (主人), proving that she is married and currently living with her husband (結婚している老人).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.18.vi: From here to the station takes about 15 minutes by car, but if you walk it takes 1 hour.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.18.gram: Sets a conditional topic ('if by car...').
Hypothetical condition ('if one walks, it takes 1 hour').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.19.vi: Right now, what I am most worried about is how long the buses will continue to run.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.19.gram: Emphatic pattern: 'The thing that ... most is that ...'.
Embedded question clause ('how long the buses will run').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.19.keys: Direct clue for Q4: Directly states the greatest concern (一番心配していること) is how long the bus will continue running, matching the fear that buses will disappear (バスがなくなってしまうこと).
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.20.vi: If the number of people riding the bus decreases, the buses will probably stop coming.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.21.vi: When we get older and can no longer drive a car, if there are no buses, what will happen to our lives? I am truly worried.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.21.gram: Expresses loss of capability ('become unable to drive').
Hypothetical condition ('if there are no buses').
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.sentences.21.keys: Clue for Q4: Stresses that lacking buses (バスがなかったら) when unable to drive will severely threaten their livelihood, explaining why this is the author's primary worry.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.outline.0.label: The town 40 years ago and child-raising years
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.outline.0.note: The town was built 40 years ago; although far from Tokyo, it was green and ideal for young couples, including the author, to settle down and raise children.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.outline.1.label: Children leaving and the town becoming aged
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.outline.1.note: As children grew up and left, residents aged past 60; distance to hospitals and emptying houses made the town lonely, with no new young arrivals.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.outline.2.label: Daily inconveniences and anxiety over bus services
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.outline.2.note: Daily life has become difficult without nearby shops; the author's greatest worry is that when they can no longer drive, bus service will cease due to fewer passengers.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t88-p1.vietnamese:
This town was built about 40 years ago. It was a very beautiful town, located about an hour by train from Tokyo and roughly 20 minutes by bus from the train station. We got married 40 years ago and bought a house in this town. It is a large house with a spacious garden. Many young married couples also moved into neighboring houses. With abundant greenery, it was a wonderful place to raise children. Our daughter also grew up healthy and lively alongside the neighborhood kids.

Eventually, the children from every household grew into adults and left the town. Most of the people currently living here are 60 or older, and it has turned into a town of elderly residents. As we age, even weeding the garden becomes hard labor. With the hospital far away, falling suddenly ill is a major worry. Because of that, some people have moved to convenient condominiums in Tokyo. There are also empty homes where no one lives because family members were hospitalized with illnesses. The town has suddenly become lonely. Being an inconvenient town, no young people move in anymore.

Lately, I have come to feel that daily life is quite tough as well. Since there are no stores nearby, I go shopping near the station in my husband's car. It takes about 15 minutes by car from here to the station, but walking takes a full hour. Right now, what worries me most is how long the buses will keep running. If ridership drops, the buses will probably stop coming altogether. When we grow too old to drive, if there are no buses either, what will become of our lives? I am truly deeply concerned.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.sentences.0.vi: This is an essay written by Tajima.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.sentences.7.vi: The man said “Thank you” to me many times.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Reports quoted words addressed to someone; に marks the listener and と marks the quotation.

An inviting or urging form of いらっしゃる; here it warmly invites the listener to return.

The invitation to return is the main referent of それ in the next sentence; it is not an invitation to a private home as in option 2 of Question 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.sentences.9.vi: Hearing that made me very happy, and I thought I would like to come and see him again.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.sentences.9.gramm: An い-adjective takes ～く before なる to express a change of state: become happy.
A verb stem before に来る expresses the purpose of coming: 会いに来る means come to see someone.
Expresses a wish felt at that time: thought one would like to do something.
Direct evidence for Question 4, answer 1: Tajima wants to see the man again.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.sentences.11.vi: I usually spend my time doing things like playing games with friends, but tomorrow I plan to visit the man.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.sentences.11.gram: Spend time doing things such as a given activity; the activity is an example.
Provides background before a contrast: usually playing games, but visiting the man tomorrow.
A verb stem + に行く expresses the purpose of going: go to see someone.
Follows a dictionary-form verb to express an intention or plan.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.sentences.11.keys: Rules out options 3 and 4 of Question 4: the usual activity is gaming with friends, not routinely visiting the man or gaming with him.
Confirms the planned visit tomorrow, linking it to the wish to see him again in sentence 9.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.sentences.12.vi: Next time, I hope to take a guitar along and sing together with him.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.sentences.12.gram: Take something along to another place; 持っていって connects it to the following clause.
歌えたら combines the potential form 歌える with conditional たら: if we can sing.
Expresses a hope: it would be nice if something could happen.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.sentences.12.keys: Tajima plans to bring the guitar; this does not support the man's owning one as stated in option 2 of Question 2.
The hoped-for activity on the next visit is singing together, not gaming as in option 4 of Question 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.outline.0.label: Introducing the visit
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces Tajima's essay, the visit to Hikari Home last Saturday, and the elderly people living there.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.outline.1.label: Meeting the 90-year-old man
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.outline.1.note: Tajima listens to the man and shares a meal with him. The man cannot walk, has five children, and sang well when young.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.outline.2.label: Helping him eat
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.outline.2.note: Since the man cannot hold a spoon, Tajima helps feed him. The man repeatedly thanks Tajima and invites Tajima to return.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.outline.3.label: Wanting to return and sing together
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.outline.3.note: Tajima feels happy and wants to see the man again, so plans to visit tomorrow and hopes to bring a guitar and sing with him.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t89-p1.vietnamese:
This is an essay written by Tajima.

Last Saturday, I went to a place called Hikari Home. Many elderly men and women who cannot live with their families live there. I listened to a 90-year-old man tell stories and shared a meal with him. Because he could not walk, he remained seated in a chair the whole time. He told me all sorts of things, such as having as many as five children who had all graduated from good universities, and being a good singer when he was young.

At lunchtime, the man could not hold a spoon, so I brought food to his mouth for him. He said “Thank you” to me many times. Then he kindly said, “If you'd like, come again.” Hearing that made me very happy, and I thought I would like to come and see him again.

Tomorrow is Saturday. I usually spend my time doing things like playing games with friends, but tomorrow I plan to visit the man. Next time, I hope to take a guitar along and sing together with him.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.0.vi: Everyone knows that getting plenty of calcium is good for building healthy bones.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Introduces what is needed or advisable to achieve a purpose.
It is good or advisable to do something; の nominalizes the action.
Turns an entire statement into a noun phrase: the fact that…
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.1.vi: However, it is not widely known that exercise is just as important as getting calcium.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.1.vocab: not very; used with a negative
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.1.gramm: To about the same degree as…
Packages the preceding statement as the topic of the sentence.
Not much or not very; does not express complete negation.
Negative passive state: is not or has not been…
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.2.vi: If people do not get enough exercise as children, their bones become more prone to breaking as they age, and they may develop osteoporosis.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.2.gramm: If one does not…; introduces a resulting consequence.
Become more likely or prone to…
Called…; introduces the name of the disease.
May or might; expresses possibility rather than certainty.
A written explanatory ending that emphasizes the statement.
Q1: introduces the condition leading to bone risks and explains why exercise matters.
Q1, option 3: exercise makes bone disease less likely. かもしれない expresses possibility, not the certainty of broken bones asserted in option 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.3.vi: Although exercise is important, that does not mean just any kind of exercise will do.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Although it is said that…; qualifies the preceding statement.
It does not mean that…; rejects an overgeneralization.
Q4: the type of exercise matters, ruling out option 1, which says any exercise will do.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.4.vi: Activities such as dancing, running, and jumping are effective for building healthy bones, while swimming is said to have little effect in this respect.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.4.vocab: not much; used with a negative
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.4.gramm: Lists representative examples without being exhaustive.
Not much…; does not mean none at all.
It is said that…; presents a commonly stated view.
Q4: provides examples of exercise that builds healthy bones, matching option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.5.vi: This is because exercise that involves supporting one's own body weight helps strengthen bones, but the human body floats in water, so there is no need to support that weight while in the water.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.5.vocab: that; referring to supporting body weight
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.5.gramm: To…; introduces what is needed to achieve a goal.
Make something…; 強くする means to make stronger.
While…; two actions occur at the same time.
Presents an explanation followed by a contrast.
This is because…; explains the preceding statement.
Q2: identifies supporting one's body weight as the feature that benefits bones.
Q2, option 2: その必要 refers to supporting body weight; it does not mean swimming requires no effort.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.6.vi: Exercise has various benefits, and exercise suited to the body makes bones thicker and stronger.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Something suited to…; 合った modifies the following noun.
Before an adjective, より means more or to a greater degree.
Q3: exercise makes bones thicker and stronger, but the passage does not say they can never break, as option 1 claims.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.7.vi: Furthermore, the muscles around the bones also become stronger, and those muscles help maintain bone strength.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Become…; expresses a change in state.
Turns an adjective into a noun expressing a quality or degree: 強い → 強さ.
Be useful for doing…; のに expresses use here, not concession.
Q3: muscles help maintain bone strength; they do not replace bones as option 4 claims.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.8.vi: Also, people who exercise regularly move quickly and can more easily prevent fractures and injuries caused by accidents and similar events than people who do not exercise at all.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.8.vocab: entirely; at all with a negative
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.8.gramm: Caused by…; modifies the following noun.
Easy to…; here, easier to prevent, not guaranteed prevention.
Q3: matches the faster body movements described in option 2.
Q3, option 2: being better able to prevent fractures and injuries is paraphrased as being less likely to suffer them.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.9.vi: Exercise for general health is beneficial regardless of the age at which it is started, but exercise for building strong bones is different.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.9.gramm: Modifies a noun with its purpose: something for…
No matter at what age one does…
Links contrasting statements about general health and building strong bones.
Q4: shifts the focus to when exercise should be done to build strong bones.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.10.vi: This is because bones finish developing during the period from birth to around age 30.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.10.gram: About, approximately; age 30 is an approximate point.
During a period…; the event is completed within that period.
Combines the passive with ～てしまう to emphasize completion.
This is because…; explains why timing matters.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.10.keys: Q4: according to the passage, bone development finishes around age 30, supporting the advice to exercise in childhood.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.11.vi: Considering this, one can see that it is better to build stronger bones during childhood in preparation for later life.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.11.voca: that; the timing of bone development
alternative, course; in an advisability pattern
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.11.gram: Considering…; draws a conclusion from preceding information.
Do something in advance for the future.
It is better to…; here combined with ～ておく in 作っておいた方がいい.
Probably or surely…; expresses an expectation and invites agreement.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.11.keys: Q4, option 3: directly recommends building stronger bones in childhood in preparation for later life.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.12.vi: To build healthy bones, it is important to do effective exercise at the right time.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.12.gram: To…; introduces what is needed to achieve a purpose.
Something that has…; の replaces が in a clause modifying a noun.
Emphasizes an explanation or conclusion after a noun or な-adjective.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.sentences.12.keys: Q4: the conclusion combines the two main requirements: appropriate timing and effective exercise.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.outline.0.label: Exercise is as important as calcium
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.outline.0.note: Starting with familiar knowledge about calcium, the author introduces the less widely known importance of exercise and the bone risks of insufficient childhood exercise.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.outline.1.label: Types of exercise that benefit bones
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.outline.1.note: Not every type of exercise is suitable. Dancing, running, and jumping are effective, while swimming has little effect on bone building because it does not require supporting body weight.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.outline.2.label: Benefits of exercise
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.outline.2.note: Exercise makes bones thicker and stronger, strengthens surrounding muscles, and enables quicker movements that help prevent fractures and injuries.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.outline.3.label: Build strong bones in childhood
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.outline.3.note: The author distinguishes exercise for general health from exercise for bone development. According to the passage, bones finish developing around age 30, so a strong foundation should be built in childhood.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.outline.4.label: Effective exercise at the right time
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.outline.4.note: The conclusion stresses combining appropriate timing with effective exercise to build healthy bones.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t90-p1.vietnamese:
Everyone knows that getting plenty of calcium is good for building healthy bones.

However, it is not widely known that exercise is just as important as getting calcium.

If people do not get enough exercise as children, their bones become more prone to breaking as they age, and they may develop osteoporosis.

Although exercise is important, that does not mean just any kind of exercise will do.

Activities such as dancing, running, and jumping are effective for building healthy bones, while swimming is said to have little effect in this respect.

This is because exercise that involves supporting one's own body weight helps strengthen bones, but the human body floats in water, so there is no need to support that weight while in the water.

Exercise has various benefits, and exercise suited to the body makes bones thicker and stronger.

Furthermore, the muscles around the bones also become stronger, and those muscles help maintain bone strength.

Also, people who exercise regularly move quickly and can more easily prevent fractures and injuries caused by accidents and similar events than people who do not exercise at all.

Exercise for general health is beneficial regardless of the age at which it is started, but exercise for building strong bones is different.

This is because bones finish developing during the period from birth to around age 30.

Considering this, one can see that it is better to build stronger bones during childhood in preparation for later life.

To build healthy bones, it is important to do effective exercise at the right time.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.0.vi: This time, we interviewed President Tanaka Mitsuo, who founded a company that introduces foreign nationals to job opportunities.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.0.gramm: Clauses placed before nouns modify them: the company that provides job referrals; President Tanaka, who founded it.
A humble expression for asking someone questions or listening to them; here, conducting an interview.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.1.vi: Q: What exactly does your company do?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.1.gramm: In 具体的には, に makes 具体的 adverbial and は highlights the perspective: in specific terms.
Asks for an explanation or further details.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.2.vi: More than 1,400 foreign nationals have registered, and, put simply, our job is to refer them to their preferred companies as far as possible.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.2.vocab: if one says; to put it
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.2.gramm: At least the stated amount, including that amount.
申し込んでいる describes the current state of having registered.
Introduces background before continuing the explanation; が is a soft connector here, not necessarily a contrast.
Conditional form; 簡単にいえば introduces a simplified explanation: put simply.
Explains or summarizes what something amounts to.
Establishes referrals to applicants’ preferred companies, providing context for the successful placements in Question 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.3.vi: In other words, you act as an intermediary between foreign nationals and companies, right?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.3.gramm: Expresses a relationship between two parties and modifies the following noun: an intermediary between foreign nationals and companies.
Checks understanding or seeks the listener’s agreement.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.5.vi: But with the recent economic downturn, isn’t that difficult?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.5.gramm: After 不景気, で connects to the following assessment and suggests a cause: because of the downturn.
An abbreviated ～のではないですか, asking for confirmation of an assumption: isn’t it …?
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.6.vi: Yes. Since even Japanese people find it difficult to get a good job, it is even tougher for foreign nationals.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.6.gramm: Even …; uses Japanese people as an example to emphasize the difficulty.
の nominalizes the preceding action: finding a good job is difficult.
Gives a reason with an explanatory, emphatic tone.
If it is …; in the case of …; here, considering foreign nationals.
Identifies the difficulty as finding employment, rather than pay or discrimination.
Identifies foreign nationals as the relevant group; in context, the difficulty is their gaining employment at Japanese companies. Question 1: option 3.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.7.vi: Only about 5% of those registered actually secure a placement, I would say.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.7.vocab: be settled; here, secure a placement
have done; be in the resulting state
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.7.gramm: Nominalizes and topicalizes the first part to identify it: those securing placements account for about 5%.
A percentage of the specified group; the denominator is the registered applicants.
Softens an estimate: I would say; perhaps.
In the job-referral context, 決まる means securing a placement, not finalizing desired conditions.
The roughly 5% refers to registered applicants who secure employment, not companies. Together with sentence 2, this supports option 3 for Question 2.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.8.vi: Q: Please give some advice to foreign nationals who hope to find employment in Japan in the future.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.8.gramm: で marks where an activity takes place, and の connects it to a noun: employment in Japan.
A polite way to request something from the listener.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.9.vi: I would like people who want to work in Japan to develop enough communication skills to be able to travel with Japanese people.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.9.gramm: Expresses a desire to perform an action: want to work.
行ける is the potential form of 行く; 旅行に行ける means being able to go on a trip.
Expresses a degree modifying a noun: communication skills sufficient to travel together.
Expresses a wish for the specified people to do something; here, develop communication skills.
Traveling together illustrates the required communication level; it is not the main request to visit more places. This rules out option 1 in Question 4.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.10.vi: What I particularly want to tell international students is that, more than their knowledge of honorific language or the size of their vocabulary, I worry about their lack of experience interacting with Japanese people.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.10.gram: States what the speaker wants to say and gently introduces the next point.
Lists examples without presenting an exhaustive list.
More than …; here, compares the degree of concern.
Specifies what the assessment refers to: the concern is the lack of interaction experience.
default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.sentences.10.keys: Honorific language and vocabulary are not the main concern, helping eliminate options 1–3 in Question 3 and identify the focus of Question 4.

default.p.6nd_dokkai_n3-t91-p1.vietnamese:
This time, we interviewed President Tanaka Mitsuo, who founded a company that introduces foreign nationals to job opportunities.

Q: What exactly does your company do?

More than 1,400 foreign nationals have registered, and, put simply, our job is to refer them to their preferred companies as far as possible.

In other words, you act as an intermediary between foreign nationals and companies, right?

Q: I see. But with the recent economic downturn, isn’t that difficult?

Yes. Since even Japanese people find it difficult to get a good job, it is even tougher for foreign nationals. Only about 5% of those registered actually secure a placement, I would say.

Q: Please give some advice to foreign nationals who hope to find employment in Japan in the future.

I would like people who want to work in Japan to develop enough communication skills to be able to travel with Japanese people.

What I particularly want to tell international students is that, more than their knowledge of honorific language or the size of their vocabulary, I worry about their lack of experience interacting with Japanese people.

But without skills such as choosing conversation topics, giving brief responses to show you are listening, and sensing the atmosphere in a situation, you will run into difficulties when working with Japanese people.

Beyond that, I would say it is also important to take an active interest in Japanese culture.
